lessons.title: Read the language
lessons.description: Strings, sets, order, and the symbols that hold a problem together.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Chapter 0 — Know what kind of thing you are talking about · chap0.pdf, pages 1–15

The whole idea

This deck gives us the grammar for talking precisely about computers. Before proving anything, ask: what objects are involved, and what exactly am I claiming about them? A bunch of notation becomes much less cursed once every symbol has a job. Pages 1–9 introduce objects and logic; pages 10–15 show how definitions become reasons in a proof.

Build the objects from scratch

A set is a collection where membership matters. {0,1} and {1,0,1} name the same set. A sequence preserves order and repetitions: 01 differs from 10, and 11 differs from 1. A tuple is a fixed-length sequence of entries. A machine's five-tuple is therefore a record with five different fields, not five arbitrary decorations.

A function gives exactly one output for every allowed input. Its output may itself be a set. That is how an NFA transition can be a perfectly valid function even though the machine has several possible next states. A relation records which pairs satisfy a condition; it need not select a single partner.

The Cartesian product lists ordered choices from two sets. If A={1,2} and B={x,y}, then A×B contains (1,x), (1,y), (2,x), (2,y). Later, “state × symbol” simply means “give me those two pieces of information together.”

Watch a definition do useful work

Pages 3–4 use “same remainder modulo 7.” Two integers are related when their difference is a multiple of 7. Why is this an equivalence relation—a way of grouping genuinely interchangeable cases?

An integer differs from itself by zero, so it relates to itself (reflexive). If i−j=7a, then j−i=7(−a), so reversing the pair preserves the relation (symmetric). If i−j=7a and j−k=7b, adding gives i−k=7(a+b), so the relationship passes through the middle number (transitive). Each fancy word has just become a checkable property.

How a proof grows out of the picture

Page 11 asks why an undirected graph's total degree is even. A vertex is a node; an edge joins endpoints; a vertex's degree counts incident edge-ends. Look at one edge. It contributes one end at each endpoint, so two contributions overall. Repeat that accounting for every edge: total degree = twice the number of edges. Twice an integer is even. Done. We counted a generic contribution, so the argument covers every finite graph, not just the drawn example. A self-loop, if allowed, contributes two to its vertex's degree.

An implication “P implies Q” says there cannot be a case with P true and Q false. It does not say Q happens only because of P. “Rain implies wet ground” allows wet ground from a sprinkler. To disprove a universal implication, find one case satisfying P but violating Q.

Source wording to separate: page 10 writes the contrapositive ¬Q→¬P under a contradiction heading. Contraposition proves that equivalent implication. Contradiction assumes the original claim fails and derives an impossibility. Pages 13–15 use contradiction: write √2=m/n in lowest terms; its square forces m even, then n even, contradicting lowest terms. Those methods are related but their opening assumptions differ.

Carry this into the next deck

A state diagram will use sets, functions and a graph to define a checker. Proofs will connect its behavior to a claim about all inputs. Your job is to track object, condition, reason before worrying about polished wording.

Connected check: explain why showing three graphs with even degree sums is weaker than the “two ends per edge” argument. Use the distinction between examples and all graphs.

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

The whole job of this course is to describe which inputs belong, then build a machine or a proof that gets that decision right. Before the machinery, we need to know what the objects are. Otherwise every formula turns into alphabet soup.

Symbols, strings, and languages

An alphabet, written Σ\SigmaΣ (“sigma”), is the finite set of symbols inputs may use. For Σ={0,1}\Sigma=\{0,1\}Σ={0,1}, the symbols are 0 and 1. A string is a finite ordered sequence of these symbols: 101 is one string. Its length is ∣101∣=3|101|=3∣101∣=3. The bars mean length, not membership or absolute value here.

A language is a set of strings. In E={1}E=\{1\}E={1}, the language has exactly one member: the one-symbol string 1. So 1 belongs; 11 does not. The letter E is just the name someone picked. Rename it A and the language stays the same. Braces collect members; they do not mean “repeat.”

Compare three different objects:

Expression What it is What it contains
1 A string One symbol
{1} A language One string, namely 1
1* as a regular expression A description of a language Zero or more consecutive 1s

The empty string, ε\varepsilonε, has zero symbols. The empty set, ∅\emptyset∅, has zero members. Thus {ε}\{\varepsilon\}{ε} has one member, a string of length zero. It's an empty package versus no package. Keep the analogy limited: the package corresponds to a member of a set.

Read a real slide's language

Pumping Lemma 1, page 1, uses

A={0n1n∣n≥0}.A=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}.A={0n1n∣n≥0}.

Read it as: “A is the set of strings made of n zeros followed by n ones, for any integer n at least zero.”

  • 0n0^n0n: n copies of 0, not the arithmetic number zero to a power.
  • Writing 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n side by side means concatenate: put the second string after the first.
  • The vertical bar inside the braces means such that. It plays a different role from the two length bars in ∣w∣|w|∣w∣.
  • The same n appears twice, so the two counts must agree.

Substitute n=0 to get ε. Substitute n=1 to get 01. Substitute n=2 to get 0011. 0101 has the same number of zeros and ones, but is not in A: the zeros must all come first. The order condition is doing real work.

Now change the rule to C={w∈{0,1}∗∣#0(w)=#1(w)}C=\{w\in\{0,1\}^*\mid \#_0(w)=\#_1(w)\}C={w∈{0,1}∗∣#0​(w)=#1​(w)}. Here #0(w)\#_0(w)#0​(w) counts zeros and #1(w)\#_1(w)#1​(w) counts ones. 0101 is in C. This is a changed language, not a new way to spell A.

Decode the glue

w∈Aw\in Aw∈A means “w is a member of A.” A⊆BA\subseteq BA⊆B means every member of A is also in B. The first compares a string with a language; the second compares two languages. A∪BA\cup BA∪B is union: strings in either language. A∩BA\cap BA∩B is intersection: strings in both.

AB={xy∣x∈A,y∈B}AB=\{xy\mid x\in A,y\in B\}AB={xy∣x∈A,y∈B} means choose a string from A and then one from B, in that order. If A={0,11} and B={1}, then AB={01,111}; BA={10,111}. No, concatenation is not a free-for-all shuffle.

A∗A^*A∗ means concatenate zero or more members of A. Zero choices produce ε, so ε always belongs to A*. For A={01}, A*={ε,01,0101,…}; 001 is not included. For A={0,1}, A* is every finite binary string. The base language changed, so the result changed.

What to write on an exam

For A={0ⁿ1ⁿ | n≥0}, a string belongs exactly when it consists of a block of zeros followed by a block of ones of the same length. The empty string is included by choosing n=0.

Notice that this sentence states both order and count, and handles the boundary n=0. That's the habit: unpack the rule into conditions before you draw anything.

A connected practice task

For B={0m1n∣m≥n≥0}B=\{0^m1^n\mid m\geq n\geq0\}B={0m1n∣m≥n≥0}, classify ε, 0, 001, 011, and 010. For each rejection, name the condition it violates. Then explain how B differs from A above.

Hint: find the two separate checks

First check whether the string is zeros-then-ones. Only after that compare the number of zeros with the number of ones. Zero-length blocks are allowed.

Show the worked answer

ε: yes (m=n=0). 0: yes (m=1,n=0). 001: yes (m=2,n=1). 011: no (1 is less than 2). 010: no (a zero occurs after a one). B permits extra zeros; A requires equality. Both require block order. A is a subset of B.

Keep: alphabet = allowed symbols; string = one ordered input; language = set of inputs. Membership depends on every condition in the definition.

lessons.title: What a machine remembers
lessons.description: States, DFA/NFA rules, and a complete subset construction.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

DFA 2 — Compress the past without losing the decision · chap1_DFA2.pdf, pages 1–14

The whole idea

The design question is: which differences between input histories can safely be forgotten? If two histories require the same behavior for every possible continuation, one state may represent both. If some continuation must distinguish them, merging them loses information. This is the reason to design state meanings before drawing arrows.

Build the picture from the slide examples

Pages 1–4 recognize nonempty strings whose first and last symbols agree. You need the first symbol permanently, and you update the current last symbol. A separate initial situation handles “nothing read yet.” One symbol such as a already has matching first and last symbols; the empty string needs its own decision.

Pages 6–8 keep the sum since the last reset, modulo 3. Modulo 3 means the remainder after division by 3: 0, 1 or 2. You can throw away the actual sum because adding the next digit affects the final remainder using only the current remainder. A reset overwrites the summary with remainder zero. This is deliberate forgetting, not random loss of memory.

One complete construction: odd many ones

Pages 11–13 ask for binary strings with an odd number of 1s. “Odd” means 1,3,5,…; “even” means 0,2,4,…. You do not need to distinguish one 1 from a thousand and one. Both require the same future toggles.

Let qₑ mean “even many ones so far,” and qₒ mean “odd many.” Start qₑ because the initial count is zero. Accept at qₒ. Reading 0 changes no count, so each state loops on 0. Reading 1 changes parity, so it switches states.

For 010101, the summaries after each symbol are even, odd, odd, even, even, odd. Accept. If you append another 1, the answer flips. That is exactly what the rule demands.

The formal computation page is a run log

On page 9, w=w₁…wₙ names the input symbols. The r₀,…,rₙ names the visited states. w entries are what we read; r entries are what we remember afterward. There are n symbols but n+1 recorded states because r₀ records the situation before reading anything.

r₀=q₀ says start correctly. δ(rᵢ,wᵢ₊₁)=rᵢ₊₁ says each adjacent row follows the update rule. rₙ∈F says the final recorded state belongs to the accepting set. “∈” means membership. It is an acceptance test, not a claim that every run must accept.

A language is regular if some finite automaton recognizes exactly its strings. That is an existence claim about a checker. A language does not become regular because its English description sounds simple.

Why this method generalizes

The odd/even invariant holds at the start and survives each symbol. That gives a proof for arbitrarily long inputs. The “contains 001” machine on page 14 uses another summary: how much of the useful suffix 001 has been matched, or whether it was already found. After 000, the useful suffix is still 00; an extra zero should not erase both zeros from memory.

The reset, parity and substring examples share one mental move: keep exactly the information needed for later decisions. Their arrows differ because their meanings differ.

Next connection: DFA3 keeps two such summaries at once. Connected check: for an odd-ones machine, justify the start, 0-arrows, 1-arrows and accepting state from their meanings, without memorizing its drawing.

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

A state is the machine's current memory summary. The circle is how we draw it. The name inside could be S, q₀, or 17; the name itself does not do the work. The transitions and accepting labels do.

A complete DFA for exactly 1

Target: E={1}E=\{1\}E={1}, input alphabet {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1}. We need to accept exactly one input. Ask what information matters after each prefix:

  • S: nothing has been read yet.
  • A: the entire prefix read so far is exactly 1.
  • D: the prefix cannot possibly be completed into exactly 1.
Current state Read 0 Read 1 Accept if input ends here?
S D A No
A D D Yes
D D D No

Read 11: start at S; first 1 takes you to A; second 1 takes you to D. You reject where you finish, not because you happened to pass through an accept state. The dead state loops on both symbols because extra input cannot fix an already-too-long string.

For ε, there are no moves and the machine stays at S, so it rejects. The start state matters even when nothing happens.

The five-part definition, with actual objects

M=(Q,Σ,δ,q0,F)M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)M=(Q,Σ,δ,q0​,F):

  1. Q = {S,A,D}: all the states.
  2. Σ = {0,1}: input symbols.
  3. δ: the transition function, here given by the table.
  4. q₀ = S: one designated start state.
  5. F = {A}: the set of accepting states.

A DFA can have many accepting states. “One next state” describes each transition's output, not how many states can be in F. Formally δ:Q×Σ→Q\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Qδ:Q×Σ→Q: give it one current state and one symbol; get one next state. A start state is one element of Q; that element can itself have a set-shaped label after a conversion. The label {q₀,q₁} can name one DFA state.

NFA: several possible runs

An NFA transition returns a set of possible next states. Its type is δ:Q×Σε→P(Q)\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q)δ:Q×Σε​→P(Q). Here Σε=Σ∪{ε}\Sigma_\varepsilon=\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}Σε​=Σ∪{ε}; an ε move consumes no input. P(Q)\mathcal P(Q)P(Q) means all subsets of Q, including the empty set. For Q={u,v}, these are ∅, {u}, {v}, {u,v}.

So an entry {v} says “the available destinations form the set containing v.” Writing just v has the wrong type for this table. ∅ says that branch has no matching move. It does not add a mysterious extra NFA state called “null.”

Acceptance means at least one run reads the whole input and finishes accepting, with ε moves allowed. A dead branch doesn't kill the other branches. An ε arrow is optional; it does not force the machine to ignore a symbol arrow.

Subset construction, from scratch

Take the NFA with start u, accept v, and only arrow u —1→ v. The DFA tracks a set of current NFA possibilities. From {u}, 1 reaches {v}; 0 reaches ∅. From {v}, either symbol reaches ∅. From ∅, either symbol stays ∅.

Set naming a DFA state 0 1 Accepting?
{u} ∅ {v} No
{v} ∅ ∅ Yes
{u,v} ∅ {v} Yes
∅ ∅ ∅ No

The full power-set construction has four states. {u,v} is unreachable from {u}, so deleting it gives our three-state DFA. If a question requires the full prescribed construction, show all subsets first and then explain deletion. Reachable-only exploration is an efficient computation method, but it doesn't replace an explicitly requested four-state diagram.

With ε arrows, define ε-closure E(S): include S and everything reachable using only ε moves, repeatedly. Start at E({q₀}). For each real symbol, collect matching destinations from every current state, then take closure. Don't retain old states merely because they were there before.

Why this is the foundation for Midterm 2

A DFA has only finitely many memory summaries. A PDA adds a stack. A TM adds a rewritable tape and a head. The pumping argument asks what must happen when finitely many states face a sufficiently long input. Machine conversion asks how another representation can preserve the same decisions. Same game, different memory.

Fresh task: change the target to “all strings ending in 1.” Give state meanings and a complete table. Explain why 11 now accepts.

Show the worked answer

Use N: empty or ends in 0, and Y: ends in 1. Start N; accept Y. From either state, 0 goes to N and 1 goes to Y. On 11 the run is N→Y→Y. This language is different from {1}: it allows arbitrary earlier symbols. The table has exactly one destination for each state/symbol pair.

“even” means 0,2,4,…. you do not need to distinguish one 1 from a thousand and one. both require the same future toggles. let qₑ mean “even many ones so far,” and qₒ mean “odd many.” start qₑ because the initial count is zero. accept at qₒ. reading 0 changes no count, so each state loops on 0. reading 1 changes parity, so it switches states. for `010101`, the summaries after each symbol are even, odd, odd, even, even, odd. accept. if you append another 1, the answer flips. that is exactly what the rule demands. ## the formal computation page is a run log on page 9, w=w₁…wₙ names the input symbols. the r₀,…,rₙ names the visited states. **w entries are what we read; r entries are what we remember afterward.** there are n symbols but n+1 recorded states because r₀ records the situation before reading anything. r₀=q₀ says start correctly. δ(rᵢ,wᵢ₊₁)=rᵢ₊₁ says each adjacent row follows the update rule. rₙ∈f says the final recorded state belongs to the accepting set. “∈” means membership. it is an acceptance test, not a claim that every run must accept. a language is **regular** if some finite automaton recognizes exactly its strings. that is an existence claim about a checker. a language does not become regular because its english description sounds simple. ## why this method generalizes the odd/even invariant holds at the start and survives each symbol. that gives a proof for arbitrarily long inputs. the “contains 001” machine on page 14 uses another summary: how much of the useful suffix `001` has been matched, or whether it was already found. after `000`, the useful suffix is still `00`; an extra zero should not erase both zeros from memory. the reset, parity and substring examples share one mental move: keep exactly the information needed for later decisions. their arrows differ because their meanings differ. **next connection:** dfa3 keeps two such summaries at once. **connected check:** for an odd-ones machine, justify the start, 0-arrows, 1-arrows and accepting state from their meanings, without memorizing its drawing.

lessons.title: Build a proof from reasons
lessons.description: Assumptions, both directions, induction, and counterexamples.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Chapter 0 — Know what kind of thing you are talking about · chap0.pdf, pages 1–15

The whole idea

This deck gives us the grammar for talking precisely about computers. Before proving anything, ask: what objects are involved, and what exactly am I claiming about them? A bunch of notation becomes much less cursed once every symbol has a job. Pages 1–9 introduce objects and logic; pages 10–15 show how definitions become reasons in a proof.

Build the objects from scratch

A set is a collection where membership matters. {0,1} and {1,0,1} name the same set. A sequence preserves order and repetitions: 01 differs from 10, and 11 differs from 1. A tuple is a fixed-length sequence of entries. A machine's five-tuple is therefore a record with five different fields, not five arbitrary decorations.

A function gives exactly one output for every allowed input. Its output may itself be a set. That is how an NFA transition can be a perfectly valid function even though the machine has several possible next states. A relation records which pairs satisfy a condition; it need not select a single partner.

The Cartesian product lists ordered choices from two sets. If A={1,2} and B={x,y}, then A×B contains (1,x), (1,y), (2,x), (2,y). Later, “state × symbol” simply means “give me those two pieces of information together.”

Watch a definition do useful work

Pages 3–4 use “same remainder modulo 7.” Two integers are related when their difference is a multiple of 7. Why is this an equivalence relation—a way of grouping genuinely interchangeable cases?

An integer differs from itself by zero, so it relates to itself (reflexive). If i−j=7a, then j−i=7(−a), so reversing the pair preserves the relation (symmetric). If i−j=7a and j−k=7b, adding gives i−k=7(a+b), so the relationship passes through the middle number (transitive). Each fancy word has just become a checkable property.

How a proof grows out of the picture

Page 11 asks why an undirected graph's total degree is even. A vertex is a node; an edge joins endpoints; a vertex's degree counts incident edge-ends. Look at one edge. It contributes one end at each endpoint, so two contributions overall. Repeat that accounting for every edge: total degree = twice the number of edges. Twice an integer is even. Done. We counted a generic contribution, so the argument covers every finite graph, not just the drawn example. A self-loop, if allowed, contributes two to its vertex's degree.

An implication “P implies Q” says there cannot be a case with P true and Q false. It does not say Q happens only because of P. “Rain implies wet ground” allows wet ground from a sprinkler. To disprove a universal implication, find one case satisfying P but violating Q.

Source wording to separate: page 10 writes the contrapositive ¬Q→¬P under a contradiction heading. Contraposition proves that equivalent implication. Contradiction assumes the original claim fails and derives an impossibility. Pages 13–15 use contradiction: write √2=m/n in lowest terms; its square forces m even, then n even, contradicting lowest terms. Those methods are related but their opening assumptions differ.

Carry this into the next deck

A state diagram will use sets, functions and a graph to define a checker. Proofs will connect its behavior to a claim about all inputs. Your job is to track object, condition, reason before worrying about polished wording.

Connected check: explain why showing three graphs with even degree sums is weaker than the “two ends per edge” argument. Use the distinction between examples and all graphs.

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

A proof is a chain of reasons that covers every case claimed. Examples help you discover an argument. They don't magically turn a claim about infinitely many inputs into something settled.

Start with the target, not fancy wording

Suppose the claim is: “If a DFA reaches the same state after strings u and v, then appending the same suffix z produces the same acceptance decision.”

What are you given? A deterministic machine, two runs ending at the same state, and one common remaining input z. What must you show? The final acceptance decisions agree. We don't need to remember the earlier strings; the current state plus the next symbol determines the next move.

Complete proof: Let q be the state reached after both u and v. The two remaining computations start at q and read the same string z. At each step, their current states and next input symbols are equal, so determinism gives equal next states. Hence their final states are equal. Since acceptance depends on whether that final state is in F, the decisions agree.

This is the engine behind the pumping lemma. Once you're back in the same state, the machine has no secret counter remembering how many laps you took. The circle is the memory. That's it.

Make the repeated-step reasoning explicit: induction

Induction proves a claim for every nonnegative integer by covering a starting case and a repeatable step. Think of a rule that lets you extend a correct run by one more symbol.

Claim: after k symbols of the common suffix above, the two machines are in the same state.

  • Base, k=0: neither suffix symbol has been read. Both states are q by assumption.
  • Induction hypothesis: assume the states agree after k symbols.
  • Step: if another symbol exists, both next symbols are the same symbol a. Apply δ to the same pair (state,a); the resulting states agree after k+1 symbols.
  • Conclusion: the states agree after all |z| symbols, including when |z|=0.

The hypothesis is a temporary assumption used to prove the next case. It is not permission to assume the final claim with no work. This pattern also proves a machine invariant: describe exactly what each state or stack represents after any processed prefix, verify the start, then verify every possible update.

Equality needs two directions

To prove a grammar generates exactly L, show:

  1. Soundness: every string the grammar generates is in L. No extra garbage gets through.
  2. Completeness: every string in L has a derivation. No valid input is excluded.

Worked example: S→0S1∣εS\to0S1\mid\varepsilonS→0S1∣ε generates exactly {0n1n∣n≥0}\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}{0n1n∣n≥0}.

Soundness: A terminating derivation uses the wrapping rule some k≥0 times and then S→ε. Each wrap adds one 0 on the left and one 1 on the right, so the result is 0ᵏ1ᵏ.

Completeness: Take any 0ⁿ1ⁿ with n≥0. Apply S→0S1 exactly n times, then S→ε. This derives the chosen string. The two inclusions prove equality.

Contradiction and counterexamples

To prove L is not regular, assume it is regular and show this forces a statement incompatible with that assumption. You must name the contradiction. “This is impossible” is not a reason by itself.

To disprove “every binary string with equal counts is zeros-then-ones,” one counterexample suffices: 0101 has equal counts but is not in block order. You do not need to show that all equal-count strings fail. Which side says “every” matters.

∀\forall∀ means “for every”; ∃\exists∃ means “there exists.” Negating “every input is accepted” gives “some input is not accepted.” Negating “some input is accepted” gives “every input is not accepted.” Swap the quantifier and negate its claim. For P⇒QP\Rightarrow QP⇒Q, only P true and Q false is a counterexample.

How to discover a proof

Write the assumption and desired conclusion in ordinary English. Expand the relevant definition. Look at a tiny example to find what stays true. Then replace its particular numbers with arbitrary variables and justify the general step. Finally attack your own proof with boundary cases: zero, empty string, smallest permitted length, and a condition changed by one.

A construction proof supplies the required object and checks it. For example, to show every integer t between n and 2n is a sum of n numbers each 1 or 2: choose t−n copies of 2 and 2n−t copies of 1. The counts are nonnegative, sum to n, and their weighted sum is 2(t−n)+(2n−t)=t. Saying “clearly every value is possible” would skip exactly the part to prove.

Fresh practice

Prove that S→aSb∣abS\to aSb\mid abS→aSb∣ab generates exactly {anbn∣n≥1}\{a^nb^n\mid n\geq1\}{anbn∣n≥1}. Explain the change from the ε-base grammar.

Hint: count wraps, then account for the base

After k wraps, the final ab contributes one additional a and one additional b. For the reverse direction, how many wraps produce a target with n of each?

Show the complete proof

Every terminating derivation uses k≥0 wrapping steps and then S→ab, giving aᵏ(ab)bᵏ=aᵏ⁺¹bᵏ⁺¹. Thus every generated string belongs to the target. Conversely, for any n≥1, use n−1 wrapping steps and then S→ab, obtaining aⁿbⁿ. The base generates one matched pair, so ε is excluded. Both directions are established.

Proof check before moving on: are the variables introduced, all cases covered, and every “there exists” backed by an actual object or argument? The formal proof should use clear English sentences, not a wall of symbols.

lessons.title: Why finite memory forces a loop
lessons.description: The mechanism, the quantifiers, and a complete nonregularity proof.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Pumping lemma: finite memory eventually repeats itself · chap1_pumpinglemma1.pdf, pages 1–9

The question: when is a finite number of states not enough?

A DFA can remember parity with two states. Could it remember the exact number of leading zeros so it can demand that many ones afterward? For {0n1n:n≥0}\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}{0n1n:n≥0}, the number may be arbitrarily large. “It needs to count” is a useful suspicion, but not yet a proof: plenty of counting tasks only need a remainder. We need a consequence that every DFA must obey.

Suppose a DFA has p states. Read p symbols. The computation has visited p+1 state positions: the initial state plus one after each symbol. With only p different states, some state was visited twice. That's the pigeonhole principle: more visits than available distinct places forces a repeat.

A repeat turns a path into a reusable loop

Split the input into three consecutive pieces. x gets us to the repeated state the first time. y takes us around the loop back to that same state. z finishes the original accepting journey.

Because the state after y is exactly the state before y, the rest of the machine cannot tell whether we took that loop zero times, once, twice, or a hundred times. Following z afterward still reaches accept. The DFA has no secret memory outside its current state. That's the whole damn mechanism.

The notation xyizxy^izxyiz means x, then i copies of y, then z. With i=0, y disappears; with i=1, it is the original string; with i=2, y is duplicated. We are editing a substring, not moving letters around.

Decode the theorem in its actual order

If L is regular, there exists a pumping length p such that every s in L with length at least p can be split as s=xyz satisfying:

  1. ∣y∣>0|y|>0∣y∣>0: the loop consumes at least one symbol.
  2. ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p: the loop fits within the first p symbols.
  3. xyiz∈Lxy^iz\in Lxyiz∈L for every integer i≥0: every repetition count still works.

∣y∣|y|∣y∣ is the number of symbols in y. ∈\in∈ means “is a member of.” The theorem promises at least one suitable split, not every split. p belongs to the assumed machine; we don't get to declare p=3 because that makes an example convenient.

Why this helps prove impossibility

To show a language is not regular, assume a DFA exists and receive its unknown p. Choose a legal long string. Then show that no allowed split can keep all repetitions in the language. That contradicts the required loop property.

Be careful with the deck's counting examples. Equal numbers of 0 and 1 is not the same requirement as equal numbers of adjacent 01 and 10. The latter can be tracked using boundary information: in a binary string, changes from 0 to 1 and back alternate. Similar-looking counts can need radically different memory.

Keep: pumping is a necessary consequence of finite state memory. It is a tool for ruling regularity out, not a general way to establish regularity. Next we turn the mechanism into a complete quantified proof.

One connected check: Why does returning to the same state matter more than merely reading the same symbol twice?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

Question: how do we prove that no DFA, however cleverly designed, can recognize a language? Showing that your own three-state attempt fails isn't enough. Some other design might work. We need a restriction shared by every finite-state machine.

Why a loop is unavoidable

Suppose a DFA has p states. Reading its first p symbols visits p+1 states when you include the start. There are more visits than available states, so two visits must be to the same state. This is the pigeonhole principle: p boxes cannot hold p+1 objects with at most one in each.

Split an accepted input into x, y, z. x gets to the repeated state; y goes around the loop and returns; z is the rest of the input leading to acceptance. The loop consumes at least one symbol because the two visits occur at different times. It finishes within the first p input symbols.

Take a concrete conditional example: 00 [0] 111. Suppose the bracketed 0 loops back to the same state. Doing that loop twice gives 00 [00] 111; doing it zero times gives 00 [] 111, or 00111. All three computations reach the same state before the final 111, so the same suffix leads to acceptance. Yet only 000111 has equal numbers of zeros and ones. This explains the mechanism. It does not claim every DFA has its loop at this exact position.

The theorem, translated before use

If A is regular, there exists an integer p≥1 such that every s in A with |s|≥p has a split s=xyz satisfying:

∣y∣>0,∣xy∣≤p,xyiz∈A for every integer i≥0.|y|>0,\qquad |xy|\leq p,\qquad xy^iz\in A\text{ for every integer }i\geq0.∣y∣>0,∣xy∣≤p,xyiz∈A for every integer i≥0.

  • p: the pumping length; the hypothetical machine supplies it.
  • s: one sufficiently long accepted string.
  • x: prefix before the loop; may be empty.
  • y: the nonempty loop's input.
  • z: suffix after the loop; may be empty.
  • i: number of copies of y. i=0 deletes y; i=1 leaves the input alone; i=2 duplicates y.

The condition is necessary for regularity. A failed attempt to break pumping does not prove a language regular. To prove regular, construct a DFA, NFA, regular expression, or use a valid closure argument.

A complete exam proof

Claim: A={0n1n∣n≥0}A=\{0^n1^n\mid n\geq0\}A={0n1n∣n≥0} is not regular.

Suppose A is regular, and let p≥1 be a pumping length. Choose s=0ᵖ1ᵖ. Then s∈A and |s|=2p≥p. Consider any split s=xyz with |xy|≤p and |y|>0. Because the first p symbols of s are zeros, y=0ᵏ for some 1≤k≤p. Set i=0. Then xy⁰z=0ᵖ⁻ᵏ1ᵖ has fewer zeros than ones, so it is not in A. This contradicts the pumping property. Therefore A is not regular.

Why each line earns its place:

Line Obligation it handles
Assume regular; get p Makes the theorem applicable
Choose s=0ᵖ1ᵖ Valid member, long enough, tailored to p
Consider any legal split Covers the theorem's possible choice of split
y=0ᵏ, 1≤k≤p Uses the location and nonempty conditions
Choose i=0 Supplies a specific repetition count
Unequal counts Shows failure of the actual language rule
Contradiction Connects the failure back to the assumption

The choice order is the whole damn game

For a nonregularity proof: arbitrary p → choose s → every legal split → choose i. You do not get to choose a convenient y and ignore other legal choices. You can name y=0ᵏ because all legal y have that form. The repetition i may depend on the split; it need not always be 0 or 2.

Practice: change the counts

Prove B={0n12n∣n≥0}B=\{0^n1^{2n}\mid n\geq0\}B={0n12n∣n≥0} is not regular. Before opening the answer, identify s, the forced form of y, i, and the condition broken.

Hint: keep the loop in the zero block

Choose s=0ᵖ1²ᵖ. Deleting k zeros leaves the ones unchanged. For a valid string, how many ones would p−k zeros require?

Show the complete proof

Suppose B is regular with pumping length p≥1. Let s=0ᵖ1²ᵖ∈B; its length is 3p≥p. For any legal split, y=0ᵏ with 1≤k≤p. Pump down with i=0 to obtain 0ᵖ⁻ᵏ1²ᵖ. It would need 2(p−k) ones to belong to B, but has 2p and k>0. Thus it is outside B, contradicting the lemma. Hence B is not regular.

Retain: the loop preserves the machine's decision; we choose a language member for which changing that loop breaks the language's rule.

get p | makes the theorem applicable | | choose s=0ᵖ1ᵖ | valid member, long enough, tailored to p | | consider any legal split | covers the theorem's possible choice of split | | y=0ᵏ, 1≤k≤p | uses the location and nonempty conditions | | choose i=0 | supplies a specific repetition count | | unequal counts | shows failure of the actual language rule | | contradiction | connects the failure back to the assumption | ## the choice order is the whole damn game for a nonregularity proof: **arbitrary p → choose s → every legal split → choose i**. you do not get to choose a convenient y and ignore other legal choices. you can name y=0ᵏ because **all** legal y have that form. the repetition i may depend on the split; it need not always be 0 or 2. ## practice: change the counts prove \(b=\{0^n1^{2n}\mid n\geq0\}\) is not regular. before opening the answer, identify s, the forced form of y, i, and the condition broken.
hint: keep the loop in the zero block

choose s=0ᵖ1²ᵖ. deleting k zeros leaves the ones unchanged. for a valid string, how many ones would p−k zeros require?

show the complete proof

suppose b is regular with pumping length p≥1. let s=0ᵖ1²ᵖ∈b; its length is 3p≥p. for any legal split, y=0ᵏ with 1≤k≤p. pump down with i=0 to obtain 0ᵖ⁻ᵏ1²ᵖ. it would need 2(p−k) ones to belong to b, but has 2p and k>0. thus it is outside b, contradicting the lemma. hence b is not regular.

**retain:** the loop preserves the machine's decision; we choose a language member for which changing that loop breaks the language's rule. pumping lemma: finite memory eventually repeats itself chap1_pumpinglemma1.pdf # pumping lemma: finite memory eventually repeats itself ## the question: when is a finite number of states not enough? a dfa can remember parity with two states. could it remember the exact number of leading zeros so it can demand that many ones afterward? for \(\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}\), the number may be arbitrarily large. “it needs to count” is a useful suspicion, but not yet a proof: plenty of counting tasks only need a remainder. we need a consequence that **every** dfa must obey. suppose a dfa has p states. read p symbols. the computation has visited p+1 state positions: the initial state plus one after each symbol. with only p different states, some state was visited twice. that's the pigeonhole principle: more visits than available distinct places forces a repeat. ## a repeat turns a path into a reusable loop split the input into three consecutive pieces. x gets us to the repeated state the first time. y takes us around the loop back to that same state. z finishes the original accepting journey. because the state after y is exactly the state before y, the rest of the machine cannot tell whether we took that loop zero times, once, twice, or a hundred times. following z afterward still reaches accept. the dfa has no secret memory outside its current state. that's the whole damn mechanism. the notation \(xy^iz\) means x, then i copies of y, then z. with i=0, y disappears; with i=1, it is the original string; with i=2, y is duplicated. we are editing a **substring**, not moving letters around. ## decode the theorem in its actual order if l is regular, there exists a pumping length p such that every s in l with length at least p can be split as s=xyz satisfying: 1. \(|y|>0\): the loop consumes at least one symbol. 2. \(|xy|\le p\): the loop fits within the first p symbols. 3. \(xy^iz\in l\) for every integer i≥0: every repetition count still works. \(|y|\) is the number of symbols in y. \(\in\) means “is a member of.” the theorem promises **at least one** suitable split, not every split. p belongs to the assumed machine; we don't get to declare p=3 because that makes an example convenient. ## why this helps prove impossibility to show a language is not regular, assume a dfa exists and receive its unknown p. choose a legal long string. then show that **no allowed split** can keep all repetitions in the language. that contradicts the required loop property. be careful with the deck's counting examples. equal numbers of `0` and `1` is not the same requirement as equal numbers of adjacent `01` and `10`. the latter can be tracked using boundary information: in a binary string, changes from 0 to 1 and back alternate. similar-looking counts can need radically different memory. **keep:** pumping is a necessary consequence of finite state memory. it is a tool for ruling regularity out, not a general way to establish regularity. next we turn the mechanism into a complete quantified proof. **one connected check:** why does returning to the same state matter more than merely reading the same symbol twice?

lessons.title: Make the pumping proof adapt
lessons.description: Squares, inequalities, ratios, and choosing a useful witness.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Pumping variations: choose a weakness, then design the witness · chap1_pumpinglemma3.pdf, pages 1–12

The mental model: control the damage, don't memorize one string

Pumping proofs have a fixed negotiation. You assume regularity; the lemma supplies p; you choose a sufficiently long member s; the hypothetical machine gets a legal split; you choose a repetition count that makes membership fail. The order matters. You must beat every legal split of your chosen s, not just a convenient one.

Write the plan in ordinary words first: “The loop is trapped in this region. Changing that region destroys this relationship.” Then translate the relationship into counts, positions, or arithmetic.

Variation 1: a word repeated twice

Let L={ww:w∈{0,1}∗}L=\{ww:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}L={ww:w∈{0,1}∗}. Here w is any binary string, and ww means two identical copies, in the same order. Choose s=0p1 0p1s=0^p1\,0^p1s=0p10p1. This is a member: its two copies are both 0p10^p10p1.

For every legal split, the bound ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p forces y=0ky=0^ky=0k with 1≤k≤p. Pump down to get 0p−k1 0p10^{p-k}1\,0^p10p−k10p1.

Why can't this be some different word repeated twice? Don't merely say “the original halves differ”—maybe the dividing point moved. There are exactly two 1s, and the whole string ends in 1. In a square tt, each identical half must therefore contain one 1 and end in 1. Each half is a block of zeros followed by one 1, with the same number of zeros. Our two zero blocks have lengths p−k and p, which differ. No alternate split can save it.

That extra argument closes a real proof gap. A drawing of two unequal old halves would not.

Variation 2: square lengths

Let L={1n2:n≥0}L=\{1^{n^2}:n\ge0\}L={1n2:n≥0}. A string belongs exactly when its length is 0,1,4,9,16,… . Choose s=1p2s=1^{p^2}s=1p2. Its length is at least p. Every legal nonempty y has length k with 1≤k≤p.

Pump up once, i=2. The new length is p²+k. It is bigger than p² but smaller than the next square:

p2<p2+k≤p2+p<(p+1)2=p2+2p+1.p^2<p^2+k\le p^2+p<(p+1)^2=p^2+2p+1.p2<p2+k≤p2+p<(p+1)2=p2+2p+1.

There is no square strictly between consecutive squares, so the pumped word is outside L. The argument works for every k in the allowed range. Pumping down is less convenient: for p=1 and k=1 it gives length zero, which is a square. Choosing i=2 avoids that boundary trap.

What the quantifiers are saying

∃\exists∃ means “there exists”; ∀\forall∀ means “for every.” The lemma says a regular language has some p that works for every long member, with some legal split working for every repetition count. To refute it, show that for every proposed p, you can find a bad member for which every legal split has some failing repetition count.

Negating the order correctly prevents the classic bullshit proof where you choose a bad split and act as though no good split exists.

Keep: control where y lives, then identify a condition that any nonzero change destroys. Pumping is about the language's structure, not just its surface notation.

One connected check: In the square-length proof, why do we need the upper bound k≤p, rather than only k>0?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

The first pumping proof teaches the structure. Exam rigor means recognizing what changes when the language changes. This lesson uses the course's square-length example and the 2021 paper's variations. The explanations are newly written; use the linked paper for its exact wording.

Square lengths: don't confuse a string with a number

D={1n2∣n≥0}D=\{1^{n^2}\mid n\geq0\}D={1n2∣n≥0} contains ε, 1, 1111, nine ones, sixteen ones, and so on. The string is made only of ones. The length must be a perfect square. 111 is out because three is not a square.

Assume regularity and get p≥1. Choose s=1ᵖ². It is long enough because p²≥p. Every legal y is 1ᵏ with 1≤k≤p. With i=2, the new length is p²+k, so

p2<p2+k≤p2+p<(p+1)2.p^2<p^2+k\leq p^2+p<(p+1)^2.p2<p2+k≤p2+p<(p+1)2.

There is no square strictly between two consecutive squares. Thus the pumped string is outside D for every legal k. That completes the contradiction.

Why choose p²? We need a member of D. Choosing 1ᵖ would fail when p isn't a square. Why use an inequality? It covers all possible loop lengths simultaneously.

The 2021 variation: can i=3 work?

Yes. Three copies replace the original one copy, so the increase is 2k, not 3k:

p2<p2+2k≤p2+2p=(p+1)2−1<(p+1)2.p^2<p^2+2k\leq p^2+2p=(p+1)^2-1<(p+1)^2.p2<p2+2k≤p2+2p=(p+1)2−1<(p+1)2.

Still trapped between adjacent squares. Same strategy; a changed calculation.

With i=0 and the same s, the length is p²−k. For p≥2,

(p−1)2<p2−p≤p2−k<p2.(p-1)^2<p^2-p\leq p^2-k<p^2.(p−1)2<p2−p≤p2−k<p2.

But when p=1, deleting y leaves ε. For n≥0, ε belongs to D, so this particular i=0 argument has a hole. If the problem changes the language to n≥1, ε is excluded and that last case works too. If a question fixes s or asks you to adapt the lecture proof, follow that restriction instead of silently replacing the setup.

Inequalities: choose a string on the boundary

2021 Problem 3(b) asks about L={0h1k∣h>5k, h,k>0}L=\{0^h1^k\mid h>5k,\ h,k>0\}L={0h1k∣h>5k, h,k>0}. The target has a strict inequality. Pick the nearest valid boundary: s=0⁵ᵖ⁺¹1ᵖ. Every legal y=0ᵗ for 1≤t≤p. Deleting y leaves h=5p+1−t≤5p=5k, violating h>5k. The original s is in L and long enough; every split is covered. Therefore L is not regular.

A random string with a huge excess of zeros might survive deletion of a short y. Choosing the boundary makes the smallest legal deletion fatal. That's how to discover s instead of memorizing it.

Ratios: turn words into counts

2021 Problem 3(a) uses nonempty binary strings with proportion of ones at most 0.9. Choose s=1⁹ᵖ0ᵖ, exactly on the allowed boundary. Any legal y=1ᵗ, 1≤t≤p. Pumping with i=2 gives proportion

9p+t10p+t>910,\frac{9p+t}{10p+t}>\frac9{10},10p+t9p+t​>109​,

because multiplying by the positive denominators reduces this to 90p+10t>90p+9t, which holds since t>0. The length remains nonzero. Thus every legal split can be broken and the language is nonregular.

Logic behind the theorem

The pumping conclusion has the pattern “there exists p, for every long member s, there exists a legal split, for every i the pumped string stays in L.” To contradict it: for every proposed p, exhibit a long member s for which every legal split has some failing i.

In the 2021 truth-table question, ¬(A∧B∧C)\neg(A\land B\land C)¬(A∧B∧C) is equivalent to (A∧B)⇒¬C(A\land B)\Rightarrow\neg C(A∧B)⇒¬C. Both are false only when A,B,C are all true. If asked for a detailed truth table, that verbal argument is not the requested deliverable: write all eight rows.

Fresh practice

For nonempty binary strings whose proportion of ones is at most 2/3, give a complete pumping proof of nonregularity.

Hint: pick an exact boundary ratio

Try two blocks whose lengths have ratio 2:1, with the ones first. Pumping up adds ones only. Compare the new ratio with 2/3 by cross multiplication.

Show the complete proof

Suppose regular with pumping length p≥1. Choose s=1²ᵖ0ᵖ; it is nonempty, has length 3p≥p, and proportion 2/3. Any legal split has y=1ᵗ for 1≤t≤p. With i=2 the proportion is (2p+t)/(3p+t)>2/3, since 3(2p+t)>2(3p+t) is equivalent to t>0. This contradicts pumping, so the language is nonregular.

Proof hygiene: bounds must include the endpoints. The legal loop bound is 1≤|y|≤p. Some printed solution lines use strict inequalities where these inclusive bounds are required; use the mathematically correct bounds.

lessons.title: Build strings with a grammar
lessons.description: Variables, derivations, grammar design, and language equality.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

CFGs: a variable is unfinished work, a terminal is finished output · chap2_CFG1.pdf, pages 1–12

Start with what a grammar is trying to do

A DFA checks a completed string. A grammar builds strings. We still care about a language—a set of completed strings—but now ask which ones the construction rules can produce. There is no input head and no accepting circle in a grammar.

The deck's grammar is:

A→0A1∣B,B→#.A\to0A1\mid B,\qquad B\to\#.A→0A1∣B,B→#.

A and B are variables: placeholders for unfinished work. 0, 1, and # are terminals: finished output symbols that stay put. A is the starting variable. The vertical bar means “or,” so A has two alternative rules. The arrow means “you may replace this variable with that right-hand side.”

Run the rules all the way to completion

Begin with A. Choose its wrapping rule three times, then finish:

A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111⇒000B111⇒000#111.A\Rightarrow0A1\Rightarrow00A11\Rightarrow000A111\Rightarrow000B111\Rightarrow000\#111.A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111⇒000B111⇒000#111.

At 00A11, the zeros and ones are already output. A is the one unfinished job between them. Applying A→0A1 replaces that A, leaving its surrounding output untouched. We didn't replace the entire line with 0A1.

Each wrapping adds one zero on the left and one one on the right. Switching to B stops the wrapping; B→# puts a separator in the middle. Therefore the generated language is {0n#1n:n≥0}\{0^n\#1^n:n\ge0\}{0n#1n:n≥0}. n is the number of wraps. With zero wraps, A→B→# gives #. ε is not generated: no rule finishes with no terminal at all.

Why this can do what a DFA cannot

The growing expression stores unfinished structure. Every additional wrap leaves one more 1 waiting on the right. A finite grammar can describe arbitrarily deep nesting because its rules can reuse a variable. The finite rulebook does not impose a fixed bound on the size of a derivation.

A parse tree records the same construction as a tree. A node labeled A has children 0, A, 1 when that rule is used. Read the terminal leaves left to right to recover the completed string. The tree preserves who created whom, which a final string alone does not show.

Decode the formal package

G=(V,Σ,R,S)G=(V,\Sigma,R,S)G=(V,Σ,R,S) names a grammar. V is its finite set of variables; Σ is its finite terminal alphabet; R is its finite rule set; S is the starting variable. In this example S—the formal slot name—is filled by the variable A. The actual start does not have to be called S.

uAv⇒uwvuAv\Rightarrow uwvuAv⇒uwv says a rule A→w can replace A wherever it appears, with the same surrounding strings u and v retained. “Context-free” means the rule does not inspect those surroundings before permitting replacement. ⇒∗\Rightarrow^*⇒∗ means zero or more derivation steps.

The last slide adds two different ways to grow structure

For S→aSb|SS|ε, interpret a as an opening parenthesis and b as a closing one. S→aSb wraps one balanced structure inside a matched pair. S→SS places two balanced structures side by side. S→ε finishes with nothing. For aabbab, one derivation is S⇒SS⇒aSbS⇒aaSbbS⇒aabbS⇒aabbaSb⇒aabbab. Each arrow replaces one S.

Equal counts alone are insufficient: ba has one of each but closes before anything opens. A balanced-parentheses string must have equal final counts and every prefix must contain at least as many openings as closings. Wrapping and concatenation preserve both conditions. Conversely, split a nonempty balanced string after the close matching its first opening: inside that pair and after it are smaller balanced strings, exactly the wrapping and side-by-side jobs. This connects grammar rules to nested structure, the reason stacks will be useful.

What a correctness proof has to establish

Every derivation here produces matching outer blocks because each wrap adds exactly one of each symbol and the only finishing option inserts #. Conversely, any desired n can be produced by choosing n wraps then finishing. This proves both “no wrong strings” and “every required string.” Merely deriving 000#111 proves only one example.

Keep: variables are pending jobs; rules replace one pending job; terminals are finished output. Next we use grammar structure to control arithmetic grouping and identify ambiguity.

One connected check: At 00A11, why can the next step produce 000A111 but not 000A11?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

A grammar builds a string. A machine reads a string. We will later convert between them while preserving the language. First, make the building process concrete.

One course example, every symbol explained

CFG 1, pages 2–5, gives:

A→0A1∣B,B→#.A\to0A1\mid B,\qquad B\to\#.A→0A1∣B,B→#.

A and B are variables: unfinished work you may replace. 0, 1, and # are terminals: actual symbols in the finished input. Here # is literally a separator character, not a counting operator. The start variable is A. The vertical bar means “or”: A may be replaced by 0A1 or by B.

The four-part formal grammar is G=(V,Σ,R,S)G=(V,\Sigma,R,S)G=(V,Σ,R,S). V={A,B} is the variable set. Σ={0,1,#} is the terminal alphabet. R is the set of rules above. S=A says that the chosen start variable is A. The formal slot is conventionally called S; the actual symbol occupying it need not be named S.

To generate 00#11:

A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒00B11⇒00#11.A\Rightarrow0A1\Rightarrow00A11\Rightarrow00B11\Rightarrow00\#11.A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒00B11⇒00#11.

At each arrow replace exactly one variable occurrence using a rule. Everything around it stays put. The last line has only terminals, so it is a finished string. ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ means one derivation step; ⇒∗\Rightarrow^*⇒∗ means zero or more steps. A rule arrow →\to→ states an allowed replacement; a derivation arrow ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ applies one inside a whole string.

Why this language is exactly 0ⁿ#1ⁿ

Each A→0A1 adds a matching outer pair. A→B and B→# end the wrapping with a separator. Any finished derivation therefore gives 0ⁿ#1ⁿ for some n≥0. Conversely, for any n≥0, take n wrapping steps then the two finishing steps. This proves both directions. With n=0, the string is #, not ε.

The recursive variable keeps the two distant blocks linked. That's the extra power compared with a finite-state memory. The grammar can nest arbitrarily many pending matching pairs.

Designing a grammar: decide what a rule contributes

Target 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n, n≥0: S→0S1 adds a matched pair, S→ε ends with zero pairs.

Target all strings made of balanced parentheses: S→(S) | SS | ε. The wrap nests one balanced string; SS puts two balanced strings side by side. A string like ()() needs the concatenation rule. A string like )( is excluded even though the counts agree. Count alone doesn't establish correct nesting.

Target 0n1n∪1n0n0^n1^n\cup1^n0^n0n1n∪1n0n: use separate variables A→0A1|ε and B→1B0|ε, then S→A|B. The start chooses which entire pattern to generate. It doesn't mix the two patterns midway.

Read a bigger grammar from the inside out

The 2023 paper starts with B→bB|ε and D→cD|ε. These generate b* and c*: any nonnegative count. X→aXb|ab generates aⁱbⁱ with i≥1. The base ab excludes ε.

Then Y→aBc|aYc generates aⁱbʲcⁱ with i≥1,j≥0: each wrap adds one a and one c, and B freely chooses the b count. Finally S→XD|Y chooses either equal a/b counts with arbitrary c's, or equal a/c counts with arbitrary b's. Work bottom-up by variable, then compose the results. Don't guess the full language from one sample string.

Fresh practice

Construct and justify a CFG for L={0m1n∣m≥n≥0}L=\{0^m1^n\mid m\geq n\geq0\}L={0m1n∣m≥n≥0}. Your proof must explain order, inequality, and why every valid pair of counts is possible.

Hint: split the zeros into two jobs

Some zeros are extra. The remaining zeros each pair with one 1. Use one variable for extra zeros and another for matched pairs, concatenated in that order.

Show construction and proof

Use S→AB, A→0A|ε, B→0B1|ε. A generates 0ᵏ with k≥0 and B generates 0ⁿ1ⁿ, so every resulting string is 0ᵏ⁺ⁿ1ⁿ and satisfies m≥n. Conversely, for any m≥n≥0 choose k=m−n extras from A and n pairs from B. This derives 0ᵐ1ⁿ. Both directions and ε are covered.

Keep: a rule is a local replacement; a derivation is a sequence of replacements; the language contains only terminal strings reachable from the start.

\(\rightarrow^*\) means zero or more steps. a rule arrow \(\to\) states an allowed replacement; a derivation arrow \(\rightarrow\) applies one inside a whole string. ## why this language is exactly 0ⁿ#1ⁿ each a→0a1 adds a matching outer pair. a→b and b→# end the wrapping with a separator. any finished derivation therefore gives 0ⁿ#1ⁿ for some n≥0. conversely, for any n≥0, take n wrapping steps then the two finishing steps. this proves both directions. with n=0, the string is `#`, **not ε**. the recursive variable keeps the two distant blocks linked. that's the extra power compared with a finite-state memory. the grammar can nest arbitrarily many pending matching pairs. ## designing a grammar: decide what a rule contributes target \(0^n1^n\), n≥0: s→0s1 adds a matched pair, s→ε ends with zero pairs. target all strings made of balanced parentheses: s→(s) | ss | ε. the wrap nests one balanced string; ss puts two balanced strings side by side. a string like `()()` needs the concatenation rule. a string like `)(` is excluded even though the counts agree. count alone doesn't establish correct nesting. target \(0^n1^n\cup1^n0^n\): use separate variables a→0a1|ε and b→1b0|ε, then s→a|b. the start chooses which entire pattern to generate. it doesn't mix the two patterns midway. ## read a bigger grammar from the inside out the 2023 paper starts with b→bb|ε and d→cd|ε. these generate b* and c*: any nonnegative count. x→axb|ab generates aⁱbⁱ with i≥1. the base ab excludes ε. then y→abc|ayc generates aⁱbʲcⁱ with i≥1,j≥0: each wrap adds one a and one c, and b freely chooses the b count. finally s→xd|y chooses either equal a/b counts with arbitrary c's, or equal a/c counts with arbitrary b's. work **bottom-up by variable**, then compose the results. don't guess the full language from one sample string. ## fresh practice construct and justify a cfg for \(l=\{0^m1^n\mid m\geq n\geq0\}\). your proof must explain order, inequality, and why every valid pair of counts is possible.
hint: split the zeros into two jobs

some zeros are extra. the remaining zeros each pair with one 1. use one variable for extra zeros and another for matched pairs, concatenated in that order.

show construction and proof

σ is its finite terminal alphabet; r is its finite rule set; s is the starting variable. in this example s—the formal slot name—is filled by the variable a. the actual start does not have to be called s. \(uav\rightarrow uwv\) says a rule a→w can replace a wherever it appears, with the same surrounding strings u and v retained. “context-free” means the rule does not inspect those surroundings before permitting replacement. \(\rightarrow^*\) means zero or more derivation steps. ## the last slide adds two different ways to grow structure for s→asb|ss|ε, interpret a as an opening parenthesis and b as a closing one. s→asb wraps one balanced structure inside a matched pair. s→ss places two balanced structures side by side. s→ε finishes with nothing. for `aabbab`, one derivation is s⇒ss⇒asbs⇒aasbbs⇒aabbs⇒aabbasb⇒aabbab. each arrow replaces one s. equal counts alone are insufficient: `ba` has one of each but closes before anything opens. a balanced-parentheses string must have equal final counts **and** every prefix must contain at least as many openings as closings. wrapping and concatenation preserve both conditions. conversely, split a nonempty balanced string after the close matching its first opening: inside that pair and after it are smaller balanced strings, exactly the wrapping and side-by-side jobs. this connects grammar rules to nested structure, the reason stacks will be useful. ## what a correctness proof has to establish every derivation here produces matching outer blocks because each wrap adds exactly one of each symbol and the only finishing option inserts #. conversely, any desired n can be produced by choosing n wraps then finishing. this proves both “no wrong strings” and “every required string.” merely deriving `000#111` proves only one example. **keep:** variables are pending jobs; rules replace one pending job; terminals are finished output. next we use grammar structure to control arithmetic grouping and identify ambiguity. **one connected check:** at `00a11`, why can the next step produce `000a111` but not `000a11`?

lessons.title: One string, two structures
lessons.description: Leftmost derivations and complete ambiguity witnesses.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Grammar structure: the same string can carry different meanings · chap2_CFG2.pdf, pages 1–12

The question: who belongs together?

The characters in a+a×a do not visibly say which operation groups first. A grammar can encode that structure. In the deck's layered grammar,

E→E+T∣T,T→T×F∣F,F→(E)∣a,E\to E+T\mid T,\quad T\to T\times F\mid F,\quad F\to(E)\mid a,E→E+T∣T,T→T×F∣F,F→(E)∣a,

E means an expression built from terms, T a multiplication-level term, and F an atomic factor: a single a or a parenthesized expression. These names are helpful meanings assigned to variables; the rules do the enforcing.

Build the example and see why precedence emerges

A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining variable:

E⇒E+T⇒T+T⇒F+T⇒a+T⇒a+T×F⇒a+F×F⇒a+a×F⇒a+a×a.E\Rightarrow E+T\Rightarrow T+T\Rightarrow F+T\Rightarrow a+T\Rightarrow a+T\times F\Rightarrow a+F\times F\Rightarrow a+a\times F\Rightarrow a+a\times a.E⇒E+T⇒T+T⇒F+T⇒a+T⇒a+T×F⇒a+F×F⇒a+a×F⇒a+a×a.

The final top-level split is E+T. The multiplication lives inside the right T. A factor can contain a whole addition only by using F→(E), which prints parentheses. That's why (a+a)×a has a different structure and different visible parentheses. The grammar is not calculating a numerical answer; it determines the syntactic grouping first.

Ambiguity means two trees, not two scheduling choices

Now use the flatter grammar E→E+E∣E×E∣(E)∣aE\to E+E\mid E\times E\mid(E)\mid aE→E+E∣E×E∣(E)∣a. It can build a+a×a with the root operation +, or with the root operation ×. The root-+ tree groups a+(a×a); the root-× tree groups (a+a)×a, even though the generated string has no parentheses.

Two corresponding leftmost derivations are:

E⇒E+E⇒a+E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a,E\Rightarrow E+E\Rightarrow a+E\Rightarrow a+E\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times a,E⇒E+E⇒a+E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a,

E⇒E×E⇒E+E×E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a.E\Rightarrow E\times E\Rightarrow E+E\times E\Rightarrow a+E\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times a.E⇒E×E⇒E+E×E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a.

That is a complete ambiguity witness: same terminal string, different parse structures, certified here by different leftmost derivations. If you merely expand independent left and right children in a different order, you may still get the same tree. That's scheduling, not ambiguity.

A grammar can be ambiguous even if another grammar for the same language is unambiguous. An inherently ambiguous language is stronger: every CFG generating it is ambiguous. Keep the object straight—one rulebook versus the whole language.

Designing a grammar by splitting the job

For {0n1n}∪{1n0n}\{0^n1^n\}\cup\{1^n0^n\}{0n1n}∪{1n0n}, a new start chooses which subgrammar to run. One wraps zeros around ones; the other wraps ones around zeros. Union means either branch may generate the string; neither branch has to satisfy both descriptions.

A DFA can also become a grammar. Give each state qᵢ a variable Rᵢ. For an arrow qᵢ—a→qⱼ, add Rᵢ→aRⱼ. For each accepting state, add Rᵢ→ε, allowing generation to finish there. A derivation now writes exactly the labels of a successful machine path. This connects checking to building.

Keep: grammar rules encode structure, not just a bag of output strings. Next, CNF standardizes the shape of those rules while preserving the language.

One connected check: Why do two different leftmost derivations give stronger evidence of ambiguity than two derivations with unrestricted expansion order?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

Ambiguity asks whether one finished string has two different grammatical structures. It does not ask whether two different strings can be generated. Of course a useful grammar usually generates lots of strings.

Why “two derivations” alone is too weak

Take S→AB, A→a, B→b. You can expand A before B or B before A. Both routes make ab, but they describe the same parse tree: S has children A and B, and those become a and b.

To remove this irrelevant choice of expansion order, require a leftmost derivation: at each step replace the leftmost remaining variable. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two distinct leftmost derivations, equivalently two distinct parse trees. One leftmost and one rightmost derivation do not automatically prove ambiguity.

A whole example from the 2022 paper

Grammar: H→bCb; C→mC | CbC | ε. Terminals b and m represent bread and meat. The start H is the whole hamburger. The string bmbmb can be built in these two leftmost ways:

H⇒bCb⇒bmCb⇒bmCbCb⇒bmbCb⇒bmbmCb⇒bmbmb.H\Rightarrow bCb\Rightarrow bmCb\Rightarrow bmCbCb\Rightarrow bmbCb\Rightarrow bmbmCb\Rightarrow bmbmb.H⇒bCb⇒bmCb⇒bmCbCb⇒bmbCb⇒bmbmCb⇒bmbmb.

H⇒bCb⇒bCbCb⇒bmCbCb⇒bmbCb⇒bmbmCb⇒bmbmb.H\Rightarrow bCb\Rightarrow bCbCb\Rightarrow bmCbCb\Rightarrow bmbCb\Rightarrow bmbmCb\Rightarrow bmbmb.H⇒bCb⇒bCbCb⇒bmCbCb⇒bmbCb⇒bmbmCb⇒bmbmb.

In the first route, the outer C first uses mC, then that remaining C splits into CbC. In the second, the outer C splits immediately, and the left child contributes the first meat. These are different structural choices, not merely doing the same independent replacements in another order. Every step shown replaces the leftmost variable, and both routes end at the identical terminal string.

That's a complete ambiguity witness. You don't need to show every string is ambiguous. The definition needs one witness.

Nullable rules can hide ambiguity

If B→BB|b|ε, the variable B can disappear directly or split and have both children disappear. So even a very short terminal string may have multiple parse structures. In the 2024 paper, S→B|BJ and J→jJb|j|ε. The string j has:

S⇒BJ⇒J⇒jS\Rightarrow BJ\Rightarrow J\Rightarrow jS⇒BJ⇒J⇒j

and

S⇒BJ⇒BBJ⇒BJ⇒J⇒j.S\Rightarrow BJ\Rightarrow BBJ\Rightarrow BJ\Rightarrow J\Rightarrow j.S⇒BJ⇒BBJ⇒BJ⇒J⇒j.

The second route has an extra B→BB subtree. Deleting ε from a written string does not delete that historical tree structure. This is why identical-looking intermediate strings can occur in distinct derivations.

Grammar versus language

“G is ambiguous” is a statement about this grammar. It does not prove its language has no unambiguous grammar. A language is inherently ambiguous when every CFG for it is ambiguous. That is a stronger claim requiring a different argument. Don't upgrade the conclusion just because the wording sounds similar.

How to work an ambiguity problem

Identify a string that can be split in two ways, or produced by two alternative start branches, or gets redundant nullable subtrees. Write two complete leftmost derivations. Underline the leftmost variable mentally before each step. Check the final terminal strings match exactly. State that the derivations are distinct and therefore the supplied grammar is ambiguous.

For arithmetic expressions, E→E+E|E×E|a permits different parse grouping of a+a×a. A grammar separating expression, term, and factor can impose precedence. It's the grammar structure doing the disambiguation; just writing “multiply first” beside an ambiguous grammar does not change its rules.

Fresh practice

For S→SS|a, prove ambiguity using aaa. Give two leftmost derivations and explain where their structures differ.

Hint: choose which child of the root grows

After S→SS, one derivation can expand the left S into SS. In the other, finish the left S as a before expanding the right S.

Show the two derivations

S⇒SS⇒SSS⇒aSS⇒aaS⇒aaa, and S⇒SS⇒aS⇒aSS⇒aaS⇒aaa. Both always expand the leftmost variable. The first groups the first two a's under the left child of the root; the second groups the last two under the right child. Thus the grammar is ambiguous.

lessons.title: CNF without losing a rule
lessons.description: Nullable occurrences, unit chains, and the full conversion recipe.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

CNF as a controlled rewrite: preserve choices at every stage · chap2_CNF2.pdf, pages 1–8

The mental model: change the wiring, keep the possible outputs

Every conversion stage should answer the same question: “How can I reconstruct an old derivation from this new one, and a new derivation from an old one?” If you only check that the final grammar looks like CNF, you can still have the wrong language. Format and equivalence are separate obligations.

We need an order because one repair can create the next kind of unwanted rule. Removing ε rules can create unit rules, so doing unit removal first would leave new handoffs behind.

Step 1: protect the start and find all nullable variables

Create S₀→S, with fresh S₀ appearing on no right-hand side. If the original grammar can generate ε, only this protected start will keep that ability in the final CNF.

Find nullable variables by repeated marking. First mark variables with a direct ε rule. Then mark A whenever it has a rule whose entire right-hand side consists of already-nullable variables. A terminal blocks this: a printed a cannot disappear. Repeat until a full pass adds nothing. This is a fixed point: further application changes nothing.

Why repeat? In A→B, B→C, C→ε, A is nullable indirectly. One left-to-right scan could miss it depending on rule order. With finitely many variables, each productive pass adds a mark and the process eventually stops.

Step 2: replace disappearing subtrees with explicit choices

For each rule, choose independently which nullable occurrences to omit. Keep the original rule too. For X→ABA with A nullable and B not nullable, the possibilities are ABA, AB, BA, B. The two As share a variable name but represent separate positions in a derivation.

Do not retain an ordinary empty right-hand side after this stage. Preserve S₀→ε exactly when the original start was nullable. Then remove the original ε rules from other variables.

Cycles need no special magic. With S→B|ε and B→S|ε, both variables are nullable; the language is just {ε}. The protected start may generate ε, but there is no terminal-producing work to invent. A conversion that manufactures a from this grammar is obviously wrong.

Here's the bit that makes the omission rule click. In an old derivation, a nullable variable might spend five steps becoming ε. In the new grammar, its parent can choose an alternative that leaves that position out immediately. Same finished word; fewer internal moves. We preserve the possible output, not the exact history of how it got printed.

Step 3: follow unit reachability, then copy real work

A unit rule has exactly one variable on its right, such as A→B. For each A, find every B reachable by zero or more unit rules. Copy every nonunit B-production onto A. Then remove unit rules.

Example: A→B, B→C, C→a|DE. A needs A→a|DE, and B needs B→a|DE. C keeps its original alternatives. The slides' CNF2 page 3 wording about removing B→u should not be read as deleting the nonunit production being copied; doing that can destroy valid outputs. Retain the useful nonunit rules.

Step 4: make terminal leaves and binary splits explicit

For X→aBCd, use U→a and V→d, then X→UBCV. Break the four-variable sequence into a chain, for example X→UH₁, H₁→BH₂, H₂→CV. Reading the leaves still gives a, then B's output, then C's, then d. Fresh helpers prevent collisions with existing variable meanings.

A rule X→a is already valid. Do not replace it by X→U unless you also remove the new unit rule afterward. The goal is standard shape, not maximum helper count.

A final audit you can actually perform

Check every right-hand side's shape; ensure only the protected start may produce ε; ensure that start never occurs on a right-hand side; inspect repeated nullable positions; inspect unit chains and cycles; compare a few boundary strings to catch errors. Finite examples can expose a mistake, but the stage-by-stage derivation argument establishes equivalence for all strings.

Keep: compute closures first, then rewrite from the complete information. Next, a PDA will execute pending grammatical work using a stack.

One connected check: Why can removing ε rules create unit rules, and why does that determine the order of the conversion stages?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

Chomsky normal form (CNF) is a standardized shape for grammar rules. The language should stay the same; the grammar's internal machinery changes. This is a repeat procedure on all six inspected Midterm 2 papers.

The destination

Each rule must have one of these shapes:

  • A→BC: exactly two variables on the right.
  • A→a: exactly one terminal on the right.
  • The start variable alone may have S₀→ε, if ε is in the language.

The start variable must not occur on the right of any rule. A→B is a unit rule and is not CNF. A→aB is not CNF because the two-symbol right side contains a terminal. A→BCD is not CNF because it has three variables. A→a is already fine; don't “fix” it into a unit rule.

Step 1: protect the start

Add a fresh start S₀ and S₀→S. “Fresh” means a symbol not already used. Keep S as an ordinary variable if needed. This lets us preserve ε using only S₀→ε and prevents the actual start symbol from being on a right side.

Step 2: eliminate ε rules without losing their choices

A variable is nullable if it can derive ε, possibly through other variables. Find them to a fixed point: first direct ε rules, then rules whose entire right side consists of nullable variables. Repeat until no new variable qualifies. Terminals never disappear this way.

For every right side, retain the original and add alternatives omitting each possible collection of nullable occurrences. Then remove ordinary ε rules; keep S₀→ε exactly when the original language contains ε.

The word “occurrences” is doing work. If A is nullable and a rule is S→ABA, the left A and right A are separate positions. Omitting one or both yields BA, AB, B, besides ABA. If B is nullable too, also AA, A, and ε are possible; duplicates count once. Keep ε only under the permitted start rule in the finished grammar.

The earlier gap, explicitly: for S→ABC with nullable A and B but nonnullable C, the alternatives are ABC, BC, AC, C. A stays/B disappears gives AC. Both disappear gives C. The C never disappears because no rule says it can.

Step 3: remove unit rules

A→B means A delegates to B without adding any terminal. Replace this delegation by B's non-unit alternatives. Keep B's productions for other uses of B. For chains and cycles, compute everything reachable by unit steps, then copy non-unit right sides from every reachable variable. This avoids looping on A→B→A.

Example: A→B, B→C|b, C→A|c. Each of A,B,C reaches all three through unit steps, so each receives alternatives b|c. Delete the unit links. The grammar becomes A→b|c, B→b|c, C→b|c.

The wording on CNF 2 page 3 can misleadingly suggest deleting the target variable's productions. That is not the language-preserving procedure. The worked examples and historical solutions retain productions needed by other variables. We implement the correct construction here.

Step 4: split long right sides and isolate terminals

For A→BCD, introduce X→CD and replace the original by A→BX. For A→aBb, introduce terminal helpers U→a,V→b, then use A→UX and X→BV. A prescribed exam order may split before replacing terminals; follow the requested stages and names. The final shape alone is not all the requested work.

A small complete conversion

Start with S→aSb|ε. Add S₀→S. Nullable S means add S→ab and S₀→ε; remove S→ε. Now:

S₀ → S | ε
S  → aSb | ab

Remove the unit S₀→S by copying S's non-unit alternatives:

S₀ → aSb | ab | ε
S  → aSb | ab

Introduce U→a,V→b,X→SV:

S₀ → UX | UV | ε
S  → UX | UV
X  → SV
U  → a
V  → b

Every rule now passes the shape test; S₀ never appears on the right. The UV base handles one pair; UX recurses; S₀→ε handles zero pairs.

Fresh practice

Convert S→AB, A→aA|ε, B→b into CNF, showing all stages. Does the start get an ε rule?

Show every stage

Add S₀→S. A is nullable, but B is not, so S is not nullable. Remove A→ε and add A→a and S→B, keeping S→AB. Eliminate S→B and S₀→S (and any induced unit links): S₀→AB|b; S→AB|b; A→aA|a; B→b. Replace the terminal in aA with U→a. Final: S₀→AB|b; S→AB|b; A→UA|a; B→b; U→a. There is no S₀→ε because every original string contains b.

Exam check: new start; all nullable-occurrence combinations; unit closure; no ordinary ε; only two variables or one terminal; intermediate stages in the requested order.
