lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Configurations: a complete snapshot, then a precise claim about termination · chap3_TM3.pdf, pages 1–14

A state name alone no longer describes the situation

For a DFA with fixed input position, the state was enough memory. For a TM, two visits to q can have different tape contents and head positions. A configuration must record all three: control state, tape, and head location. Otherwise a trace can silently lose the information that determines the next move.

The notation uqvu q vuqv writes the tape prefix u to the left of the head, inserts state q at the head position, and writes the scanned symbol as the first symbol of v. q is not a tape symbol; it is an annotation in the snapshot.

Decode one transition completely

Suppose a configuration is a q bc: the tape contains abc, the head reads b, and the state is q. If δ(q,b)=(r,x,R), the new configuration is ax r c. The b was overwritten by x; the head moved to c; the state became r.

If instead δ(q,b)=(r,x,L), the result is r axc: the head now reads the a to the left. The entire tape is still axc; only the placement of the state annotation differs. At the left boundary there is no earlier cell to move into, so that case follows the boundary rule separately.

This is why copying only the state sequence is not a full TM trace. You need the tape edits and head movement too.

Three possible outcomes, not two

A TM may accept, reject, or keep running forever. A recognizer for L must accept every member and must never accept a nonmember. On a nonmember it may reject or loop. A decider must halt on every input, accepting members and rejecting nonmembers.

Every decider is a recognizer. Calling a recognizer “an algorithm that answers yes or no” overstates its guarantee: on some no-instances it may never answer. You cannot turn it into a decider by getting impatient after a million steps; a genuine accepting run might take a million and one.

Read the deck's constructions as phase programs

The w#w machine alternates marking, crossing, comparing, and returning. Its return states need different jobs on the two sides of #; reaching a marked symbol on the right is not the same as reaching the last processed symbol on the left. State meanings explain why several apparently similar left-moving states exist.

The slide language is aibjcka^ib^jc^kaibjck with ij=k and i,j,k≥1: all three blocks must be nonempty. Check that format first, then use repeated matching: for each a, traverse the b-block and account for j c-symbols. Restore temporary b-marks before the next a, while keeping track of c-symbols already spent. The a-count controls the number of repetitions, and the b-count controls each repetition's cost. A final check rejects unused or insufficient c's. The slide's positivity condition rejects zero-size blocks at the format check. A variation allowing zero would need different boundary handling; don't silently change the supplied language.

Reuse the comparison routine on a whole list

Pages 13–14 ask that the binary blocks in #x₁#x₂…#xₗ all differ. Compare every pair, not only neighbors. For #0#1#0, the first and second differ, and the second and third differ, but the first and third are equal. Mark the two selected separators, copy or compare their blocks using the earlier matching routine, then advance to the next pair. With l blocks there are l(l−1)/2 pairs, so a systematic finite pair schedule terminates. The subscripts identify positions in the list, not bits inside one block.

A high-level solution still owes a proof

For any construction, state the invariant tying the marks to completed work. Then show why acceptance implies the required relation and why a valid input can complete the procedure. Finally show termination using finite scans and a finite number of progressing rounds. “It keeps trying until it works” is not a halting argument.

Keep: a configuration is a snapshot; a recognizer may loop on nonmembers; a decider always finishes. Next, multiple tapes make programs easier to organize without changing which languages are computable.

One connected check: Why does a repeated control state fail to prove a TM is looping, while a repeated complete configuration of a deterministic TM does prove it?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

This lesson reconstructs the 2025 Midterm 2 masking machine from its prescribed algorithm and diagram. It is a worked example, so count this question as exposed after reading it. Use other questions or fresh variants for a later independent check.

First translate the exact task

Input has the form text#mask#. The text uses a,b; the mask uses 0,1; their lengths are promised equal. Keep a text character if its corresponding mask bit is 1. Append the kept characters after the second #. The problem permits erasing processed text and mask positions and requires at most eleven states excluding reject.

Example: ab#01# must append b. The a pairs with 0 and is discarded; the b pairs with 1 and is copied. This is not a recognizer checking equal strings; it is a transducer computing an output.

Assign one job to each state

State Job / information remembered
q₀ Find the next text character, or finish at the first #
q₁ / q₂ Remember a / b while scanning to the first #
q₃ / q₄ Remember a / b while finding the next unprocessed mask bit
q₅ / q₆ Remember a / b while scanning to the output's end
q₇ Return left through output to the second #
q₈ Return left through the mask area to the first #
q₉ Return left through remaining text to the erased-prefix boundary
qₐ Halt accepting

Remembering a versus b requires different states while traveling, because the erased source character can't be reread. Return phases can be shared once that remembered symbol has been written or discarded.

Complete transition table

Each row means current state, read symbol(s), write, move, next. “Same” means keep the scanned symbol. Unlisted pairs go to reject. The promised input format means we do not add a separate format validator.

Current Read Write Move Next
q₀ a ⊔ R q₁
q₀ b ⊔ R q₂
q₀ # # R qₐ
q₁ a,b same R q₁
q₂ a,b same R q₂
q₁ # # R q₃
q₂ # # R q₄
q₃ ⊔ ⊔ R q₃
q₄ ⊔ ⊔ R q₄
q₃ 0 ⊔ L q₈
q₄ 0 ⊔ L q₈
q₃ 1 ⊔ R q₅
q₄ 1 ⊔ R q₆
q₅ 0,1,#,a,b same R q₅
q₆ 0,1,#,a,b same R q₆
q₅ ⊔ a L q₇
q₆ ⊔ b L q₇
q₇ a,b same L q₇
q₇ # # L q₈

To draw the diagram from this table, draw each state once and one arrow for each row. Combine labels only when source, destination, write behavior, and movement agree. qₐ is a halting state; the course uses a labeled single circle for TM halting states. Use its convention.

Why blank means different things in different phases

At q₃/q₄ a blank is a processed mask bit, so scan right. At q₅/q₆, after the current bit, there are no processed mask blanks ahead: remaining mask bits, separator, then output are nonblank. The first blank is the output end. At q₉, the first blank reached from the right is the processed-text boundary, so turn right. The state tells you which meaning is relevant. Without the phase, the same blank symbol is ambiguous.

Correctness and halting

After k rounds, the first k text symbols and first k mask bits are erased. The output equals exactly the kept characters among those k positions, in their original order. Remaining text and mask suffixes are unchanged. In round k+1, q₀ remembers the next text character, q₃/q₄ finds the corresponding first unprocessed mask bit, and the branch either appends that character or skips it. The return phases restore the head to the next text symbol. Hence the invariant holds for k+1.

When all text is erased, q₀ reads the first # and accepts. Equal promised lengths ensure all mask positions have also been processed. Each round processes one pair; every scan crosses a finite region to a guaranteed boundary. Therefore the machine halts. The empty case ## accepts with empty output.

Fresh variation

Change the task to keeping a character exactly when its mask bit is 0. Which transitions change? Explain why the rest of the invariant survives.

Show the modification

Swap the roles of input 0 and 1 at q₃ and q₄. Reading 1 now erases and moves left to q₈; reading 0 erases and moves right to q₅ or q₆. All scanning, appending and return rules stay the same. The invariant changes only from “kept by bit 1” to “kept by bit 0.” State meanings that remember a/b remain unchanged.

Exam habit: after drawing, simulate the requested input through the actual final halting transition. The past solutions repeatedly require the entire trace, not an ellipsis near the end.

lessons.title: More tapes, more branches, same power
lessons.description: Simulations, simultaneous updates, and breadth-first search.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

One tape simulates many: encode the whole situation, then update it · chap3_multitapeTM2.pdf, pages 1–5

The job: replace convenient hardware with an encoding

A multitape machine has k tapes and k head positions. A single tape can store their finite used contents as separated blocks, for example #block₁#block₂#…#blockₖ#. Use a marked version of a symbol to indicate each simulated head's position. The delimiter and marked symbols are extra members of the simulator's finite tape alphabet.

The representation must retain both the data and the head locations. Merely joining the tape contents loses which cell each simulated head reads next. That's the same lesson as configurations: an encoding has to preserve everything needed to determine the next step.

Simulate one joint step in phases

First sweep across the encoded blocks and read each marked symbol. Remember the k-symbol tuple in the simulator's finite control. This is possible because k and the simulated tape alphabet are fixed for this machine, so there are only finitely many possible tuples.

Use the simulated transition function to determine the new state, writes, and movements. Make another sweep to update each marked cell and move the head marker to its neighbor. Different blocks may move their heads in different directions, but all updates come from the same old snapshot.

For example, if the simulated heads read (0,1) and the rule writes (x,0) with movements (R,L), the simulator must find those two marked cells, replace their contents, and move the two markers appropriately. It must not let the new x influence the choice of the second write.

What if a simulated tape needs more room?

If a head moves past its block's currently represented end, insert a blank cell into that block. Shift later encoded cells right to make space. A finite-control carry can move symbols one by one; this is tedious but implementable. The block remains a faithful representation of a tape with additional blank cells available.

The simulation is allowed to use many real steps for one simulated step. Computability asks whether the same answers can be produced at all, not whether the hardware has identical speed.

The invariant is the proof

At the beginning of each simulated step, the single-tape encoding represents exactly the multitape machine's complete configuration. Initialization establishes this. Reading the stored head tuple and applying the same transition preserves it. Therefore each finite accepting or rejecting computation is reproduced, and an endless simulated computation continues rather than being falsely turned into a halt.

Conversely, a multitape machine can ignore extra tapes and behave like a one-tape machine. The two simulations establish equal recognition and decision power.

Why this matters later

We can design algorithms using convenient multiple tapes, then know a standard TM can implement them. In complexity theory we revisit this exact construction and count its cost: scanning and shifting a growing representation can turn t simulated steps into roughly quadratic work. Same computability is compatible with different efficiency.

Keep: encode complete configurations; preserve them one simulated step at a time. The proof is an invariant plus a way to implement each update.

One connected check: What information would be lost if the encoding included tape contents and separators but no marked head positions?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

Different machine models can look wildly different and still recognize exactly the same languages. “Equivalent” concerns what can be computed, not whether the diagrams, running time, or number of states are identical.

Two tapes: one simultaneous move

A k-tape transition reads k symbols, writes k symbols, and moves k heads, while changing one shared control state. For two tapes,

δ(q,a,b)=(r,c,d,R,L)\delta(q,a,b)=(r,c,d,R,L)δ(q,a,b)=(r,c,d,R,L)

reads a on tape 1 and b on tape 2, writes c,d respectively, moves head 1 right and head 2 left, and enters r. Do not run the tape-1 line as one machine step and the tape-2 line as another. They are one joint instruction.

The course allows a stay move S for multitape machines. The input starts on tape 1; all other tapes are blank. Any extra left marker you want must be a permitted symbol, and its initialization must be part of the construction.

A concrete copy routine

Suppose the tape alphabet permits a marker $. First write $ at the beginning of tape 2 and move its head right, leaving tape 1 at the first input character. For each a∈{0,1}, read a on tape 1 and blank on tape 2; write a on tape 2 and move both heads right. At tape-1 blank, the copy is complete. Move tape-2 head left over copied symbols until $, then right. Now tape 2 is positioned at the copy's first symbol.

This illustrates initialization, simultaneous updates, and boundary detection. It is not a substitute for a past question that restricts Γ={0,1,#,⊔} and forbids $. Under such a restriction you must use the permitted marking strategy or boundary behavior.

Simulating many tapes with one

Encode each tape's used region as a block separated by #. Mark the scanned cell in each block using a dotted version of its symbol. A one-tape simulator scans the blocks to learn the k scanned symbols, remembers that finite tuple in its control, then scans again to perform the prescribed writes and move the marks. If a simulated head needs a fresh cell, insert a blank in that block and shift later material right.

For fixed k and finite Γ, the tuple of scanned symbols has finitely many possibilities, so finite control can remember it. Each simulated step takes finitely many scans. This proves simulation of arbitrary computations, not just a sample trace. The reverse direction is immediate: a one-tape machine is a special case of a multitape machine.

A stay move can also be simulated: write the requested symbol, move right into an intermediate state, then move left while preserving that next cell. Choosing right then left avoids problems at the left boundary.

Nondeterministic TM: why breadth-first matters

An NTM accepts if at least one branch accepts. A depth-first simulator may follow one infinite branch forever while another branch accepts after five steps. So enumerate the tree fairly, by depth: all paths of length 0, then 1, then 2, and so on. Each layer is finite because each configuration has finitely many next moves.

If an accepting branch exists, it has a finite length d, and the breadth-first simulator eventually visits it. Thus a deterministic TM can recognize the same language. This is not NFA subset construction into finitely many control states; TM configurations include arbitrarily long tape contents.

If every branch halts on every input, finite branching implies the computation tree for a fixed input is finite (the relevant consequence of König's lemma). Then exhaustive breadth-first simulation can also reject after all branches finish. This establishes equivalence for deciders too. “Every branch is finite” alone would not imply a finite tree if infinite branching were allowed; finite branching is essential.

Fresh practice

An NTM's left branch loops forever; its right branch accepts after three steps. Describe what a depth-first simulator and a breadth-first simulator might do, and whether the NTM accepts.

Show the answer

The NTM accepts because its right branch accepts. A depth-first simulator choosing the left branch first can loop forever and never discover this. Breadth-first explores all finite depths fairly, so it eventually reaches the right branch's accepting configuration at depth three. This explains recognizer equivalence; it does not make the original NTM a decider, because one branch fails to halt.

lessons.title: Connect the whole course map
lessons.description: Memory models, regular closure, GNFA, and reusable proof structure.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Algorithms and the Church–Turing thesis: what counts as an effective method? · chap3_Hilbert.pdf, pages 1–13

The whole-course question gets bigger

We've shown that several formal machine designs have the same computability power. Now connect them to the informal word algorithm: a finite, mechanical procedure whose individual steps can be carried out effectively. The Church–Turing thesis says that effectively computable procedures are captured by Turing machines.

This is a thesis linking an informal notion to a formal model, not a theorem proved by manipulating two formal definitions. Equivalence between one-tape and multitape TMs is a theorem; the claim that the model captures every effective method has a different logical status.

Searching for an integer root: yes can be easier than no

Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, try integer inputs and evaluate it. For one variable, test 0,1,−1,2,−2,… . If an integer root exists, this enumeration eventually finds it. If none exists, an unbounded search alone runs forever. It is a recognizer-style strategy for the yes-instances, not automatically a decider.

For a univariate polynomial of positive degree with nonzero leading coefficient, a computable bound on root magnitude turns this into a finite search. Once every integer within a valid bound has been checked, there are no other possible integer roots to miss. For the slide example 4x3−2x2+x−74x^3-2x^2+x-74x3−2x2+x−7, a bound such as |x|≤7 suffices. Constant and zero polynomials are handled separately rather than dividing by a nonexistent leading term.

The critical extra ingredient is the stopping certificate supplied by the bound. “I haven't found a root yet” is not the same information as “I've exhausted every possible root.”

Why the multivariable result is deeper

For polynomial equations in several integer variables, enumerating all integer tuples still recognizes existence of a solution. Hilbert's tenth problem asked for a general deciding procedure. The negative result says no such algorithm exists for all instances. This does not follow just from the fact that our current brute-force search may loop; a bad algorithm doesn't prove all algorithms impossible. An impossibility theorem needs a reduction or other general argument.

Three levels of describing a TM

A formal description lists states and transitions. An implementation-level description explains tape layouts, head movements, and marking. A high-level description uses algorithmic steps such as “search the finite graph,” while making those steps effective and termination clear.

For graph connectivity, begin with one marked vertex, repeatedly mark neighbors of marked vertices, and stop when a whole pass adds nothing. A finite graph has only finitely many vertices to add. Accept if all are marked. The algorithm's monotone progress explains termination; the reachability invariant explains correctness.

An input encoding, written with angle brackets such as ⟨G⟩, turns an abstract object into a finite string. Invalid encodings must have specified treatment. The machine reads symbols, not a Platonic graph floating in the void.

Keep: distinguish an effective procedure, a formal simulation theorem, and the Church–Turing thesis. Existence search needs a separate reason to stop on no-instances. Next, we ask which questions about encoded machines are decidable.

One connected check: What extra fact turns the univariate integer-root enumeration into a decider, and why does “it worked on many examples” not provide that fact?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

This page connects the whole map. Use it after the worked lessons, or jump to a missing definition from another lesson. It is a summary with proof ideas, not a replacement for producing the constructions yourself.

Three levels of memory

Finite automata: finite state only. DFA, NFA, and regular expressions describe the regular languages. An NFA can branch but does not gain language-recognition power over a DFA.

Pushdown automata: finite control plus one unbounded stack. Nondeterministic PDAs and CFGs describe the context-free languages. Every regular language is context-free: a PDA can simulate a DFA while ignoring its stack. Some context-free languages, such as 0ⁿ1ⁿ, are not regular. DPDAs recognize a proper subclass of CFLs.

Turing machines: rewritable tape with a moving head. Multitape and nondeterministic variants have the same recognition power as ordinary deterministic TMs. Deciders halt on every input; recognizers may loop on nonmembers. The ability to simulate another model establishes containment; separating examples establish that a containment is strict.

The published course explicitly omits the detailed non-context-free-language discussion at the end of PDA 5. CFL pumping was absent as a direct task in the six inspected Midterm 2 papers. It is not part of this site's core practice route unless current class information adds it. Regular-language pumping is a separate theorem and must not be used to prove a language is not context-free.

Regular-language closure: what “closed” means

A class is closed under an operation if applying that operation to languages in the class always produces another language in the class. “Open” is not the usual opposite term here; say “not closed.” One result being regular does not establish closure of the whole class.

Inputs regular Result Construction / proof idea
A,B A∪B regular NFA with fresh ε-branching start
A,B A∩B regular Product DFA tracks both states; accept when both accept
A,B AB regular NFA ε-links from A's finals to B's start
A A* regular Fresh accepting start; enter A and repeat from its finals
A Complement regular In a complete DFA over fixed Σ, swap accepting and rejecting states
A,B A−B regular Intersect A with complement of B

For the product, after reading w the state is (state of M_A after w, state of M_B after w). This invariant holds initially and is preserved by each paired transition. The accepting pair condition therefore implements intersection exactly. For union, accept if either component accepts. Same transitions, changed final set.

Do not complement an NFA by flipping circles: existential acceptance does not become universal rejection that way. Convert to a complete DFA first.

Regular expressions and GNFA elimination

RE operations are union, concatenation and star. ε denotes the language {ε}; ∅ denotes the empty language. Therefore Rε=R, R∅=∅, R∪∅=R, and ∅*=ε. Concatenation order matters.

Both DFA→GNFA and NFA→GNFA can be done directly. Add a new start with an ε edge to the old start, a new sole accept reached by ε from old finals, union parallel edges, and label missing edges ∅. An NFA's symbol and ε labels are already regular expressions. Subset construction is not required for this route.

When removing state k, update each remaining i→j label to

Rij ∪ Rik(Rkk)∗Rkj.R_{ij}\ \cup\ R_{ik}(R_{kk})^*R_{kj}.Rij​ ∪ Rik​(Rkk​)∗Rkj​.

The old edge handles paths bypassing k. The new term enters k, loops there zero or more times, then leaves. This explains the star and the order. Update from the old labels for that elimination step, not labels partly overwritten during the same step.

A proof template that travels

For any conversion, write: what does a state/variable/configuration represent; why is that true at the start; how is it preserved by each move/rule; why does the ending condition correspond to membership? For a decider, add why the process halts. For equivalence, cover both directions. For impossibility, identify a property forced by every candidate machine and construct an input that violates it.

The Church–Turing thesis connects the informal notion of an effective algorithm with Turing computation. It is a thesis about that informal notion, not a mathematical theorem proved by checking a few programs. The course's Hilbert deck uses integer-root search to contrast a recognizer with a bounded terminating decision procedure.

Fresh practice

Someone claims: “A and B are nonregular, so A∪B must be nonregular.” Disprove this using a language L and its complement over the same alphabet, and explain why both can be nonregular.

Show the counterexample

Take L={0ⁿ1ⁿ | n≥0}, which is nonregular, and its complement over {0,1}*. The complement is also nonregular: if it were regular, closure of regular languages under complement would make L regular, a contradiction. Yet their union is {0,1}*, which is regular. Closure promises concern inputs inside the class; they do not give this claimed rule for nonregular inputs.

Repair the star example without changing its language

Keep the base language fixed as A={01}. Its NFA is u —0→ v —1→ w, with u starting and w accepting. To recognize A*, add a fresh accepting start s, an ε arrow s→u, and an ε arrow w→u. Keep w accepting. No other arrows exist.

State 0 1 ε Accepting?
s ∅ ∅ {u} Yes
u {v} ∅ ∅ No
v ∅ {w} ∅ No
w ∅ ∅ {u} Yes

The fresh s accepts ε. A completed 01 finishes at w and may begin another complete copy through u. The strings 01 and 0101 accept; 001 and 01001 reject. There is no zero self-loop here. Adding a zero self-loop at u would make 001 possible; that would change the language and break this construction. The accepting new start does not grant arbitrary extra input a free pass: some path still has to consume the entire input.

models.title: Chapter 0 — Know what kind of thing you are talking about
models.html:
The whole idea

This deck gives us the grammar for talking precisely about computers. Before proving anything, ask: what objects are involved, and what exactly am I claiming about them? A bunch of notation becomes much less cursed once every symbol has a job. Pages 1–9 introduce objects and logic; pages 10–15 show how definitions become reasons in a proof.

Build the objects from scratch

A set is a collection where membership matters. {0,1} and {1,0,1} name the same set. A sequence preserves order and repetitions: 01 differs from 10, and 11 differs from 1. A tuple is a fixed-length sequence of entries. A machine's five-tuple is therefore a record with five different fields, not five arbitrary decorations.

A function gives exactly one output for every allowed input. Its output may itself be a set. That is how an NFA transition can be a perfectly valid function even though the machine has several possible next states. A relation records which pairs satisfy a condition; it need not select a single partner.

The Cartesian product lists ordered choices from two sets. If A={1,2} and B={x,y}, then A×B contains (1,x), (1,y), (2,x), (2,y). Later, “state × symbol” simply means “give me those two pieces of information together.”

Watch a definition do useful work

Pages 3–4 use “same remainder modulo 7.” Two integers are related when their difference is a multiple of 7. Why is this an equivalence relation—a way of grouping genuinely interchangeable cases?

An integer differs from itself by zero, so it relates to itself (reflexive). If i−j=7a, then j−i=7(−a), so reversing the pair preserves the relation (symmetric). If i−j=7a and j−k=7b, adding gives i−k=7(a+b), so the relationship passes through the middle number (transitive). Each fancy word has just become a checkable property.

How a proof grows out of the picture

Page 11 asks why an undirected graph's total degree is even. A vertex is a node; an edge joins endpoints; a vertex's degree counts incident edge-ends. Look at one edge. It contributes one end at each endpoint, so two contributions overall. Repeat that accounting for every edge: total degree = twice the number of edges. Twice an integer is even. Done. We counted a generic contribution, so the argument covers every finite graph, not just the drawn example. A self-loop, if allowed, contributes two to its vertex's degree.

An implication “P implies Q” says there cannot be a case with P true and Q false. It does not say Q happens only because of P. “Rain implies wet ground” allows wet ground from a sprinkler. To disprove a universal implication, find one case satisfying P but violating Q.

Source wording to separate: page 10 writes the contrapositive ¬Q→¬P under a contradiction heading. Contraposition proves that equivalent implication. Contradiction assumes the original claim fails and derives an impossibility. Pages 13–15 use contradiction: write √2=m/n in lowest terms; its square forces m even, then n even, contradicting lowest terms. Those methods are related but their opening assumptions differ.

Carry this into the next deck

A state diagram will use sets, functions and a graph to define a checker. Proofs will connect its behavior to a claim about all inputs. Your job is to track object, condition, reason before worrying about polished wording.

Connected check: explain why showing three graphs with even degree sums is weaker than the “two ends per edge” argument. Use the distinction between examples and all graphs.

models.title: DFA 1 — A state is the information you keep
models.html:
The whole idea

The automatic door on pages 1–3 is the cleanest starting point: the same sensor reading can require different behavior depending on whether the door is already open or closed. A state stores the relevant situation from before this instant. The circle is the drawing of that stored situation. It is not the memory concept itself.

Build the machine before the notation

A door controller receives a sensor category such as front, rear, both or neither. Its current state plus that reading determines the next state. You do not need the entire history of everyone who walked past. You need the small summary that makes the next decision possible.

A DFA applies the same idea to a string: read one symbol, update the summary, repeat. “Deterministic” means a current state and symbol specify exactly one next state. “Finite” means the list of available summaries is fixed and finite. It cannot invent a new state every time the input gets longer.

Acceptance is checked after all input is read. An accepting state may have outgoing arrows because the current prefix might be valid while a longer string is not. Walking through an accepting state halfway through is not an early victory lap.

Follow the actual slide example

Pages 9–10 ask for strings ending in 1. What must survive from the past? Only whether the most recently read symbol is 1. Use q₁ for “no last 1” and q₂ for “last symbol was 1.” Initially q₁: no symbol has been read, and the empty string does not end in 1.

Current summary      Read 0       Read 1
q₁: not ending in 1   q₁           q₂
q₂: ending in 1       q₁           q₂

For 1010, start q₁. Read 1→q₂, 0→q₁, 1→q₂, 0→q₁. End in q₁, so reject. Notice why both rows agree: whatever happened before, a new final 0 makes the current prefix end in zero. The update rule follows from the state's meaning.

Now decode the five pieces

The tuple (Q,Σ,δ,q₀,F) names the same machine in five fields. Q is the finite set of states; Σ is the input alphabet; δ is the update function; q₀ is the chosen starting state; F is the set of accepting states. In this example Q={q₁,q₂}, Σ={0,1}, q₀=q₁ and F={q₂}. The subscript 0 in q₀ means “designated start,” so its actual label can be q₁. Annoying notation, yes; no mathematical conflict.

δ(q₁,1)=q₂ reads “from q₁, on input 1, go to q₂.” Its type Q×Σ→Q means it consumes a pair and returns one state. It says nothing about how many accepting states are permitted. F may contain several states or none.

Why this works

After every nonempty prefix, the machine is at q₂ exactly when that prefix ends in 1. Check the first symbol, then notice each update preserves the statement. At the end, F selects exactly the required strings. This statement is the machine's invariant: its maintained meaning.

Pages 4–8 use a different three-state language: at least one 1, with an even number of zeros after the last 1. Do not silently reuse the two-state interpretation there. Different target, different information to remember.

Next connection: DFA2 turns “remember the relevant summary” into a construction method. Connected check: explain why “ends in 1” needs no exact count of all earlier ones, while “exactly one 1” needs a different summary.

models.title: DFA 2 — Compress the past without losing the decision
models.html:
The whole idea

The design question is: which differences between input histories can safely be forgotten? If two histories require the same behavior for every possible continuation, one state may represent both. If some continuation must distinguish them, merging them loses information. This is the reason to design state meanings before drawing arrows.

Build the picture from the slide examples

Pages 1–4 recognize nonempty strings whose first and last symbols agree. You need the first symbol permanently, and you update the current last symbol. A separate initial situation handles “nothing read yet.” One symbol such as a already has matching first and last symbols; the empty string needs its own decision.

Pages 6–8 keep the sum since the last reset, modulo 3. Modulo 3 means the remainder after division by 3: 0, 1 or 2. You can throw away the actual sum because adding the next digit affects the final remainder using only the current remainder. A reset overwrites the summary with remainder zero. This is deliberate forgetting, not random loss of memory.

One complete construction: odd many ones

Pages 11–13 ask for binary strings with an odd number of 1s. “Odd” means 1,3,5,…; “even” means 0,2,4,…. You do not need to distinguish one 1 from a thousand and one. Both require the same future toggles.

Let qₑ mean “even many ones so far,” and qₒ mean “odd many.” Start qₑ because the initial count is zero. Accept at qₒ. Reading 0 changes no count, so each state loops on 0. Reading 1 changes parity, so it switches states.

For 010101, the summaries after each symbol are even, odd, odd, even, even, odd. Accept. If you append another 1, the answer flips. That is exactly what the rule demands.

The formal computation page is a run log

On page 9, w=w₁…wₙ names the input symbols. The r₀,…,rₙ names the visited states. w entries are what we read; r entries are what we remember afterward. There are n symbols but n+1 recorded states because r₀ records the situation before reading anything.

r₀=q₀ says start correctly. δ(rᵢ,wᵢ₊₁)=rᵢ₊₁ says each adjacent row follows the update rule. rₙ∈F says the final recorded state belongs to the accepting set. “∈” means membership. It is an acceptance test, not a claim that every run must accept.

A language is regular if some finite automaton recognizes exactly its strings. That is an existence claim about a checker. A language does not become regular because its English description sounds simple.

Why this method generalizes

The odd/even invariant holds at the start and survives each symbol. That gives a proof for arbitrarily long inputs. The “contains 001” machine on page 14 uses another summary: how much of the useful suffix 001 has been matched, or whether it was already found. After 000, the useful suffix is still 00; an extra zero should not erase both zeros from memory.

The reset, parity and substring examples share one mental move: keep exactly the information needed for later decisions. Their arrows differ because their meanings differ.

Next connection: DFA3 keeps two such summaries at once. Connected check: for an odd-ones machine, justify the start, 0-arrows, 1-arrows and accepting state from their meanings, without memorizing its drawing.

models.title: DFA 3 — Combine rules by remembering both summaries
models.html:
The whole idea

You already have two working checkers. Can you combine their languages without reinventing everything? Pages 1–4 define the language operations; pages 5–10 prove one combination works. Closure means an operation never takes you outside the class when you start inside it. It is a statement about all suitable languages, not a “closed” state in a diagram.

First distinguish the three jobs

Union A∪B means the whole input belongs to A or B, possibly both. Concatenation A◦B means the input can be split into a first piece from A and a second piece from B, in that order. Star A* means concatenate zero or more pieces from A. Zero pieces produce ε, the empty string.

The slide's A={good,bad}, B={boy,girl} makes the roles visible. goodgirl is in A◦B; girlgood is not. goodbadgood is in A*, because each piece belongs to A. You may choose the sequence of pieces, but you do not shuffle characters inside a chosen piece. The star counts repetitions of whole members, not necessarily single symbols.

The slide combines “odd many 1s” with “odd many 0s.” After a prefix, the first machine knows one parity and the second knows the other. Store the ordered pair of their states. Four combinations are possible: (even,even), (even,odd), (odd,even), (odd,odd).

models.title: NFA 1 — Keep several guesses alive
models.html:
The whole idea

A DFA commits to one next state. An NFA may have several legal moves. The useful picture is a collection of candidate runs: one candidate can die while another succeeds. The definition says accept if at least one complete run consumes the whole input and ends accepting. It is not a probability, a majority vote, or a machine that magically knows the future.

Why guessing helps

Pages 6–7 ask whether the third symbol from the end is 1. While reading left to right, you do not yet know where the end will be. An NFA can continue scanning and, whenever it sees a 1, also start a candidate that says, “maybe this is the third-last position.” That candidate must then consume exactly two further symbols and finish.

The diagram has q₁ looping on 0 and 1; q₁ also goes to q₂ on 1; q₂→q₃ and q₃→q₄ each consume either symbol. Only q₄ accepts, with no outgoing moves. Those missing moves are part of the design: if more input remains, that candidate guessed too early and must die.

Follow the candidates all the way

Use the slide's accepted input 0100. Begin with candidate set {q₁}. After 0: {q₁}. After 1: {q₁,q₂}, because the run can keep scanning or start its guess. After the next 0: {q₁,q₃}. After the final 0: {q₁,q₄}. One candidate finishes at q₄, so accept.

Now 0010: after 0,0,1 the set is {q₁,q₂}; after the last 0 it is {q₁,q₃}. No accepting candidate remains. Reject. The 1 was second-last, not third-last. Reaching q₂ was only a hypothesis, not success.

What ε adds

Pages 2–5 also use ε-arrows. ε means move without consuming an input symbol. If a candidate can follow an ε-arrow, include that possibility while retaining the possibility of taking zero ε-moves. The ε-closure collects everything reachable that way. After consuming the next real symbol, take closure again. Old states do not stay merely because you remember seeing them; they stay only if a legal continuation reaches them at the current input position.

The tree is a record of possible paths. A row can collect possibilities at a common input position, including free ε movement. Actual hardware need not create infinitely many parallel workers; this is a mathematical definition of accepted strings.

Why the DFA can still do this

Pages 8–10 show eight DFA states remembering the latest three bits. That DFA stores enough history to answer at the end without guessing. Leading zeros in the initial q₀₀₀ do not create a false accepting third-last 1 for a short input. Nondeterminism made the design compact; it did not enlarge the regular-language class. Subset construction will prove the general equivalence.

The modified ε version on pages 12–13 asks a different question: is some one among the last three symbols a 1? Zero, one or two remaining symbols may finish the guessed path. Changing arrows changes the permitted completion lengths, hence the language.

Connected check: explain why giving q₄ a loop on both symbols would destroy the “third from the end” test. Trace one input that reveals the problem.

models.title: NFA 2 — A transition returns a collection of options
models.html:
The whole idea

We need a precise way to write “zero, one, or several possible next states.” The output of an NFA transition is a set. The function still gives one answer for each request; that answer is the entire option set. This repairs the informal “δ isn't a function anymore” wording in NFA1.

Build the types before reading the formula

For a DFA, asking “from q on 1?” returns one state, say r. For an NFA it may return {r,s}, {r}, or ∅. Braces say “a set containing these states.” ∅ says “there are no options.” The accepting set F is a separate object listing states where a fully consumed run may finish.

The power set 𝒫(Q) is the collection of all subsets of Q. If Q={a,b}, its possible output sets are ∅, {a}, {b}, {a,b}. Each state has an in/out choice, hence 2×2=4 subsets. With three states there are 2³=8. The power set is where the function's answers live; it is not a new kind of accepting state.

Σ names actual input symbols. Σε means Σ∪{ε}, allowing the table to ask about a no-input move as well. Thus δ:Q×Σε→𝒫(Q) reads: state plus a symbol-or-ε request goes in; a set of possible destinations comes out.

Work the slide's actual table

Pages 8–9 have four states. From q₁ on 1 the answer is {q₁,q₂}. From q₂ on ε it is {q₃}. From q₃ on 1 it is {q₄}, and q₄ accepts.

Trace 11. Start {q₁}. The first 1 reaches q₁ and q₂; the free q₂→q₃ move adds q₃. Current possibilities are {q₁,q₂,q₃}. On the second 1, q₁ contributes {q₁,q₂}; q₂ contributes ∅; q₃ contributes {q₄}. Combine those destinations, then close under ε: {q₁,q₂,q₃,q₄}. Accept because q₄ is possible after the whole string.

Notice the empty contribution from q₂. Union with ∅ adds nothing. We do not insert an object called ∅ into the set of NFA states. “No candidate from this branch” is different from “a candidate at a state named empty set.” The latter becomes a useful name only in the converted DFA.

Why the formal run can be longer than the string

Page 10 allows w=y₁…yₘ with each yᵢ either a real symbol or ε. For input 11, one accepting path can be labeled 1,ε,1. Concatenating those labels still gives 11: the ε contributes zero characters. The state sequence has a step for every move, so m need not equal the number of input characters.

The condition rᵢ₊₁∈δ(rᵢ,yᵢ₊₁) says the chosen next state must be one of the legal options. A run chooses one option each time; the acceptance definition asks whether any suitable run exists.

Next connection: NFA3 makes the whole current option set into one DFA state. Connected check: distinguish δ(q₁,1)={q₁,q₂} from F={q₄}: what question does each set answer?

models.title: NFA 3 — One DFA state can store the entire candidate set
models.html:
The whole idea

The NFA branches, but its set of states is finite. So we can ask a deterministic machine to keep a checklist: which NFA states are still possible after the input read so far? Every possible checklist gets one DFA state. That is subset construction. The braces label the contents of one memory record; they do not turn the new DFA into a branching machine.

Here's the mental switch: the DFA is the clerk holding the whole checklist, not one of the candidates on it. {q₁,q₂} is one clerk's current record. Reading a symbol deterministically produces the next record. That's why a circle with braces can still be one ordinary DFA state.

Build the update rule

Suppose the current checklist is R and the next input symbol is a. Look at every state r in R, follow its a-arrows, collect the destinations, then include every state reachable from those destinations by ε moves. That creates one uniquely determined next checklist.

The start checklist is E({q₀}), where E means ε-closure: include q₀ and all states reachable by zero or more ε-arrows. A checklist accepts when it contains at least one NFA accepting state. Nothing more complicated is hidden in the formula R∩F≠∅: intersection keeps members shared by R and F; “not empty” says at least one accepting possibility survives.

Trace the exact slide example

The three-state NFA on page 3 starts at q₁, which has an ε move to q₃; q₁ is accepting. Therefore the converted start is {q₁,q₃}, already accepting because ε has an accepting run at q₁.

Pages 10–11 give baa:

before input       {q₁,q₃}
after b            {q₂}
after ba           {q₂,q₃}
after baa          {q₁,q₂,q₃}

The final set contains q₁, so accept. To see one union explicitly, page 6 starts with {q₁,q₂} and reads a: q₁ contributes no destination; q₂ contributes q₂ and q₃. The result is {q₂,q₃}. ∅∪{q₂,q₃}={q₂,q₃}. An empty contribution doesn't create an extra candidate.

What the empty DFA state means

If the checklist becomes ∅, every NFA candidate has died. Another symbol cannot restart a nonexistent run. Thus ∅→∅ on every symbol in the DFA. This is a real state whose remembered fact is “no candidates remain.” In the old NFA, a missing arrow meant a branch died. Same behavior, different representation.

With three original states there are eight possible subsets. The textbook construction includes all of them; some are unreachable from the start. Here any subset containing q₁ but omitting q₃ is unreachable because closure would immediately include q₃. Remove unreachable states only after satisfying any exam requirement to display the complete prescribed construction.

Why the proof works for every input

At zero symbols, closure records exactly the possible starts. Assume the checklist is exact after a prefix. Every legal next run must consume the next symbol from one of those states, followed by any ε moves; the update lists exactly those possibilities. No legal run is omitted and no impossible run is invented. Induction gives the exact checklist after every prefix. The final “contains an accepting state” test then agrees with NFA acceptance.

In the formula δ′(R,a)=⋃ᵣ∈ᴿ E(δ(r,a)), the prime marks the new transition function and ⋃ means collect the members from all the listed sets. It is the table procedure written compactly.

Connected check: explain why starting at {q₁} would already be wrong in this example before processing the first symbol. Then say which start-state property the proof would lose.

models.title: NFA 4 — Use free handoffs to assemble whole-language machines
models.html:
The whole idea

Union, concatenation and star are instructions about whole accepted pieces. We want machine wiring that respects those instructions. ε-arrows let us hand control from one component to another without secretly adding an extra character. That is their job here. They are not decorative buffers.

Derive the three constructions

For union, the complete input may belong to either language. Add a fresh start with ε-arrows to both old starts. Preserve both components' accepting states. One successful component is enough.

For concatenation, the input must be a valid first piece followed by a valid second piece. Add ε-arrows from each first-component accept to the second start. Keep only second-component accepts as final accepts. A candidate may guess a boundary at any successful first-piece endpoint; another candidate may keep reading in the first component. A successful run must eventually finish both obligations.

For star, the input is zero or more complete pieces from one language. Add a fresh accepting start to handle zero pieces, with an ε-arrow into the old start. From old accepting states, add ε-arrows back to the old start so another piece may begin. Keep the old accepting states accepting too: you may finish after a complete positive number of pieces.

Follow one stable example

Use A={01} throughout this example. Its NFA has S→T on 0 and T→U on 1, with S starting and U accepting. Other symbol moves are absent. For A*, add accepting start Z, Z→S on ε, and U→S on ε.

The input 0101 has a successful run:

Z --ε--> S --0--> T --1--> U --ε--> S --0--> T --1--> U

All four symbols are consumed and U accepts. The empty string accepts at Z. Input 001 fails: after its first zero the candidate is at T, which has no zero move. “Repeat pieces” does not mean you may repeat arbitrary fragments of a piece. 001 cannot be cut into complete 01 blocks.

Why the extra start matters

The slides' pages 13–14 warn against simply making the old start accepting. A different original machine might return to its start after a nonempty string that it previously rejected. Changing that state's status would newly accept the string, even if it is not a concatenation of valid old pieces.

Here is a separate counterexample, with its changed target stated explicitly: an NFA for 01 has old start S looping on 0, then S→T on 1, with T accepting. Making S accepting would accept 0. But (01)* contains no nonempty all-zero string, since every nonempty piece ends in 1. A fresh accepting start avoids that bug. It provides exactly the zero-piece option without changing the meaning of visits to old S.

Read the case definition as “whose state is this?”

The piecewise δ table preserves an old state's old moves except at the handoff points. Set union adds the new ε destination without deleting existing ε destinations. The fresh start has no ordinary input moves; its ε moves enter components. Q is the combined state set; F separately specifies where a completed input may accept. Rename overlapping component state labels first so they really are distinct states.

A correctness argument cuts an accepting run at the handoffs to recover valid pieces. In reverse, join accepting runs for valid pieces using those handoffs. That's why the construction recognizes exactly the combined language.

Next connection: regular expressions describe these same three operations as formulas. Connected check: for concatenation, explain what would go wrong if first-component accepting states remained accepting even when the second language does not contain ε.

a correctness argument cuts an accepting run at the handoffs to recover valid pieces. in reverse, join accepting runs for valid pieces using those handoffs. that's why the construction recognizes **exactly** the combined language.

models.title: Regular expressions: a recipe for a whole set of strings
models.html:
The job: describe patterns without drawing every state

A machine reads a string and gives a verdict. A regular expression describes which strings belong. Same target, different tool: a checker versus a compact recipe. Don't read a regular expression as one giant literal word. Its operations build sets of possible words.

Start with the slide expression (0∪1)0∗(0\cup1)0^*(0∪1)0∗. The first parentheses say “choose 0 or 1.” The final part says “append zero or more copies of 0.” That generates 0, 1, 00, 10, 000, 100, and so on. It cannot generate 101: after the first position, only zeros are permitted. It cannot generate the empty string: the first choice still owes us one symbol.

Three building blocks, three operations

A literal a describes the one-element language {a}. The expression ε describes {ε}, a set containing one string of length zero. The expression ∅ describes the empty language: no choices at all. Those last two are different as hell: an order containing a zero-length item versus no available item.

Operation What you actually do Example
Union R∪SR\cup SR∪S Choose a string from either recipe 0 ∪ 1 gives 0 or 1
Concatenation RSRSRS Choose from R, then from S; join in that order (0 ∪ 1)1 gives 01 or 11
Star R∗R^*R∗ Choose zero, one, or more R-strings and join them (01)* gives ε, 01, 0101, …

Star repeats its whole operand. 01* means a mandatory 0 followed by any number of ones. (01)* repeats pairs. Parentheses are doing actual work here.

The language of an expression R is written L(R)L(R)L(R). So L(1)={1}L(1)=\{1\}L(1)={1}, while L(1∗)={ε,1,11,111,…}L(1^*)=\{\varepsilon,1,11,111,\ldots\}L(1∗)={ε,1,11,111,…}. A language name such as A or E does not secretly add a star.

Build one from the requirement

“Exactly one 1” gives us three jobs: any zeros before it, the one mandatory 1, any zeros after it. Therefore 0∗10∗0^*10^*0∗10∗. For 00100, choose two zeros, then 1, then two zeros. For 00110, no choice can account for the second 1. That explains both inclusion and exclusion.

“Even length” becomes ((0∪1)(0∪1))∗((0\cup1)(0\cup1))^*((0∪1)(0∪1))∗: each repetition contributes two symbols. Zero repetitions contributes length zero, which is even. If the question requires positive even length, one pair must be mandatory. Check the boundary before celebrating.

Why machines and expressions match

For each basic expression, draw a tiny NFA. For union, concatenate, or star, use the corresponding ε-handoff construction. A complicated expression is assembled from smaller expressions; its NFA is assembled in the same shape. This is structural induction: prove the base pieces, then prove each assembly operation preserves the claim. You aren't checking infinitely many expressions one by one.

The decimal-number example, assembled from its requirements

Let D stand for a decimal digit choice, 0 through 9. The slide expression is

(+∪−∪ε)(DD∗∪DD∗.D∗∪D∗.DD∗).(+\cup-\cup\varepsilon)(DD^*\cup DD^*.D^*\cup D^*.DD^*).(+∪−∪ε)(DD∗∪DD∗.D∗∪D∗.DD∗).

The first parentheses choose a plus sign, a minus sign, or no sign. The three body alternatives cover an integer such as 72; digits followed by a dot and optional more digits such as 2.1 or 7.; or optional digits, a dot, then at least one digit such as .01. Here the dot is a literal decimal point, not a wildcard. DD* means at least one digit because its first D is mandatory.

Why not simply D*.D*? Both starred parts could choose zero digits, accepting . by itself. The mandatory D in each decimal alternative prevents that. For -.01, choose minus, then the third body alternative with zero digits before the dot and two afterward. Every chunk now has a reason.

Keep: expression operators manipulate languages; concatenation preserves order; star includes zero repetitions. Next we actually assemble an NFA from a recipe.

One connected check: In (0 ∪ 1)0*, which exact part prevents ε, and which exact part prevents 11?

models.title: RE to NFA: make each piece of the recipe executable
models.html:
The whole idea: an expression has a structure; the machine follows it

The deck builds an NFA for (ab∪a)∗(ab\cup a)^*(ab∪a)∗. Read that from the outside inward: repeat a block zero or more times; each block is either ab or a. So the machine needs a place where one block ends and another may begin. That place must also accept, because zero blocks is allowed.

Use q₁ as the start and accepting state, and q₂ as “we consumed the a of an ab block and still owe a b.” Now the arrows have reasons:

State Read a Read b
q₁ {q₁, q₂} ∅
q₂ ∅ {q₁}

From q₁ on a, one branch finishes the single-letter block a and returns to q₁. Another branch treats that same a as the first half of ab and goes to q₂. It is one input symbol consumed along two alternative interpretations. We didn't duplicate the input or require both branches to work.

Follow a whole string, including the dead branches

Trace aba. Start with {q₁}. After the first a, candidates are {q₁,q₂}. On b, q₁ contributes nothing and q₂ contributes q₁, leaving {q₁}. On the final a, candidates are {q₁,q₂} again. q₁ is present, so accept. Its successful interpretation is ab followed by a.

Trace abb. After ab, only q₁ remains. It has no b arrow, so the set becomes ∅ and the input rejects. An NFA doesn't get to resurrect a dead branch because the remaining letter is inconvenient.

ε accepts immediately at q₁. b rejects. aa accepts as a + a. These checks cover different reasons the construction might fail; they are not a proof for every string.

Where the bigger slide construction comes from

The mechanical conversion can use more states and ε arrows: build ab, build a, join them by union, then wrap the result in star. Those ε arrows route control without consuming a letter. The compact table above packages the same language more efficiently. Different state counts do not mean different answers; compare accepted strings.

To justify correctness, follow completed blocks. Every successful return to q₁ consumes either a or ab, so an accepting run spells a concatenation of permitted blocks. Conversely, any chosen sequence of those blocks has a path: take the self-return interpretation for a, or the q₂ detour for ab. That is the two-direction argument: no extras, none missing.

The reverse problem is coming

An NFA with an a-loop before a mandatory b, then arbitrary a or b afterward, has expression a∗b(a∪b)∗a^*b(a\cup b)^*a∗b(a∪b)∗. You can see it by reading the stages. Messier diagrams need a general method: remove a state while preserving the paths that used to go through it. That is the next deck's job.

Keep: give every state an unfinished obligation. The arrows become consequences of that meaning instead of random doodles.

One connected check: Does aab have a successful block decomposition? Identify it before tracing the table.

models.title: State elimination: compress journeys without losing their labels
models.html:
The job: remove a circle, preserve every possible journey

A GNFA is a finite graph whose arrows carry regular expressions. One arrow may stand for a whole chunk of input. The point is to summarize longer and longer paths until only a start and an accept state remain. Their connecting expression then describes the language.

Picture a station k that we want to erase. A trip from i to j can either avoid k or enter k, loop there some number of times, and leave. Those are the only two kinds of trip we need to account for at this elimination step.

Call the entry label R₁, loop label R₂, exit label R₃, and existing direct label R₄. The replacement is

R1R2∗R3∪R4.R_1R_2^*R_3\cup R_4.R1​R2∗​R3​∪R4​.

Read it as a sentence: enter, do any number of loops, exit; OR use the old route. This is not a spell to memorize without knowing what each chunk pays for.

Work the slide example one edge at a time

After state 1 is removed in Example 1.68, the relevant labels include:

Journey Label
start s → 2 a
2 → 2 aa ∪ b
2 → 3 ab
s → 3 b
3 → 2 ba ∪ a
3 → 3 bb
2 → accept ε
3 → accept ε

Now remove state 2. For s → 3, enter on a, loop on (aa ∪ b)*, exit on ab. Keep the direct b route too. New label: a(aa∪b)∗ab∪ba(aa\cup b)^*ab\cup ba(aa∪b)∗ab∪b.

For 3 → 3, entering 2 costs (ba ∪ a), its loop is unchanged, and returning to 3 costs ab. Keep old bb. New loop: (ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗ab∪bb(ba\cup a)(aa\cup b)^*ab\cup bb(ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗ab∪bb.

For s → accept, use a(aa ∪ b)*ε, which simplifies to a(aa ∪ b)*. For 3 → accept, keep the old ε option as well: (ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗∪ε(ba\cup a)(aa\cup b)^*\cup\varepsilon(ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗∪ε.

Notice the discipline: each new label is explained by an actual route. We don't rearrange the letters because concatenation is ordered.

Recombine the remaining routes

To finish, give the four remaining labels short temporary names: P for s→3, T for 3's loop, U for 3→accept, and V for s→accept. Removing state 3 gives PT*U ∪ V. Substitute the expressions just calculated if the question requests the full final RE. The giant final formula is only “enter, loop, exit, or go directly” again; its size hides no new operation.

Two easy places to break the construction

No edge means ∅, not ε. ∅ says “this journey is impossible.” ε says “the journey is possible while consuming nothing.” Replacing a missing edge by ε creates free travel and can change the language.

But a missing loop contributes ∅∗={ε}\emptyset^*=\{\varepsilon\}∅∗={ε} as a language: take zero loops. Thus an entry and exit can still form a route even if k has no self-loop. Zero visits around the loop is different from a free entrance into k.

Update every remaining ordered pair, including self-loops, using the labels before deleting k. Then remove k and its incident edges. Mixing half-updated labels can accidentally account for paths multiple times or produce the wrong expression structure.

Keep: eliminate a state by replacing its possible journeys, not by deleting its behavior. The next deck makes this route argument a formal conversion algorithm.

One connected check: If i→k is a, k has no loop, k→j is b, and i→j is c, what two kinds of journey must the new label preserve?

models.title: GNFA conversion: why the elimination algorithm preserves the language
models.html:
The mental model: each arrow is a summary of hidden paths

At the beginning, most labels are single symbols. After states are removed, an arrow summarizes all the ways to travel between its endpoints through the already-removed states. That sentence is the invariant: the fact we maintain after every step. It is what makes the final expression trustworthy.

A regular expression on an arrow describes a set of strings, not one action like a DFA's single-symbol move. Traversing an ε-labeled arrow consumes nothing; an ∅ label permits no traversal. A run can split its input into chunks matching its arrow labels.

First put the graph in the required shape

Add a fresh start s with an ε arrow to the old start. Add a fresh sole accept f; put ε arrows from each old accepting state to f. Old accepting states become ordinary states. Now no arrow needs to enter s, and no arrow needs to leave f. The fresh endpoints prevent us from accidentally deleting the boundary of an accepting computation.

If two arrows share endpoints, combine labels by union. Fill missing permitted connections with ∅. This gives a label for every ordered pair whose source is not f and whose destination is not s.

The formal line

δ:(Q−{f})×(Q−{s})→R\delta:(Q-\{f\})\times(Q-\{s\})\to\mathcal Rδ:(Q−{f})×(Q−{s})→R

says: choose a source state other than f and a destination other than s; receive a regular expression. Here Q is the state set; − removes the named element; × forms ordered pairs; R\mathcal RR means the collection of regular expressions. Unlike a DFA transition table, the second input to this δ is a destination state, not an alphabet symbol.

DFA and NFA use the same preparation

A DFA already has single-symbol labels. An NFA may have parallel arrows and ε arrows. Both can be put into the GNFA shape directly. NFA→GNFA does not require subset construction first: the GNFA still allows alternative paths. Subset construction solves a different job—making a deterministic one-symbol-at-a-time machine.

For example, if an NFA has both 0 and ε arrows from p to q, the GNFA label is 0 ∪ ε. It means either consume one zero or consume nothing on that connection. It does not mean consume both.

Why one elimination is valid

Remove k. Any old path between surviving states can be split at its encounters with surviving states. A segment through k consists of entry, zero or more k-loops, and exit. The replacement expression records exactly those segments. Conversely, any string chosen from a replacement label can be expanded back into an old path. Both directions matter: preserving old paths alone would still permit accidentally adding new ones.

Each step removes one state. Since the graph began finite, eventually just s and f remain. Their edge describes exactly the original accepting paths. That proves termination and correctness for different reasons: fewer states gives termination; preserved path language gives correctness.

Keep: DFA/NFA→GNFA→RE compresses paths. NFA→DFA tracks candidate states. Different destination objects, different construction.

One connected check: Why would adding a fresh accepting state with a 1 arrow, instead of ε, change the language?

models.title: Pumping lemma: finite memory eventually repeats itself
models.html:
The question: when is a finite number of states not enough?

A DFA can remember parity with two states. Could it remember the exact number of leading zeros so it can demand that many ones afterward? For {0n1n:n≥0}\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}{0n1n:n≥0}, the number may be arbitrarily large. “It needs to count” is a useful suspicion, but not yet a proof: plenty of counting tasks only need a remainder. We need a consequence that every DFA must obey.

Suppose a DFA has p states. Read p symbols. The computation has visited p+1 state positions: the initial state plus one after each symbol. With only p different states, some state was visited twice. That's the pigeonhole principle: more visits than available distinct places forces a repeat.

A repeat turns a path into a reusable loop

Split the input into three consecutive pieces. x gets us to the repeated state the first time. y takes us around the loop back to that same state. z finishes the original accepting journey.

Because the state after y is exactly the state before y, the rest of the machine cannot tell whether we took that loop zero times, once, twice, or a hundred times. Following z afterward still reaches accept. The DFA has no secret memory outside its current state. That's the whole damn mechanism.

The notation xyizxy^izxyiz means x, then i copies of y, then z. With i=0, y disappears; with i=1, it is the original string; with i=2, y is duplicated. We are editing a substring, not moving letters around.

Decode the theorem in its actual order

If L is regular, there exists a pumping length p such that every s in L with length at least p can be split as s=xyz satisfying:

  1. ∣y∣>0|y|>0∣y∣>0: the loop consumes at least one symbol.
  2. ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p: the loop fits within the first p symbols.
  3. xyiz∈Lxy^iz\in Lxyiz∈L for every integer i≥0: every repetition count still works.

∣y∣|y|∣y∣ is the number of symbols in y. ∈\in∈ means “is a member of.” The theorem promises at least one suitable split, not every split. p belongs to the assumed machine; we don't get to declare p=3 because that makes an example convenient.

Why this helps prove impossibility

To show a language is not regular, assume a DFA exists and receive its unknown p. Choose a legal long string. Then show that no allowed split can keep all repetitions in the language. That contradicts the required loop property.

suppose a dfa has p states. read p symbols. the computation has visited p+1 state positions: the initial state plus one after each symbol. with only p different states, some state was visited twice. that's the pigeonhole principle: more visits than available distinct places forces a repeat.

The job: make the machine's promised loop impossible

We will prove L={0n1n:n≥0}L=\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}L={0n1n:n≥0} is not regular. Membership requires two things: all zeros precede all ones, and their counts match. 0011 belongs; 0101 has equal counts but the wrong order; 001 has the right order but wrong counts.

A proof must handle an unknown machine, unknown pumping length, and whichever legal split the theorem might supply. Checking one favorite split won't cut it. The trick is to choose a string that pins all legal loops into a useful region.

One complete proof, with the reasons exposed

Assume L is regular. Then it has a pumping length p≥1. Choose s=0p1ps=0^p1^ps=0p1p. This choice depends on p: whatever finite memory the supposed machine has, we give it that many zeros followed by that many ones. s is in L, and its length 2p is at least p, so the lemma applies.

Take any split s=xyz satisfying ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p and ∣y∣>0|y|>0∣y∣>0. The first p symbols of s are all zeros. Since x together with y ends within those first p positions, y contains only zeros. Since it is nonempty, y=0ky=0^ky=0k for some k with 1≤k≤p.

Choose i=0. The pumped string is xz=0p−k1pxz=0^{p-k}1^pxz=0p−k1p. It has fewer zeros than ones because k≥1. Therefore xz is not in L. But the pumping lemma promised that every repetition count, including zero, remains in L. Contradiction. Thus L is not regular.

Where the proof actually earns its conclusion

The phrase “take any split” is backed by the argument about the first p positions. We never selected x or y ourselves. If someone gives us a different legal x and y, its y still consists of k≥1 zeros, and the same failure still happens.

For a concrete illustration, let p=4 and s=00001111. Maybe y is the first zero; maybe it is the middle two zeros; maybe it is all four. Deleting it always leaves fewer than four zeros and still four ones. The illustration helps you see the mechanism; the variable-k argument proves all p and all legal splits.

Why the exact language matters

The slide discussion also considers strings with equal numbers of zeros and ones in any order. If a proof says “pumping creates a 0 after a 1, so reject,” that only works for the ordered-block language. It fails for the unordered equal-count language: order is allowed there.

The prefix-bound proof above still works for that second language. Choose the same witness, force y to contain only zeros, and break the counts. Notice the repair: we used a condition that actually defines the target language.

What to write under exam conditions

State the assumption; introduce the unknown p; choose and validate s; describe every legal y; choose i; show a precise failed membership condition; conclude contradiction. Those are logical obligations, not decorative sentences.

Keep: the witness is your choice; the decomposition is not. Use the prefix bound to control every decomposition. Next we adapt this strategy when the failed condition is duplication or a square length.

One connected check: If the target language were all strings containing at least one 1, which line of this proof would stop giving a contradiction?

models.title: Pumping variations: choose a weakness, then design the witness
models.html:
The mental model: control the damage, don't memorize one string

Pumping proofs have a fixed negotiation. You assume regularity; the lemma supplies p; you choose a sufficiently long member s; the hypothetical machine gets a legal split; you choose a repetition count that makes membership fail. The order matters. You must beat every legal split of your chosen s, not just a convenient one.

Write the plan in ordinary words first: “The loop is trapped in this region. Changing that region destroys this relationship.” Then translate the relationship into counts, positions, or arithmetic.

Variation 1: a word repeated twice

Let L={ww:w∈{0,1}∗}L=\{ww:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}L={ww:w∈{0,1}∗}. Here w is any binary string, and ww means two identical copies, in the same order. Choose s=0p1 0p1s=0^p1\,0^p1s=0p10p1. This is a member: its two copies are both 0p10^p10p1.

For every legal split, the bound ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p forces y=0ky=0^ky=0k with 1≤k≤p. Pump down to get 0p−k1 0p10^{p-k}1\,0^p10p−k10p1.

Why can't this be some different word repeated twice? Don't merely say “the original halves differ”—maybe the dividing point moved. There are exactly two 1s, and the whole string ends in 1. In a square tt, each identical half must therefore contain one 1 and end in 1. Each half is a block of zeros followed by one 1, with the same number of zeros. Our two zero blocks have lengths p−k and p, which differ. No alternate split can save it.

That extra argument closes a real proof gap. A drawing of two unequal old halves would not.

Variation 2: square lengths

Let L={1n2:n≥0}L=\{1^{n^2}:n\ge0\}L={1n2:n≥0}. A string belongs exactly when its length is 0,1,4,9,16,… . Choose s=1p2s=1^{p^2}s=1p2. Its length is at least p. Every legal nonempty y has length k with 1≤k≤p.

Pump up once, i=2. The new length is p²+k. It is bigger than p² but smaller than the next square:

p2<p2+k≤p2+p<(p+1)2=p2+2p+1.p^2<p^2+k\le p^2+p<(p+1)^2=p^2+2p+1.p2<p2+k≤p2+p<(p+1)2=p2+2p+1.

There is no square strictly between consecutive squares, so the pumped word is outside L. The argument works for every k in the allowed range. Pumping down is less convenient: for p=1 and k=1 it gives length zero, which is a square. Choosing i=2 avoids that boundary trap.

What the quantifiers are saying

∃\exists∃ means “there exists”; ∀\forall∀ means “for every.” The lemma says a regular language has some p that works for every long member, with some legal split working for every repetition count. To refute it, show that for every proposed p, you can find a bad member for which every legal split has some failing repetition count.

Negating the order correctly prevents the classic bullshit proof where you choose a bad split and act as though no good split exists.

Keep: control where y lives, then identify a condition that any nonzero change destroys. Pumping is about the language's structure, not just its surface notation.

One connected check: In the square-length proof, why do we need the upper bound k≤p, rather than only k>0?

models.title: CFGs: a variable is unfinished work, a terminal is finished output
models.html:
Start with what a grammar is trying to do

A DFA checks a completed string. A grammar builds strings. We still care about a language—a set of completed strings—but now ask which ones the construction rules can produce. There is no input head and no accepting circle in a grammar.

The deck's grammar is:

A→0A1∣B,B→#.A\to0A1\mid B,\qquad B\to\#.A→0A1∣B,B→#.

A and B are variables: placeholders for unfinished work. 0, 1, and # are terminals: finished output symbols that stay put. A is the starting variable. The vertical bar means “or,” so A has two alternative rules. The arrow means “you may replace this variable with that right-hand side.”

Run the rules all the way to completion

Begin with A. Choose its wrapping rule three times, then finish:

A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111⇒000B111⇒000#111.A\Rightarrow0A1\Rightarrow00A11\Rightarrow000A111\Rightarrow000B111\Rightarrow000\#111.A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111⇒000B111⇒000#111.

At 00A11, the zeros and ones are already output. A is the one unfinished job between them. Applying A→0A1 replaces that A, leaving its surrounding output untouched. We didn't replace the entire line with 0A1.

Each wrapping adds one zero on the left and one one on the right. Switching to B stops the wrapping; B→# puts a separator in the middle. Therefore the generated language is {0n#1n:n≥0}\{0^n\#1^n:n\ge0\}{0n#1n:n≥0}. n is the number of wraps. With zero wraps, A→B→# gives #. ε is not generated: no rule finishes with no terminal at all.

Why this can do what a DFA cannot

The growing expression stores unfinished structure. Every additional wrap leaves one more 1 waiting on the right. A finite grammar can describe arbitrarily deep nesting because its rules can reuse a variable. The finite rulebook does not impose a fixed bound on the size of a derivation.

A parse tree records the same construction as a tree. A node labeled A has children 0, A, 1 when that rule is used. Read the terminal leaves left to right to recover the completed string. The tree preserves who created whom, which a final string alone does not show.

Decode the formal package

G=(V,Σ,R,S)G=(V,\Sigma,R,S)G=(V,Σ,R,S) names a grammar. V is its finite set of variables; Σ is its finite terminal alphabet; R is its finite rule set; S is the starting variable. In this example S—the formal slot name—is filled by the variable A. The actual start does not have to be called S.

uAv⇒uwvuAv\Rightarrow uwvuAv⇒uwv says a rule A→w can replace A wherever it appears, with the same surrounding strings u and v retained. “Context-free” means the rule does not inspect those surroundings before permitting replacement. ⇒∗\Rightarrow^*⇒∗ means zero or more derivation steps.

The last slide adds two different ways to grow structure

For S→aSb|SS|ε, interpret a as an opening parenthesis and b as a closing one. S→aSb wraps one balanced structure inside a matched pair. S→SS places two balanced structures side by side. S→ε finishes with nothing. For aabbab, one derivation is S⇒SS⇒aSbS⇒aaSbbS⇒aabbS⇒aabbaSb⇒aabbab. Each arrow replaces one S.

Equal counts alone are insufficient: ba has one of each but closes before anything opens. A balanced-parentheses string must have equal final counts and every prefix must contain at least as many openings as closings. Wrapping and concatenation preserve both conditions. Conversely, split a nonempty balanced string after the close matching its first opening: inside that pair and after it are smaller balanced strings, exactly the wrapping and side-by-side jobs. This connects grammar rules to nested structure, the reason stacks will be useful.

What a correctness proof has to establish

Every derivation here produces matching outer blocks because each wrap adds exactly one of each symbol and the only finishing option inserts #. Conversely, any desired n can be produced by choosing n wraps then finishing. This proves both “no wrong strings” and “every required string.” Merely deriving 000#111 proves only one example.

Keep: variables are pending jobs; rules replace one pending job; terminals are finished output. Next we use grammar structure to control arithmetic grouping and identify ambiguity.

One connected check: At 00A11, why can the next step produce 000A111 but not 000A11?
