models.title: Grammar structure: the same string can carry different meanings
models.html:
The question: who belongs together?

The characters in a+a×a do not visibly say which operation groups first. A grammar can encode that structure. In the deck's layered grammar,

E→E+T∣T,T→T×F∣F,F→(E)∣a,E\to E+T\mid T,\quad T\to T\times F\mid F,\quad F\to(E)\mid a,E→E+T∣T,T→T×F∣F,F→(E)∣a,

E means an expression built from terms, T a multiplication-level term, and F an atomic factor: a single a or a parenthesized expression. These names are helpful meanings assigned to variables; the rules do the enforcing.

Build the example and see why precedence emerges

A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining variable:

E⇒E+T⇒T+T⇒F+T⇒a+T⇒a+T×F⇒a+F×F⇒a+a×F⇒a+a×a.E\Rightarrow E+T\Rightarrow T+T\Rightarrow F+T\Rightarrow a+T\Rightarrow a+T\times F\Rightarrow a+F\times F\Rightarrow a+a\times F\Rightarrow a+a\times a.E⇒E+T⇒T+T⇒F+T⇒a+T⇒a+T×F⇒a+F×F⇒a+a×F⇒a+a×a.

The final top-level split is E+T. The multiplication lives inside the right T. A factor can contain a whole addition only by using F→(E), which prints parentheses. That's why (a+a)×a has a different structure and different visible parentheses. The grammar is not calculating a numerical answer; it determines the syntactic grouping first.

Ambiguity means two trees, not two scheduling choices

Now use the flatter grammar E→E+E∣E×E∣(E)∣aE\to E+E\mid E\times E\mid(E)\mid aE→E+E∣E×E∣(E)∣a. It can build a+a×a with the root operation +, or with the root operation ×. The root-+ tree groups a+(a×a); the root-× tree groups (a+a)×a, even though the generated string has no parentheses.

Two corresponding leftmost derivations are:

E⇒E+E⇒a+E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a,E\Rightarrow E+E\Rightarrow a+E\Rightarrow a+E\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times a,E⇒E+E⇒a+E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a,

E⇒E×E⇒E+E×E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a.E\Rightarrow E\times E\Rightarrow E+E\times E\Rightarrow a+E\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times E\Rightarrow a+a\times a.E⇒E×E⇒E+E×E⇒a+E×E⇒a+a×E⇒a+a×a.

That is a complete ambiguity witness: same terminal string, different parse structures, certified here by different leftmost derivations. If you merely expand independent left and right children in a different order, you may still get the same tree. That's scheduling, not ambiguity.

A grammar can be ambiguous even if another grammar for the same language is unambiguous. An inherently ambiguous language is stronger: every CFG generating it is ambiguous. Keep the object straight—one rulebook versus the whole language.

Designing a grammar by splitting the job

For {0n1n}∪{1n0n}\{0^n1^n\}\cup\{1^n0^n\}{0n1n}∪{1n0n}, a new start chooses which subgrammar to run. One wraps zeros around ones; the other wraps ones around zeros. Union means either branch may generate the string; neither branch has to satisfy both descriptions.

Keep: grammar rules encode structure, not just a bag of output strings. Next, CNF standardizes the shape of those rules while preserving the language.

now use the flatter grammar \(e\to e+e\mid e\times e\mid(e)\mid a\). it can build `a+a×a` with the root operation `+`, or with the root operation `×`. the root-`+` tree groups `a+(a×a)`; the root-`×` tree groups `(a+a)×a`, even though the generated string has no parentheses.

two corresponding leftmost derivations are:

\[e\rightarrow e+e\rightarrow a+e\rightarrow a+e\times e\rightarrow a+a\times e\rightarrow a+a\times a,\]

\[e\rightarrow e\times e\rightarrow e+e\times e\rightarrow a+e\times e\rightarrow a+a\times e\rightarrow a+a\times a.\]

that is a complete ambiguity witness: **same terminal string, different parse structures**, certified here by different leftmost derivations. if you merely expand independent left and right children in a different order, you may still get the same tree. that's scheduling, not ambiguity.

a grammar can be ambiguous even if another grammar for the same language is unambiguous. an **inherently ambiguous language** is stronger: every cfg generating it is ambiguous. keep the object straight—one rulebook versus the whole language.

## designing a grammar by splitting the job

for \(\{0^n1^n\}\cup\{1^n0^n\}\), a new start chooses which subgrammar to run. one wraps zeros around ones; the other wraps ones around zeros. union means either branch may generate the string; neither branch has to satisfy both descriptions.

a dfa can also become a grammar. give each state qᵢ a variable rᵢ. for an arrow qᵢ—`a`→qⱼ, add rᵢ→arⱼ. for each accepting state, add rᵢ→ε, allowing generation to finish there. a derivation now writes exactly the labels of a successful machine path. this connects checking to building.

**keep:** grammar rules encode structure, not just a bag of output strings. next, cnf standardizes the shape of those rules while preserving the language.

**one connected check:** why do two different leftmost derivations give stronger evidence of ambiguity than two derivations with unrestricted expansion order?

models.title: CNF: turn every big job into two smaller jobs or one finished symbol
models.html:
Why the hell are we rewriting the grammar?

A rule can currently do several things at once: print terminals, create three pending jobs, hand off to one other variable, or produce nothing. That flexibility is convenient for writing a grammar, but awkward for algorithms that must reason about every derivation.

Chomsky normal form, CNF, limits a rule to one of two ordinary shapes:

A→BCorA→a.A\to BC\qquad\text{or}\qquad A\to a.A→BCorA→a.

The first splits one pending job into two pending jobs. The second finishes one job by printing one terminal. Capital letters here stand for variables, lowercase a for a terminal. They are shape examples, not the only letters allowed.

If ε belongs to the language, the new start may also have a rule to ε; that start must not appear on a right-hand side. CNF is a format for a grammar. It does not mean the language becomes regular, deterministic, or unambiguous.

Picture a job ticket. “Print a” completes it. “Do B, then C” tears it into two ordered subtickets. A variable is the ticket's label, not output printed on the page. This analogy maps only the pending-work structure: it does not introduce a real worker, time cost, or a rule that jobs must take equal time. CNF makes every ticket use one of those two shapes.

First understand what “can disappear” means

Use the slide grammar:

S→ASA∣aB,A→B∣S,B→b∣ε.S\to ASA\mid aB,\quad A\to B\mid S,\quad B\to b\mid\varepsilon.S→ASA∣aB,A→B∣S,B→b∣ε.

B can finish with nothing via B→ε, so B is nullable. A can disappear too: A→B→ε. S cannot: every completed S derivation eventually uses an aB, so at least one a remains.

Nullable does not mean “delete this variable everywhere.” B can also produce b. Removing that possibility would mutilate the language. Nullable means we must preserve both choices: it may contribute something, or contribute nothing.

The crucial example: two A occurrences are two independent jobs

In S→ASA, the left A and right A are separate occurrences. Each may disappear. So retain these four right-hand sides:

Left A Right A Result
keep keep ASA
keep omit AS
omit keep SA
omit omit S

The middle S stays: it is not nullable. Do not omit it just because its letter looks like another variable. The choices are based on derivability of ε, not typography.

S→aB additionally supplies S→a when B disappears. We are replacing the effect of an ε-producing subtree with a shorter parent rule. That is why deleting ε rules after adding alternatives preserves nonempty strings.

Remove handoffs, then package large right-hand sides

A unit rule A→B only delegates to another variable without printing anything. Replace it by B's possible nonunit work. For chains, follow all reachable unit links. For cycles, collect reachable variables once; looping around forever contributes no completed terminal output.

Then aB must become two variables: introduce U→a and replace it by UB. ASA has three variables; introduce A₁→SA and replace it by AA₁. The helper is a package for the last two jobs. It does not reorder them.

With a fresh start S₀ and the slide's simplifications, a final CNF grammar is:

S0→AA1∣UB∣a∣AS∣SAS→AA1∣UB∣a∣AS∣SAA→b∣AA1∣UB∣a∣AS∣SAA1→SAU→aB→b. \begin{aligned} S_0&\to AA_1\mid UB\mid a\mid AS\mid SA\\ S&\to AA_1\mid UB\mid a\mid AS\mid SA\\ A&\to b\mid AA_1\mid UB\mid a\mid AS\mid SA\\ A_1&\to SA\qquad U\to a\qquad B\to b. \end{aligned} S0​SAA1​​→AA1​∣UB∣a∣AS∣SA→AA1​∣UB∣a∣AS∣SA→b∣AA1​∣UB∣a∣AS∣SA→SAU→aB→b.​

Each ordinary right-hand side is two variables or one terminal. There is no S₀→ε because the original language did not contain ε.

What the normal form buys us

For a nonempty string of length n, a CNF parse tree has n terminal-producing leaves and n−1 binary splits: 2n−1 rule applications. The grammar may still have many possible trees, but each tree's size is now tied to the input length. Later, this gives finite algorithms for membership.

Keep: nullable removal preserves disappearing jobs; unit removal bypasses pure handoffs; helpers preserve ordered work while standardizing its size. Next we make these operations systematic enough to survive cycles and repeated variables.

One connected check: Why does replacing ASA only by AS lose a possibility, even though AS is one correct alternative?

models.title: CNF as a controlled rewrite: preserve choices at every stage
models.html:
The mental model: change the wiring, keep the possible outputs

Every conversion stage should answer the same question: “How can I reconstruct an old derivation from this new one, and a new derivation from an old one?” If you only check that the final grammar looks like CNF, you can still have the wrong language. Format and equivalence are separate obligations.

We need an order because one repair can create the next kind of unwanted rule. Removing ε rules can create unit rules, so doing unit removal first would leave new handoffs behind.

Step 1: protect the start and find all nullable variables

Create S₀→S, with fresh S₀ appearing on no right-hand side. If the original grammar can generate ε, only this protected start will keep that ability in the final CNF.

Find nullable variables by repeated marking. First mark variables with a direct ε rule. Then mark A whenever it has a rule whose entire right-hand side consists of already-nullable variables. A terminal blocks this: a printed a cannot disappear. Repeat until a full pass adds nothing. This is a fixed point: further application changes nothing.

Why repeat? In A→B, B→C, C→ε, A is nullable indirectly. One left-to-right scan could miss it depending on rule order. With finitely many variables, each productive pass adds a mark and the process eventually stops.

Step 2: replace disappearing subtrees with explicit choices

For each rule, choose independently which nullable occurrences to omit. Keep the original rule too. For X→ABA with A nullable and B not nullable, the possibilities are ABA, AB, BA, B. The two As share a variable name but represent separate positions in a derivation.

Do not retain an ordinary empty right-hand side after this stage. Preserve S₀→ε exactly when the original start was nullable. Then remove the original ε rules from other variables.

Cycles need no special magic. With S→B|ε and B→S|ε, both variables are nullable; the language is just {ε}. The protected start may generate ε, but there is no terminal-producing work to invent. A conversion that manufactures a from this grammar is obviously wrong.

Here's the bit that makes the omission rule click. In an old derivation, a nullable variable might spend five steps becoming ε. In the new grammar, its parent can choose an alternative that leaves that position out immediately. Same finished word; fewer internal moves. We preserve the possible output, not the exact history of how it got printed.

Step 3: follow unit reachability, then copy real work

A unit rule has exactly one variable on its right, such as A→B. For each A, find every B reachable by zero or more unit rules. Copy every nonunit B-production onto A. Then remove unit rules.

Example: A→B, B→C, C→a|DE. A needs A→a|DE, and B needs B→a|DE. C keeps its original alternatives. The slides' CNF2 page 3 wording about removing B→u should not be read as deleting the nonunit production being copied; doing that can destroy valid outputs. Retain the useful nonunit rules.

Step 4: make terminal leaves and binary splits explicit

For X→aBCd, use U→a and V→d, then X→UBCV. Break the four-variable sequence into a chain, for example X→UH₁, H₁→BH₂, H₂→CV. Reading the leaves still gives a, then B's output, then C's, then d. Fresh helpers prevent collisions with existing variable meanings.

A rule X→a is already valid. Do not replace it by X→U unless you also remove the new unit rule afterward. The goal is standard shape, not maximum helper count.

A final audit you can actually perform

Check every right-hand side's shape; ensure only the protected start may produce ε; ensure that start never occurs on a right-hand side; inspect repeated nullable positions; inspect unit chains and cycles; compare a few boundary strings to catch errors. Finite examples can expose a mistake, but the stage-by-stage derivation argument establishes equivalence for all strings.

Keep: compute closures first, then rewrite from the complete information. Next, a PDA will execute pending grammatical work using a stack.

One connected check: Why can removing ε rules create unit rules, and why does that determine the order of the conversion stages?

models.title: PDA: finite control plus a stack of unfinished obligations
models.html:
Why give a machine a stack?

For 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n, after reading n zeros the machine owes n matching ones. A DFA has only finitely many states, so it cannot keep a different state for every possible debt. A PDA adds a stack: a potentially unbounded pile where we can touch only the top. Push one marker per zero; pop one per one. Now the size of the debt is stored outside the finite control.

The state remembers the phase—still reading zeros, or already matching ones. The stack remembers the amount owed. Mixing those jobs makes diagrams feel random. Separating them makes the arrows follow from the requirement.

Think of each pushed zero as an IOU: “a future 1 must pay for this.” The $ marker says there are no more IOUs underneath. The control state says whether issuing new IOUs is still allowed. Once payment starts, a new zero isn't “more of the same”; it violates the required block order. That's why we need both the stack and the phase state.

Build the deck's counted-block machine

Use $ as a fresh bottom marker. It is a stack symbol, not an input symbol. Push it before processing a nonempty candidate. During the zero phase, each input 0 pushes a 0. The first 1 changes to the matching phase and pops a 0. Further ones keep popping. When the top becomes $, an ε move can remove it and enter accept.

There are no input-consuming transitions for 0 after the matching phase begins: that enforces block order. There is no matching 1 transition when only $ remains: that prevents too many ones. The original start is accepting to include ε when n=0.

Trace 0011, writing the stack top first:

Work completed Stack Meaning
initialize $ no zeros owed yet
read first 0 0$ owe one 1
read second 0 00$ owe two
read first 1 0$ owe one
read second 1 $ debt paid
finish by ε move empty enter accept with input consumed

001 leaves an unpaid marker. 00111 has an extra input symbol after the markers run out. 0101 tries to return to the zero phase. All reject, for different clauses of the language.

Read an arrow without guessing

A label a, b → c says: consume input symbol a, pop stack-top b, push c. ε in the input position consumes nothing. ε in the pop position means do not pop, not “test that the stack is empty.” ε in the push position means push nothing.

So 0, ε → 0 reads a zero and adds a marker without removing the old top. 1, 0 → ε reads a one and removes a zero marker. ε, $ → ε tests for and removes the actual bottom marker without reading input.

The formal symbols describe those three jobs

A PDA is (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,F)(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,F)(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0​,F). Q, Σ, q₀, F still mean states, input alphabet, start, accepting states. Γ is the stack alphabet. The transition type

δ:Q×Σε×Γε→P(Q×Γε)\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\times\Gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q\times\Gamma_\varepsilon)δ:Q×Σε​×Γε​→P(Q×Γε​)

takes a state, an input choice, and a pop choice; returns a set of (next state, push choice) pairs. The power set P\mathcal PP allows zero, one, or several alternatives. It is not an unordered representation of the stack—the stack itself remains ordered.

Acceptance requires some run to consume all input and finish in an accepting state. General final-state acceptance does not also require an empty stack; this construction uses $ to enforce the intended balance before accepting.

Keep: state = phase; stack = ordered pending obligations. Next we use nondeterminism when the input does not tell us which obligation to check or where the midpoint lies.

One connected check: For 001, which obligation is still on the stack, and why does entering an accepting state early not magically consume it or the remaining input?

models.title: PDA branching: one stack per candidate explanation
models.html:
The problem: the input may not announce the right plan

Consider {aibjck:i,j,k≥0, i=j or i=k}\{a^ib^jc^k:i,j,k\ge0,\ i=j\text{ or }i=k\}{aibjck:i,j,k≥0, i=j or i=k}. Read it carefully: there are three blocks in order, and either the a-count matches the b-count or it matches the c-count. Both equalities may hold, but both are not required.

A nondeterministic PDA can branch into two plans. Both store the a-count on the stack. One matches it against b's, then scans c's. The other scans b's without spending the stored markers, then matches against c's. Each branch has its own stack history. There is no shared pile that the first branch can damage for the second.

Follow a concrete case

For aabcc, the counts are i=2, j=1, k=2. The a=b branch spends one of its two markers on the sole b and still owes a b when c begins, so that branch fails. The a=c branch ignores the b, spends two markers on the two c's, and succeeds at the end of input. Therefore the NFA-style acceptance rule—at least one complete successful run—accepts the string.

A single rejecting branch does not reject the whole input. A branch that reaches an accepting state with unread input also does not accept the whole input. Keep the complete condition intact.

Another missing boundary: the midpoint of a palindrome

For {wwR:w∈{0,1}∗}\{ww^R:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}{wwR:w∈{0,1}∗}, wRw^RwR means w reversed. The first half must be matched against its reverse, so a stack's last-in-first-out behavior fits perfectly. Push the first half. At a guessed midpoint, switch by ε to popping and comparing.

Trace 0110. Push 0, then 1, giving stack 10$ top-first. Guess the midpoint. Read the next 1 and pop 1; read the last 0 and pop 0; finish at $ with no input left. The successful guess consumed exactly two symbols before switching.

Why not switch after just the first 0? The next symbol would be 1, but the stack expects 0, so that branch dies. Why not push all four symbols? Then no input remains to discharge the four markers. A bad guess failing is fine; a correct complete path is enough.

What a node in your trace must contain

A PDA configuration needs three pieces: current state, unread input, and entire stack. Two branches at the same state with different stacks are not the same configuration. Merging them as if this were NFA subset construction loses information.

A tree is useful: each node is a full configuration; each edge is one allowed transition. A table is useful too, provided each row retains all three fields. The representation is a tool, not the algorithm's definition. For an exam, label enough that a reader can check the pop condition and input consumption at every step.

Why this connects to grammars

A grammar also chooses among alternatives, some of which cannot generate the desired terminal string. A PDA can store the grammar's pending work and guess which production to use. That's the next deck: not an unrelated trick, but these same branching obligations applied to derivations.

Keep: a PDA branch carries its own state, remaining input, and stack. Nondeterminism guesses a plan; acceptance still demands that the whole plan works.

One connected check: If two branches have the same state and unread input but stacks 01$ and 10$, why can't you combine them into one stack set {0,1,$}?

for `aabcc`, the counts are i=2, j=1, k=2. the a=b branch spends one of its two markers on the sole b and still owes a b when c begins, so that branch fails. the a=c branch ignores the b, spends two markers on the two c's, and succeeds at the end of input. therefore the nfa-style acceptance rule—**at least one complete successful run**—accepts the string.

a single rejecting branch does not reject the whole input. a branch that reaches an accepting state with unread input also does not accept the whole input. keep the complete condition intact.

## another missing boundary: the midpoint of a palindrome

for \(\{ww^r:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}\), \(w^r\) means w reversed. the first half must be matched against its reverse, so a stack's last-in-first-out behavior fits perfectly. push the first half. at a guessed midpoint, switch by ε to popping and comparing.

trace `0110`. push `0`, then `1`, giving stack `10$` top-first. guess the midpoint. read the next `1` and pop `1`; read the last `0` and pop `0`; finish at `$` with no input left. the successful guess consumed exactly two symbols before switching.

why not switch after just the first `0`? the next symbol would be `1`, but the stack expects `0`, so that branch dies. why not push all four symbols? then no input remains to discharge the four markers. a bad guess failing is fine; a correct complete path is enough.

## what a node in your trace must contain

a pda configuration needs three pieces: current state, unread input, and **entire stack**. two branches at the same state with different stacks are not the same configuration. merging them as if this were nfa subset construction loses information.

a tree is useful: each node is a full configuration; each edge is one allowed transition. a table is useful too, provided each row retains all three fields. the representation is a tool, not the algorithm's definition. for an exam, label enough that a reader can check the pop condition and input consumption at every step.

## why this connects to grammars

a grammar also chooses among alternatives, some of which cannot generate the desired terminal string. a pda can store the grammar's pending work and guess which production to use. that's the next deck: not an unrelated trick, but these same branching obligations applied to derivations.

**keep:** a pda branch carries its own state, remaining input, and stack. nondeterminism guesses a plan; acceptance still demands that the whole plan works.

**one connected check:** if two branches have the same state and unread input but stacks `01$` and `10$`, why can't you combine them into one stack set `{0,1,$}`?

models.title: CFG to PDA: run the grammar as a stack of pending output
models.html:
The bridge: generating a string and checking a string can cooperate

A grammar chooses how to build output. A PDA can guess those grammar choices while checking them against the supplied input. Its stack means: this is the sequence still owed by the current derivation. The next owed symbol belongs on top, so we can deal with it first.

The deck's grammar is S→aTb∣bS\to aTb\mid bS→aTb∣b, T→Ta∣εT\to Ta\mid\varepsilonT→Ta∣ε. S either produces a single b, or an a, then T's output, then b. T can produce any number of a's. So the language consists of b and all strings of one or more a's followed by one b.

The stack is the machine's to-do list, with the next job on top. Expanding a variable breaks a job into smaller jobs. Matching a terminal checks off finished output against the actual input. Don't let the notation blur those actions together: planning an a and reading an a are two different damn steps.

There are only two kinds of work

If the stack top is a variable, replace it using a grammar production. This consumes no input, because choosing how to produce a symbol is not the same as matching an actual symbol.

If the top is a terminal, it must equal the next input symbol. Consume that input symbol and pop the matching terminal. If they disagree, that branch has no matching move. A terminal cannot be expanded into something more convenient.

Initialize with S above a fresh bottom marker $. Finish when the pending work is exhausted, by removing $ and entering accept. Input must also be fully consumed.

A complete trace of aaab

Write the stack top first; omit $ in this table only to make the pending work visible.

Move Unread input Pending stack
initialize aaab S
choose S→aTb aaab aTb
match a aab Tb
choose T→Ta aab Tab
choose T→Ta aab Taab
choose T→ε aab aab
match a ab ab
match a b b
match b ε empty

Now $ can be removed and the run can accept. Notice how T→Ta adds a pending a after T. Expanding the variable repeatedly builds more work without consuming input; terminal matching pays it off afterward.

Why pushes appear reversed on the diagram

To leave aTb top-first, physically push b first, then T, then a. The last pushed symbol is on top. That is a consequence of stack order, not a rule that reverses the generated language. If a diagram abbreviates a multi-symbol push, expand it into single pushes in that order using fresh intermediate states.

With a wrong production choice, the machine may get stuck. It can also keep choosing T→Ta forever. Such a branch does not accept. A finite successful derivation supplies a finite successful branch; existence of other bad branches doesn't invalidate it.

Why the conversion is correct

After matching a prefix of the input, the stack records the ungenerated/unmatched remainder of a chosen leftmost derivation. Variable expansion changes that remainder exactly as a grammar step would. Terminal matching removes the next symbol only when it agrees with the input.

Thus a successful run describes a grammar derivation of the entire input. Conversely, a derivation of the input tells the PDA which productions to choose, giving a successful run. This is the two-way language-equality proof; tracing aaab alone is only an illustration.

Keep: expand variables without input; match terminals with input. Next we reverse the bridge: describe a PDA's balanced stack behavior with grammar variables.

One connected check: Why would consuming an a while applying S→aTb, and then consuming another when popping that terminal a, be wrong?

models.title: PDA to CFG: name a balanced stretch of computation
models.html:
What the sixteen variables are actually for

With four PDA states, the standard conversion introduces one variable Aₚᵩ for each ordered pair of states p,q: 4×4=16 variables. That does not mean the PDA suddenly has sixteen states. We are building a grammar whose variables summarize different kinds of journey through the original machine.

Aₚᵩ means: strings consumed by a run that starts in p with an empty stack and ends in q with an empty stack. The same run pattern can sit above a protected existing stack: it may build and clear extra work but never pop below that baseline. Merely having the same stack at both endpoints is not enough if the run disturbed the protected contents in between.

The PDA first needs a single accepting state, empty-stack completion, and transitions that each push or pop one symbol. The next deck explains that normalization carefully.

Think of a balanced segment as a subroutine that promises: “Whatever stack was underneath me, I'll leave it alone and clean up everything I add.” Aₚᵩ names that contract together with its entry and exit states. The grammar doesn't store a stack snapshot. It describes strings that can be read while honoring that contract.

Two ways a balanced journey can be built

A balanced journey can consist of two balanced journeys in sequence. If r is the intermediate state, add

Apq→AprArq.A_{pq}\to A_{pr}A_{rq}.Apq​→Apr​Arq​.

The right side says: do p→r work, then r→q work. For each p,q,r, this is a possible decomposition. It doesn't say every input takes every route.

Or the journey pushes a symbol t, performs some balanced work above it, then pops that same t. If a push transition goes p→r while consuming a, and a matching pop goes s→q while consuming b, add

Apq→aArsb.A_{pq}\to aA_{rs}b.Apq​→aArs​b.

a and b may be ε. The inner variable covers the part between the push and its matching pop. The pushed symbol's identity must match; a push of 0 cannot be paired with a pop of $ just because the state arrows line up.

Finally Aₚₚ→ε permits doing nothing: same start and end state, no stack change, no input consumed.

Work the deck's four-state example

The normalized machine for positive 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n pushes $ from state 1 to 2, pushes zeros in state 2, begins popping zeros on the move to state 3, continues popping there, and pops $ from 3 to accepting 4.

Pair the outside $ push and pop: A14→A23A_{14}\to A_{23}A14​→A23​. Their input labels are both ε, so nothing is printed around the inner variable.

Pair a zero push 2→2 with the zero pop 3→3: A23→0A231A_{23}\to0A_{23}1A23​→0A23​1. Pair that push with the first zero pop 2→3: A23→0A221A_{23}\to0A_{22}1A23​→0A22​1. Use A₂₂→ε to finish the smallest balanced interior.

Now derive 0011:

A14⇒A23⇒0A231⇒00A2211⇒0011.A_{14}\Rightarrow A_{23}\Rightarrow0A_{23}1\Rightarrow00A_{22}11\Rightarrow0011.A14​⇒A23​⇒0A23​1⇒00A22​11⇒0011.

Every rule is tied to an actual push/pop pair. The matching grammar nesting reflects matching stack lifetimes.

Decode the four subscripts by their jobs

Letter Where it sits in the wrapped run
p before the outside push
r immediately after that push
s immediately before its matching pop
q after that pop

So Aₚᵩ names the whole wrapped journey, while Aᵣₛ names just the inside. The source's table lists p,r,s,q in this order to keep those roles visible. The p and q in one rule are allowed to coincide with other listed states; these letters name roles, not necessarily four distinct circles.

With four states, the full construction also lists 4³=64 concatenation rules, one for each choice of p,q,r, and four Aₚₚ→ε rules. An exam may require the complete construction even if most variables later prove useless. Counts come from choices of endpoints and middle states, not from new PDA states appearing out of nowhere.

Why the general construction needs concatenation too

A run may return to its baseline halfway through, then start a new balanced section. That isn't one push wrapped around the entire run. The concatenation rules capture these side-by-side sections. If a nonempty balanced run has no intermediate return to baseline, its first push must be matched by its final pop, which gives the wrapping case. This decomposition supports an induction on run length.

The reverse direction follows the grammar: empty rule does nothing; concatenation joins two valid runs; wrapping adds a matching push and pop around a valid inner run. That establishes exact correspondence, not just a few example strings.

Keep: Aₚᵩ is a name for balanced work between states. Four states give sixteen such names because both endpoints matter.

One connected check: In Aₚᵩ→aAᵣₛb, which two transitions determine p,r,s,q, and why must their stack symbols agree?

models.title: PDA normalization: make completion safe before converting
models.html:
The hidden issue: accepting state does not mean the stack is empty

Our general PDA accepts when a run consumes all input and finishes in an accepting state. It may still have stack contents. But the PDA→CFG construction summarizes balanced empty-to-empty runs. We therefore need an equivalent PDA that finishes with an empty stack at one designated accepting state.

This is a change of representation, not permission to change which strings accept. A cleanup gadget is correct only if it cannot help the original machine do extra input processing that used to be impossible.

Why “just add pop loops” is broken

Suppose an old accepting state has stack ba$, top first, and a future input transition needs to pop a. In the original machine that transition is blocked by the top b. If we add arbitrary ε-pop loops directly to this state, it can discard b, expose a, and resume the original transition. We have handed the machine a new way to process unread input. Shit—that changes behavior before completion, not just afterward.

The deck illustrates precisely this danger: cleanup mixed into the old control can accept a string the original PDA rejects. A final-state label is not a magical barrier against later transitions.

The safe gadget is a one-way exit

Add a fresh bottom marker under the original stack contents. Add a fresh drain state. From each old accepting state, allow an ε handoff into this drain. There, pop original stack symbols using ε transitions. When the fresh bottom marker appears, pop it and enter the sole new accepting state.

There is no way back to the old machine and no input-consuming transition in the drain. If a branch guesses completion too early, unread input remains forever, so it cannot accept. If an old accepting run has actually consumed the whole input, it can safely drain and finish. Those two observations establish the language-preserving role of the gadget.

The marker must be fresh: an old computation must not confuse it with one of its legitimate stack symbols. It marks the baseline that the old machine cannot cross.

Normalize individual transitions too

The grammar construction wants each transition to perform exactly one push or one pop. For a transition that both pops b and pushes c, use a fresh intermediate state: first perform the pop (and any input consumption), then perform an ε push of c. The intermediate state has only the intended continuation, so no other old transition can interrupt the halfway state.

For a transition that changes state but neither pushes nor pops, insert a push of a fresh temporary symbol followed by its pop. This creates a balanced two-step version of the same action. Consume the input only once across the two steps.

Fresh states and symbols are not decoration. Reusing an old state could create extra exits; reusing a marker carelessly could allow a wrong pop to match.

How this closes the CFG/PDA connection

CFG→PDA stores pending derivation work. Normalized PDA→CFG summarizes balanced runs. Together they show that context-free languages are exactly the languages recognized by PDAs. A DFA can be simulated by a PDA that ignores its stack, so every regular language is context-free. The reverse inclusion fails: the stack can handle 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n, which the pumping argument ruled out for DFAs.

Keep: cleanup must be an irreversible commitment to stop reading. Normalize safely, then apply the balanced-run grammar recipe.

One connected check: Why is an early jump to the fresh drain harmless, while early popping at an old accepting state can be harmful?

models.title: DPDA: determinism is about competing enabled moves
models.html:
One table cell isn't the whole decision

For a DFA, the current state and next input symbol select exactly one move. For a PDA, a move may read input or ε, and may pop the top or ε. Several differently labeled transitions can therefore be enabled at the same situation. Determinism must rule out those competing actions, not merely forbid two answers in one cell.

Suppose the machine is in q, the next input is 0, and the stack top is X. It could potentially use any of these:

Transition lookup What it would do
δ(q,0,X) read the zero and pop X
δ(q,0,ε) read the zero without popping
δ(q,ε,X) pop X without reading
δ(q,ε,ε) move without reading or popping

If two are available, the machine has a choice right now. Different labels do not make that choice disappear.

Read the course definition precisely

This course's DPDA definition requires exactly one of those four entries to be nonempty, for every state q, input symbol a, and stack symbol x. Each nonempty entry returns one pair (next state, symbol to push) rather than a set of alternative pairs.

Some treatments use “at most one” and permit partial transitions. For these slides and exam questions, use the stated exactly-one convention. The next deck completes missing cases with rejecting behavior.

An entry equal to ∅ means there is no transition. A pair such as (r,ε) is an actual transition to r that pushes nothing. Those are very different: no action versus a legal action with no push.

Work one collision

Suppose δ(q,0,ε)=(r,X): read 0, push X. Also suppose δ(q,ε,X)=(s,ε): pop X without reading. When the next input is 0 and the current top is X, both can run. One consumes input and increases the stack; the other consumes nothing and decreases it. Each individual entry has one output, but the machine is nondeterministic.

To repair the design, the state must distinguish the phases in which those actions are allowed, or one of the conflicting moves must be removed while preserving the intended language. Writing the arrows farther apart on the page doesn't fix the collision.

Deterministic does not mean “will accept or reject quickly”

An ε cycle may keep running without consuming the next input symbol. A configuration may become stuck when the input or stack is empty and its required action is unavailable. The four-way condition is stated over actual alphabet symbols; ε is the no-consumption option, not a real member of the input alphabet.

Acceptance is still about a computation that has consumed the whole input and is in an accepting state. Visiting an accepting state while unread input remains isn't enough. This is unlike a Turing machine's accepting halt state, which will be introduced later.

The broader connection

Nondeterminism adds no language-recognition power to DFAs versus NFAs, but deterministic PDAs are more restricted than general PDAs. A stack does not make every midpoint guess deterministic. The absence of a visible separator can matter because the machine may not know when to stop pushing and start popping.

Keep: check the four entries together for every concrete situation. The source's definition controls the required completeness. Next we apply that test to the counted-block PDA.

One connected check: Why can an ε transition conflict with a 0 transition even though ε and 0 are different labels?

models.title: Completing a DPDA: make every required choice unambiguous
models.html:
Start from the language, then audit the formal definition

The deck revisits the PDA for 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n. Its useful behavior is already clear: initialize a bottom marker, push zeros, pop for ones, and finish when the debt is paid. Now we ask a different question: does its transition table meet the course's strict DPDA definition for every state/input/top combination?

A familiar diagram can recognize the correct language yet fail that formal completeness requirement. This is why an exam may ask for a transition table, not just a plausible sketch.

Initialization controls every other possibility

If q₁ has δ(q₁,ε,ε)=(q₂,$), that action is enabled without reading or popping. For any next input a and top x, it already occupies the one allowed choice among the four entries. Thus the other potentially competing entries from q₁ must be empty. The bottom marker is pushed once, then the machine changes phase.

In q₂, zeros are read and pushed. When reading a 1, the machine must have a zero marker to pop before entering q₃. If the top is $ instead, there is no owed zero to match; send that required case to rejecting behavior.

A rejecting completion is part of the machine

Use a rejecting state qᵣ for cases that must be defined but cannot lead to acceptance. Its subsequent actions must also obey the four-way condition and prevent a return to useful accepting computation. It is not enough to scribble “reject” in a table if the formal transition type expects a pair. The deck's shortened qᵣ entries stand for a specified pair such as (qᵣ,ε) where appropriate.

Adding reject behavior is safe because it handles situations in which the original partial construction had no successful accepting continuation. It should never steal a case needed by a valid string.

Trace the subtle 011 case

Read 0: one zero marker is pushed. Read the first 1: that marker is popped, leaving $ in q₃. The ε move on $ then enters q₄ and removes the marker. But one input 1 remains.

This is not acceptance. In the slide construction, the remaining situation has no legal way to consume that final symbol and finish successfully. Reaching q₄ didn't cause a TM-style halt that ignores unread input. The whole-input condition still applies.

Also notice the determinism constraint at q₃ with top $. The ε-pop action is already the enabled choice, so an input-consuming action that also competes there must not be added. Otherwise we would break determinism while trying to “complete” the table.

A reliable way to check your answer

For each state q, each actual input symbol a, and each actual stack symbol x, examine the four entries from the previous deck as one group. Count nonempty entries; under this course definition the count must be exactly one. Separately check that each output is one legal pair, that labels use the stated alphabets, and that the start/accepting states are identified.

Then trace ε, a valid nonempty example, too few ones, too many ones, and an out-of-order zero. Those traces catch different failures. They don't replace a general invariant: zeros create obligations, ones discharge them, and phase changes forbid later zeros.

Keep: determinism, completeness, and language correctness are three checks with different jobs. Next, Turing machines replace the stack's top-only access with a rewritable tape and movable head.

One connected check: Why can filling an empty table entry with a useful transition accidentally violate determinism even if that cell previously contained ∅?

models.title: Turing machines: a finite program with a rewritable workspace
models.html:
What changes when the stack isn't enough?

A PDA can only inspect the top of its stack. A Turing machine, or TM, has a tape and a head that moves left or right. It can read a cell, overwrite it, move, and come back later. The finite state still stores the current phase of the program; the tape stores the growing work.

The tape has no fixed upper bound on usable cells. That does not mean infinitely many cells are processed in one move. At every finite point in a computation, only finitely much work has happened. “Unbounded workspace” and “infinite work for free” are completely different claims.

One transition does three specific things

δ(q,a)=(r,b,R)\delta(q,a)=(r,b,R)δ(q,a)=(r,b,R) means: in state q reading tape symbol a, write b in this cell, move the head one cell right, and enter r. With L, move left instead. At the tape's left boundary, the course model keeps the head there when it attempts to move farther left.

A blank is an actual tape symbol. ε is a zero-length string or no-consumption notation in other models. A blank cell is not “no cell,” and writing a blank is a real write operation. Tape symbols may include marks such as x that never appear in the original input alphabet.

Build the slide's matching idea: w#w

The separator # tells us where the first copy ends. On input 01#01, mark the first unprocessed left symbol, remember whether it was 0 or 1 in the finite control, cross the separator, and compare it with the first unprocessed right symbol. Mark that symbol too. Return to the left portion and repeat.

After the first round, marks stand where the two zeros were. After the second, both ones are marked too. Finally verify that no extra unmatched symbol remains on the right. Accept only then.

For 01#00, the second comparison fails. For 01#010, the first two comparisons succeed but the final leftover check fails. For malformed input with a missing or extra separator, the machine must reject through its format checks. Matching the examples isn't enough; each clause of the language needs a reason in the program.

What belongs in the seven-part definition?

(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,qaccept,qreject)(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,q_{accept},q_{reject})(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0​,qaccept​,qreject​): states; input alphabet; tape alphabet; transition rule; start; accepting halt state; rejecting halt state. Γ includes the blank and all input symbols. Σ excludes the blank. The accepting and rejecting states are distinct and halt immediately when entered.

This differs from a finite automaton or PDA: visiting their accepting state does not necessarily end the run, and acceptance is evaluated after the input is consumed. A TM's program must arrange its checks before entering accept.

The proof has two separate jobs

Correctness says successful comparisons and the final leftover check establish exactly two equal blocks. Halting says the procedure finishes: each round marks another left input symbol; each sweep crosses a finite occupied region; there are only finitely many unmarked left symbols. A convincing trace of 01#01 proves neither claim for every input, but it makes the invariant visible.

Keep: state = program phase; tape = editable memory; head = current location. Next we use repeated marking to test a numerical pattern in the input length.

One connected check: Why must the w#w machine check for extra right-side symbols after all left-side symbols have been matched?

models.title: Repeated halving: encode a numerical test as marking passes
models.html:
Read the language before reading the arrows

The deck's language is {02n:n≥0}\{0^{2^n}:n\ge0\}{02n:n≥0}. The number of zeros must be a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … . This is not 02n0^{2n}02n, which describes even lengths. 000000 has even length six, but six is not a power of two. ε has length zero and is also excluded.

The numerical idea is simple: one is a power of two; a larger odd count isn't; a larger even count is a power of two exactly when its half is. So repeatedly halve an even count until either one remains or an odd count greater than one appears.

The tape is doing the counting for us. The finite controller only needs to remember “keep this one” versus “cross this one out.” So the trick isn't stuffing the number eight or eight billion into a state label; it's leaving the work distributed across the tape and shrinking it by a rule we can justify.

How a tape implements “halve the count”

Scan the live zeros and mark every other one. States alternate between “keep the next live zero” and “cross out the next live zero.” Marks are ignored on later passes; they are old work, not new zeros. The head returns to the left boundary to start another pass.

The state alternation records parity during one sweep. It does not store the whole count. The surviving unmarked cells carry the reduced count between sweeps. This is a recurring theme: use finite control for a small phase distinction, external memory for an unbounded amount.

Follow numbers first, then align with the actual diagram

For eight zeros, the conceptual counts go 8→4→2→1, so accept. For six, they go 6→3, so reject on the odd count greater than one. For one zero, accept without demanding an even count. That last exception matters: “reject all odd counts” would reject the successful stopping condition too.

The slide machine has a representation detail: it erases the first zero to make a left marker and treats that reserved contribution as part of the represented count. Consequently, the remaining visible live zeros represent the current count minus one. Don't stare at a row with three visible live zeros and conclude the represented count must be three; it may represent four under this convention.

In the diagram, q₂ begins a pass by marking the first remaining live zero, q₃ and q₄ alternate through subsequent live zeros, and q₅ returns left. The one-zero case is detected when the reserved initial zero has no remaining live partner. The conceptual halving test and the diagram are the same algorithm with different bookkeeping.

Here is the physical bookkeeping for input 0000, at successive pass boundaries:

Tape's used portion Live zeros after the left marker Represented count
⊔000 after initialization 3 4
⊔x0x after one halving pass 1 2
⊔xxx after the next pass 0 1

⊔ is the blank used as the left marker, and x means crossed out. On the final scan q₂ finds no remaining live zero and reaches accept. This table is the bridge between the arithmetic 4→2→1 and the marks actually visible in the slide trace.

Why rejection and halting follow

If an odd represented count greater than one appears, repeated exact division by two cannot lead to one without a fractional step. Reject. If an even represented count appears, halving preserves the property of being a power of two. Every successful nonfinal round strictly decreases a positive integer count, so it cannot continue forever. Each tape pass itself traverses only a finite used region.

That is the proof skeleton: a property preserved by a transformation, a failed condition causing rejection, and a decreasing measure causing termination. These are reusable tools, not facts unique to this TM.

How to read a dense transition diagram

Annotate each state with its phase before tracing. Record state, head position, and full changed tape—not just the input symbols consumed, because this machine revisits cells. When a trace seems to contradict the high-level plan, check the encoding convention before changing the mathematics.

Keep: powers of two are detected by repeated parity checks and halving; the tape stores the shrinking population through marks. Next we formalize a whole machine snapshot and distinguish recognition from guaranteed termination.

One connected check: Why is a single even-length check insufficient for this language, and why must length one be treated separately?

models.title: Configurations: a complete snapshot, then a precise claim about termination
models.html:
A state name alone no longer describes the situation

For a DFA with fixed input position, the state was enough memory. For a TM, two visits to q can have different tape contents and head positions. A configuration must record all three: control state, tape, and head location. Otherwise a trace can silently lose the information that determines the next move.

The notation uqvu q vuqv writes the tape prefix u to the left of the head, inserts state q at the head position, and writes the scanned symbol as the first symbol of v. q is not a tape symbol; it is an annotation in the snapshot.

Decode one transition completely

Suppose a configuration is a q bc: the tape contains abc, the head reads b, and the state is q. If δ(q,b)=(r,x,R), the new configuration is ax r c. The b was overwritten by x; the head moved to c; the state became r.

If instead δ(q,b)=(r,x,L), the result is r axc: the head now reads the a to the left. The entire tape is still axc; only the placement of the state annotation differs. At the left boundary there is no earlier cell to move into, so that case follows the boundary rule separately.

This is why copying only the state sequence is not a full TM trace. You need the tape edits and head movement too.

Three possible outcomes, not two

A TM may accept, reject, or keep running forever. A recognizer for L must accept every member and must never accept a nonmember. On a nonmember it may reject or loop. A decider must halt on every input, accepting members and rejecting nonmembers.

Every decider is a recognizer. Calling a recognizer “an algorithm that answers yes or no” overstates its guarantee: on some no-instances it may never answer. You cannot turn it into a decider by getting impatient after a million steps; a genuine accepting run might take a million and one.

Read the deck's constructions as phase programs

The w#w machine alternates marking, crossing, comparing, and returning. Its return states need different jobs on the two sides of #; reaching a marked symbol on the right is not the same as reaching the last processed symbol on the left. State meanings explain why several apparently similar left-moving states exist.

The slide language is aibjcka^ib^jc^kaibjck with ij=k and i,j,k≥1: all three blocks must be nonempty. Check that format first, then use repeated matching: for each a, traverse the b-block and account for j c-symbols. Restore temporary b-marks before the next a, while keeping track of c-symbols already spent. The a-count controls the number of repetitions, and the b-count controls each repetition's cost. A final check rejects unused or insufficient c's. The slide's positivity condition rejects zero-size blocks at the format check. A variation allowing zero would need different boundary handling; don't silently change the supplied language.

Reuse the comparison routine on a whole list

Pages 13–14 ask that the binary blocks in #x₁#x₂…#xₗ all differ. Compare every pair, not only neighbors. For #0#1#0, the first and second differ, and the second and third differ, but the first and third are equal. Mark the two selected separators, copy or compare their blocks using the earlier matching routine, then advance to the next pair. With l blocks there are l(l−1)/2 pairs, so a systematic finite pair schedule terminates. The subscripts identify positions in the list, not bits inside one block.

A high-level solution still owes a proof

For any construction, state the invariant tying the marks to completed work. Then show why acceptance implies the required relation and why a valid input can complete the procedure. Finally show termination using finite scans and a finite number of progressing rounds. “It keeps trying until it works” is not a halting argument.

Keep: a configuration is a snapshot; a recognizer may loop on nonmembers; a decider always finishes. Next, multiple tapes make programs easier to organize without changing which languages are computable.

models.title: Multiple tapes: give each part of the job its own workspace
models.html:
The mental model: several work surfaces, one finite controller

A multitape TM has several tapes, each with its own head. It can keep the input on one tape and scratch work on another. This can make a program much easier to describe. It does not mean separate independent machines are voting on an answer: one control state selects a joint transition from the symbols currently under all heads.

For k tapes, a transition reads a k-tuple of symbols and returns a new state, k replacement symbols, and k movement choices. A tuple is ordered. The first entry belongs to tape 1, the second to tape 2, and so on. Swapping the entries can change the computation.

One step uses one shared snapshot

Suppose two heads currently read (0, blank). A transition may write (x,0) and move (R,R). Both decisions are based on the original pair. Do not write x on tape 1 and then use some half-updated situation to choose tape 2's action. The transition is one joint instruction.

A stay-put movement S is a convenient extension. It can be simulated in a left/right-only model using a right move followed by a left move, with an intermediate state preserving the required control information. The order matters at the left boundary: left then right would not restore the original position there.

The slide example: even positive unary input

The deck works with input 02n0^{2n}02n, n≥1, and constructs a machine that doubles it. This is an even-positive-length requirement, not the earlier powers-of-two language 02n0^{2^n}02n. 000000 meets the input pattern here even though its length is not a power of two.

models.title: One tape simulates many: encode the whole situation, then update it
models.html:
The job: replace convenient hardware with an encoding

A multitape machine has k tapes and k head positions. A single tape can store their finite used contents as separated blocks, for example #block₁#block₂#…#blockₖ#. Use a marked version of a symbol to indicate each simulated head's position. The delimiter and marked symbols are extra members of the simulator's finite tape alphabet.

The representation must retain both the data and the head locations. Merely joining the tape contents loses which cell each simulated head reads next. That's the same lesson as configurations: an encoding has to preserve everything needed to determine the next step.

Simulate one joint step in phases

First sweep across the encoded blocks and read each marked symbol. Remember the k-symbol tuple in the simulator's finite control. This is possible because k and the simulated tape alphabet are fixed for this machine, so there are only finitely many possible tuples.

Use the simulated transition function to determine the new state, writes, and movements. Make another sweep to update each marked cell and move the head marker to its neighbor. Different blocks may move their heads in different directions, but all updates come from the same old snapshot.

For example, if the simulated heads read (0,1) and the rule writes (x,0) with movements (R,L), the simulator must find those two marked cells, replace their contents, and move the two markers appropriately. It must not let the new x influence the choice of the second write.

What if a simulated tape needs more room?

If a head moves past its block's currently represented end, insert a blank cell into that block. Shift later encoded cells right to make space. A finite-control carry can move symbols one by one; this is tedious but implementable. The block remains a faithful representation of a tape with additional blank cells available.

The simulation is allowed to use many real steps for one simulated step. Computability asks whether the same answers can be produced at all, not whether the hardware has identical speed.

The invariant is the proof

At the beginning of each simulated step, the single-tape encoding represents exactly the multitape machine's complete configuration. Initialization establishes this. Reading the stored head tuple and applying the same transition preserves it. Therefore each finite accepting or rejecting computation is reproduced, and an endless simulated computation continues rather than being falsely turned into a halt.

Conversely, a multitape machine can ignore extra tapes and behave like a one-tape machine. The two simulations establish equal recognition and decision power.

Why this matters later

We can design algorithms using convenient multiple tapes, then know a standard TM can implement them. In complexity theory we revisit this exact construction and count its cost: scanning and shifting a growing representation can turn t simulated steps into roughly quadratic work. Same computability is compatible with different efficiency.

Keep: encode complete configurations; preserve them one simulated step at a time. The proof is an invariant plus a way to implement each update.

One connected check: What information would be lost if the encoding included tape contents and separators but no marked head positions?

models.title: Nondeterministic TMs: a tree of possible complete computations
models.html:
What branches now?

An NTM can have several legal actions for the same state and scanned symbol. Each action creates a possible next configuration: state, tape contents, and head position. As choices accumulate, the computation forms a tree. Branches are alternative histories, not multiple heads sharing one mutable tape.

A string accepts if at least one branch reaches accept after finitely many steps. A rejecting branch alone doesn't settle the input. A branch that loops also doesn't accept. The whole existential claim is: is there a finite successful computation somewhere in the tree?

A pattern example makes the guessing concrete

To recognize strings containing aab, one branch can keep scanning while another guesses “the occurrence starts here.” The checking branch then demands a, a, b in sequence. A wrong guess fails locally; a correct occurrence supplies a successful branch. This is the NFA idea with TM configurations behind it.

The word “guess” is mathematical shorthand for allowing all permitted choices as branches. It is not a probability claim and not a promise that a real computer luckily picks the right one.

A more useful guess: a factorization witness

For unary compositeness, input 0ⁿ represents the integer n. Guess integers p and q with 2≤p,q≤n−1, then verify pq=n. For n=6, the branch choosing p=2,q=3 succeeds. Guesses such as 2 and 2 fail their multiplication check. For a prime input, no legal pair succeeds.

The range bound matters. If the machine generates arbitrarily long guesses with no stopping bound, some branches may guess forever. For an NTM decider, every branch must halt. Bounding the guesses and using terminating arithmetic checks gives that guarantee. Acceptance can be existential while termination is required branch by branch.

Why tracing just the states is especially wrong here

Two branches may reach the same control state with different guessed factors on tape. Their later verification differs. You cannot merge them merely because both circles are named q. An NFA's finite state-set method does not directly apply to TMs: tape configurations can be arbitrarily large and there can be infinitely many of them.

A trace tree should show enough of each configuration to distinguish the guesses or edits. When proving correctness, identify what an accepting branch certifies: here, two nontrivial integer factors whose product is exactly the input number.

The obvious simulation idea has a trap

A deterministic simulator might try the first branch to completion, then the second. But the first can loop forever while the second accepts in ten steps. Waiting for completion would miss an available yes-answer. We need a fair schedule that never lets one infinite branch hog all the attention. That's why the next deck uses breadth-first exploration.

Keep: nondeterminism means existence of a successful branch; a branch carries a full configuration; a decider must halt on every branch.

One connected check: If one branch rejects, one loops, and one accepts after twenty steps, what determines the NTM's acceptance—and why would depth-first simulation be dangerous?

models.title: Fair simulation: don't let one endless branch hide a short success
models.html:
The problem is scheduling, not lucky guessing

To simulate an NTM deterministically, we must eventually inspect every finite candidate computation. A depth-first strategy can get trapped following an infinite branch. Breadth-first search explores all branches to depth 0, then 1, then 2, and so on. A successful branch of depth d is eventually inspected because only finitely many nodes occur at each earlier depth.

The finite branching condition matters: the transition table supplies finitely many choices per step. Without it, “finish this level before the next” might itself require infinite work.

How the three-tape simulation organizes the work

One tape preserves the original input. Another simulates a candidate branch's working tape. A third records an address: a finite sequence of transition-choice numbers. If at most three choices are available, addresses begin 1,2,3,11,12,13,21,… in length order.

To inspect address 213, reset the work tape to the input, choose option 2 on the first step, option 1 on the second, and option 3 on the third. If a requested option doesn't exist, discard that candidate. If accept is reached along the replay, accept. Then move on to the next address. No single replay is allowed to run past the address's finite length.

These addresses describe choices, not tape cell positions. Replaying from the original input prevents edits from one branch contaminating another.

Why every accepting branch is eventually found

Suppose the NTM accepts in d steps along choices c₁…c_d. There are finitely many shorter addresses and finitely many addresses of length d before that one. Each replay takes finitely many steps. Eventually the simulator replays the successful sequence and accepts.

If the NTM never accepts, the simulator never invents acceptance: every replay uses actual legal transitions. It may search forever. That is acceptable when simulating a recognizer, whose no-instances need not halt.

What changes for a decider?

If every NTM branch halts on a fixed input, and branching is finite, the whole computation tree is finite. The reason is subtler than “each branch is finite, so there are finitely many branches.” If a finitely branching tree had nodes at arbitrarily large depths, one child of the root would have arbitrarily deep descendants; then one child of that child would too; continuing would construct an infinite branch. That contradicts the all-branches-halt assumption.

A breadth-first simulator can therefore maintain the live frontier and reject when no live configuration remains and none accepted. It must actually detect exhaustion; endlessly enumerating meaningless longer addresses without checking completion would not itself be a decider.

What the theorem does and doesn't establish

Deterministic and nondeterministic TMs recognize the same languages and decide the same languages. This is about eventual answerability. The deterministic search may explore exponentially many branches before finding a witness. The later complexity decks ask whether this cost can always be avoided efficiently—an entirely different question.

Keep: bounded-depth replay gives every finite branch a turn. Fairness preserves recognition; finite-tree exhaustion supplies rejection for deciders.

One connected check: Why does replaying only a finite prefix of each branch avoid the failure of depth-first search?

models.title: Algorithms and the Church–Turing thesis: what counts as an effective method?
models.html:
The whole-course question gets bigger

We've shown that several formal machine designs have the same computability power. Now connect them to the informal word algorithm: a finite, mechanical procedure whose individual steps can be carried out effectively. The Church–Turing thesis says that effectively computable procedures are captured by Turing machines.

This is a thesis linking an informal notion to a formal model, not a theorem proved by manipulating two formal definitions. Equivalence between one-tape and multitape TMs is a theorem; the claim that the model captures every effective method has a different logical status.

Searching for an integer root: yes can be easier than no

Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, try integer inputs and evaluate it. For one variable, test 0,1,−1,2,−2,… . If an integer root exists, this enumeration eventually finds it. If none exists, an unbounded search alone runs forever. It is a recognizer-style strategy for the yes-instances, not automatically a decider.

For a univariate polynomial of positive degree with nonzero leading coefficient, a computable bound on root magnitude turns this into a finite search. Once every integer within a valid bound has been checked, there are no other possible integer roots to miss. For the slide example 4x3−2x2+x−74x^3-2x^2+x-74x3−2x2+x−7, a bound such as |x|≤7 suffices. Constant and zero polynomials are handled separately rather than dividing by a nonexistent leading term.

The critical extra ingredient is the stopping certificate supplied by the bound. “I haven't found a root yet” is not the same information as “I've exhausted every possible root.”

Why the multivariable result is deeper

For polynomial equations in several integer variables, enumerating all integer tuples still recognizes existence of a solution. Hilbert's tenth problem asked for a general deciding procedure. The negative result says no such algorithm exists for all instances. This does not follow just from the fact that our current brute-force search may loop; a bad algorithm doesn't prove all algorithms impossible. An impossibility theorem needs a reduction or other general argument.

Three levels of describing a TM

A formal description lists states and transitions. An implementation-level description explains tape layouts, head movements, and marking. A high-level description uses algorithmic steps such as “search the finite graph,” while making those steps effective and termination clear.

For graph connectivity, begin with one marked vertex, repeatedly mark neighbors of marked vertices, and stop when a whole pass adds nothing. A finite graph has only finitely many vertices to add. Accept if all are marked. The algorithm's monotone progress explains termination; the reachability invariant explains correctness.

An input encoding, written with angle brackets such as ⟨G⟩, turns an abstract object into a finite string. Invalid encodings must have specified treatment. The machine reads symbols, not a Platonic graph floating in the void.

Keep: distinguish an effective procedure, a formal simulation theorem, and the Church–Turing thesis. Existence search needs a separate reason to stop on no-instances. Next, we ask which questions about encoded machines are decidable.

One connected check: What extra fact turns the univariate integer-root enumeration into a decider, and why does “it worked on many examples” not provide that fact?

models.title: Deciding questions about automata: inspect the finite object
models.html:
The shift: the input can be a machine description

Until now, a machine usually received a word such as 0011. It can also receive an encoding of another machine, perhaps together with a word. ⟨B,w⟩\langle B,w\rangle⟨B,w⟩ means a finite string describing the pair “machine B and input w.” Angle brackets are encoding notation, not a transition or a set.

For ADFAA_{DFA}ADFA​, the question is whether the encoded DFA B accepts w. A decider checks the encoding, simulates one transition per input symbol, then checks whether the final state is accepting. There are |w| input symbols, so this simulation finishes. Empty w simply asks whether the start state accepts.

Reuse conversions when they come with termination

For NFA acceptance, convert to a DFA or directly update the finite candidate-state set while reading w. For regular-expression acceptance, compile the expression to an NFA, then use the NFA procedure. These are finite constructions. This is an early example of solving one problem by translating it into another already-solved problem.

The important claim is not “it feels computable.” We can identify each finite step and why the process ends.

Emptiness is not an infinite list of membership tests

EDFAE_{DFA}EDFA​ asks whether a DFA's language is empty. Trying ε, then all length-one strings, then all length-two strings will find a member if one exists, but may search forever if the language is empty. A decider needs a way to certify that no word works.

Treat the DFA as a finite directed graph. Mark the start. Repeatedly mark every state reachable by one outgoing arrow from a marked state. Stop when no new state is marked. If any accepting state is marked, a path to it spells an accepted string; otherwise none is reachable and the language is empty.

There are finitely many states, so marks can be added only finitely many times. A start state that already accepts makes the language nonempty via ε. That's an easy boundary case to miss if you only inspect arrows.

Equivalence becomes a search for disagreement

EQDFAEQ_{DFA}EQDFA​ asks whether two DFAs accept exactly the same strings. Build a product machine that tracks both states. Make a pair accepting exactly when one component accepts and the other rejects. This is exclusive-or, not union and not intersection.

For each input w, the product's final pair records both original verdicts. Thus its language consists exactly of disagreement witnesses. If that language is empty, the machines agree on every string; if nonempty, a member proves they differ. Run the finite emptiness algorithm on the product.

A product accepting when both components accept would answer a different question: whether they share a member. Machines may share many members and still disagree elsewhere.

The reusable reasoning pattern

Membership used a bounded run on one supplied word. Emptiness used reachability over a finite graph. Equivalence converted universal agreement into absence of a counterexample. These are three different reasons termination is available. Learn the reason, not just the conclusion “decidable.”

Keep: machine descriptions are finite inputs; finite graph structure can settle infinitely many possible words at once. Next, CFGs need different finite summaries because their derivations can grow without bound.

One connected check: Why does checking accepted strings one by one fail to decide DFA emptiness, while marking finitely many states succeeds?

\(e_{dfa}\) asks whether a dfa's language is empty. trying ε, then all length-one strings, then all length-two strings will find a member if one exists, but may search forever if the language is empty. a decider needs a way to certify that no word works.

treat the dfa as a finite directed graph. mark the start. repeatedly mark every state reachable by one outgoing arrow from a marked state. stop when no new state is marked. if any accepting state is marked, a path to it spells an accepted string; otherwise none is reachable and the language is empty.

there are finitely many states, so marks can be added only finitely many times. a start state that already accepts makes the language nonempty via ε. that's an easy boundary case to miss if you only inspect arrows.

## equivalence becomes a search for disagreement

\(eq_{dfa}\) asks whether two dfas accept exactly the same strings. build a product machine that tracks both states. make a pair accepting exactly when **one** component accepts and the other rejects. this is exclusive-or, not union and not intersection.

for each input w, the product's final pair records both original verdicts. thus its language consists exactly of disagreement witnesses. if that language is empty, the machines agree on every string; if nonempty, a member proves they differ. run the finite emptiness algorithm on the product.

a product accepting when both components accept would answer a different question: whether they share a member. machines may share many members and still disagree elsewhere.

## the reusable reasoning pattern

membership used a bounded run on one supplied word. emptiness used reachability over a finite graph. equivalence converted universal agreement into absence of a counterexample. these are three different reasons termination is available. learn the reason, not just the conclusion “decidable.”

**keep:** machine descriptions are finite inputs; finite graph structure can settle infinitely many possible words at once. next, cfgs need different finite summaries because their derivations can grow without bound.

**one connected check:** why does checking accepted strings one by one fail to decide dfa emptiness, while marking finitely many states succeeds?

models.title: CFG decision problems: bound the proof or summarize productivity
models.html:
The obstacle: a grammar can keep expanding forever

Given a grammar G and a string w, blindly enumerate derivations. A left-recursive rule can keep producing longer sentential forms without finishing. Even if w is not generated, that search may never run out of work. To decide membership, we need a justified finite boundary.

CNF provides one. For a nonempty target of length n, each parse tree has n terminal-producing leaves and n−1 binary splits. Therefore a successful derivation uses exactly 2n−1 rule applications. With finitely many productions, there are finitely many derivations of that length to inspect. ε is handled separately using the protected start's ε rule.

Work the size argument rather than memorize 2n−1

A binary split increases the number of pending leaves by one: replace one variable by two. Starting from one variable, it takes n−1 splits to create n final positions. Each position then uses one terminal rule, contributing n more applications. Total: (n−1)+n.

For a three-symbol word, the tree uses two binary splits and three terminal productions: five applications. The shape can vary, and there may be many candidate trees, but none needs an arbitrarily long chain of unit or ε productions because CNF removed those ordinary rules.

The resulting exhaustive algorithm may be slow. “Finite” establishes decidability, not polynomial efficiency. A later deck states the stronger fact that CFL membership has polynomial-time algorithms.

Emptiness uses a different summary: can this variable finish?

For ECFGE_{CFG}ECFG​, mark variables capable of producing terminal-only strings. Initially mark variables with terminal-only right-hand sides, including ε. Then mark A if a rule A→α has every variable in α already marked. Terminals in α are already finished output. Repeat to a fixed point.

If the start is marked, some completed word can be generated. If it isn't, the language is empty. For A→BC, B→b, C→c, B and C become marked first, then A. For A→B, B→A with no finishing production, neither ever becomes productive. A cycle alone does not manufacture output.

Why is the test complete? Any finite parse tree has productive terminal leaves, then productive parents, working upward. Why is it sound? Each new mark is justified by combining actual terminal derivations for the rule's children. Finitely many variables guarantee termination.

Why DFA equivalence doesn't transfer automatically

For DFAs, disagreement was represented by complement, intersection, and union constructions. Context-free languages are not generally closed under complement or intersection, so that route is unavailable for arbitrary CFGs. The deck states that CFG equivalence is undecidable. Failure of this one construction is not itself a proof of undecidability; the impossibility claim needs a separate theorem.

This also explains why a PDA with ε loops can recognize a decidable language. We need not use its possibly nonterminating branches as our deciding algorithm. Convert to a CFG and use a terminating membership procedure.

Keep: bound successful derivation size for membership; compute productivity for emptiness. Different questions may need different finite summaries.

One connected check: Why does a cycle A→B→A not make A productive unless some reachable rule can actually finish in terminals?
