models.title: Counting programs and languages: infinity has different sizes
models.html:
The question: could every language have a program?

A language is a set of finite strings. A TM is a finite description. Even before constructing a specific impossible problem, we can compare how many descriptions and how many languages there are. If there are more languages than programs, some languages have no recognizing program at all.

“Both collections are infinite” does not settle the comparison. Infinite sets can have different cardinalities—different sizes in the sense of whether their elements can be paired one-to-one.

Countable means listable, not finite

A set is countably infinite when its elements can be listed as first, second, third, and so on without missing any. All finite strings over a finite alphabet can be listed by increasing length, and within each length in a fixed order. Every particular string eventually appears.

TM descriptions are some of those finite strings. We can enumerate candidate encodings and discard malformed ones. Thus there are only countably many TMs. Program length has no fixed maximum, but every individual program is finite.

A bijection pairs each element on one side with exactly one on the other, using every element of both. Equal cardinality does not mean the sets contain the same objects. Integers and finite machine encodings are not literally the same set.

Diagonalization shows that some collections cannot be listed

Suppose someone lists infinite binary sequences as rows. Build a new sequence whose nth bit differs from the nth bit of row n. It differs from row 1 in position 1, row 2 in position 2, and so on. Therefore it is absent from the supposedly complete list.

The construction defeats every row for a specific reason, not by vaguely saying “there must be another one.” In the real-number version, choosing safe decimal digits avoids the ambiguity of two decimal representations such as a trailing sequence of 9s. The logical engine is the same: disagreement on the diagonal.

Connect the counting argument to languages

List all finite input strings as s₁,s₂,s₃,… . A language determines an infinite membership sequence: bit i is 1 if sᵢ belongs, 0 otherwise. Conversely, each such sequence defines a language. Since these infinite sequences cannot all be listed, neither can all languages.

Countably many programs cannot cover uncountably many languages. Some languages are not even recognizable. This is an existence result; it does not yet tell us a particular familiar language with no algorithm.

Keep the named problems distinct

ATMA_{TM}ATM​ consists of pairs ⟨M,w⟩ where M accepts w. HALTTMHALT_{TM}HALTTM​ asks whether M halts on w, either accepting or rejecting. These are different languages, although both are undecidable. If M rejects w, that is a no-instance of acceptance and a yes-instance of halting.

The next deck gives an explicit contradiction for A_TM, then uses recognizability and complement to sharpen the picture. Counting proves there are impossible tasks; diagonal self-reference identifies one.

Keep: finite programs are listable; arbitrary languages correspond to unlistable infinite bit sequences. “Infinite” alone is not a size comparison.

One connected check: For a machine that halts and rejects w, how do its A_TM and HALT_TM membership answers differ?

models.title: The acceptance contradiction: build a program that flips its own predicted answer
models.html:
Assume the impossible helper precisely

Suppose a decider H answers whether any encoded machine M accepts any input w. H always halts. On a yes-instance it says yes; on a no-instance it says no. “No” includes both M rejecting and M looping forever. H would have to settle both cases correctly.

We are assuming this helper exists to derive a contradiction. We are not claiming we can already implement it, and we are not waiting for a looping machine to finish.

Build the challenger D

On input ⟨M⟩, D asks H about ⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩\langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩: does M accept its own description? If H says yes, D rejects. If H says no, D accepts. Because the assumed H always halts, D also halts.

A machine description can be input data just like any other string. M is a machine; ⟨M⟩ is its encoded description. Feeding code to a program is not mystical self-awareness—it's ordinary data processing.

H is the supposed perfect predictor; D is the deliberately contrary program. D doesn't have to be clever. Its entire move is “whatever H predicts about acceptance, do the opposite.” The contradiction arrives only when the predictor is asked about that very contrary program on its own code. Keep those roles fixed before substituting D for M.

Now give D its own description

Ask what D does on ⟨D⟩.

If H predicts “D accepts ⟨D⟩,” D follows its rule and rejects. The prediction is wrong.

If H predicts “D does not accept ⟨D⟩,” D follows its rule and accepts. Again the prediction is wrong.

These two cases exhaust H's possible answers. Therefore the assumed universal acceptance decider cannot exist. The contradiction is not “D loops somehow.” D was defined to halt using H; it is the correctness of H that becomes impossible.

Recognition still exists

A universal simulator can recognize A_TM: decode M and w, simulate M on w, and accept if M accepts. If M rejects, reject; if M loops, the simulation may loop. This satisfies recognition but not decision. Undecidable does not mean no useful yes-verifier or simulator exists.

Why complements expose the missing guarantee

The complement of a language contains exactly the input strings outside it, within the fixed encoding universe. If both L and its complement have recognizers, run the two recognizers in alternating steps on the same input. Exactly one side contains that input, so its recognizer eventually accepts. If L's recognizer accepts, answer yes; if the complement's accepts, answer no. This always terminates and decides L.

For A_TM, a recognizer exists but a decider does not. Therefore its complement cannot also be recognizable. This is a logical consequence of the parallel-recognizer construction.

Why not simply swap accept and reject in an A_TM recognizer? Because loops remain loops. A no-instance that used to loop doesn't become an accepted complement member. Swapping halting verdicts works for deciders, which have no third outcome to worry about.

Keep: self-reference creates a specific forced disagreement; recognizers may leave no-instances unanswered; two complementary recognizers together would settle every input.

One connected check: Which line of the contradiction would fail if H were merely a recognizer instead of a decider?

models.title: Reductions: turn a hypothetical solver into an impossible solver
models.html:
The direction is the whole game

To prove a new problem B undecidable, start with a known undecidable problem A. Show how a solver for B would let you decide A. In words: hard input in, translate it, call the supposed B solver, translate its answer back. If that worked, it would contradict A's known impossibility.

The arrow goes from the known hard problem toward the target problem. Showing that B can be solved using an A oracle says little about B's impossibility; easy problems can also wastefully call a hard oracle.

The deck's target: is a TM's language empty?

ETM={⟨M⟩:L(M)=∅}E_{TM}=\{\langle M\rangle:L(M)=\emptyset\}ETM​={⟨M⟩:L(M)=∅}. This asks whether M accepts no input at all. A machine that loops on every input has an empty accepted language. “Empty” refers to the set of accepted strings, not whether the program runs or the tape starts blank.

Assume a decider R for E_TM exists. Given an acceptance instance ⟨M,w⟩, construct a new machine M₁:

  1. On input x, if x≠w, reject.
  2. If x=w, simulate M on w.
  3. Accept if that simulation accepts; if it rejects, reject; if it loops, keep simulating.

M and w are hardcoded into M₁'s description. Constructing that description is finite; we do not need to run M first to decide which code to write.

The wrapper is a booby-trapped test case for the supposed emptiness checker: the single candidate w gets through only if the embedded simulation accepts. Every other candidate is rejected at the door. That is the mechanism linking one execution question to a property of an entire language. The code is easy to write; knowing which behavior eventually happens is the hard part the hypothetical checker would have to solve.

Work both cases before deciding the answer flip

If M accepts w, M₁ accepts exactly w, so L(M1)={w}L(M_1)=\{w\}L(M1​)={w}, which is nonempty—even if w happens to be ε.

If M does not accept w, M₁ accepts nothing, so L(M1)=∅L(M_1)=\emptysetL(M1​)=∅. For x≠w it rejects immediately; for x=w it rejects or loops. Neither outcome is acceptance.

Thus R's “empty” answer means the original acceptance answer is no; R's “nonempty” answer means yes. We flip R's emptiness verdict to decide A_TM, a contradiction.

Why this isn't circular

M₁ may loop. That's allowed: R was assumed to decide a property of any encoded TM, including looping ones. Our overall hypothetical A_TM decider does not execute M₁ to completion; it gives M₁'s finite description to R, which is assumed to halt.

The reduction itself must be effective and terminating. Writing a wrapper program around ⟨M,w⟩ satisfies that. “Wait to see whether M accepts, then output one of two machines” would not: it might wait forever and fail to produce the transformed instance.

What a rigorous reduction answer contains

Name the assumed target decider, define the constructed machine for every input, analyze the source yes-case and no-case, show how the target answer yields the source answer, and explain why the construction and oracle use would terminate. The two-case table is the bridge between intuition and proof.

Keep: you don't solve the hard instance while constructing the wrapper. You encode its eventual behavior into a property the hypothetical solver is supposed to decide.

One connected check: Why does M looping on w still make M₁'s language empty rather than leave the mathematical set L(M₁) “unknown”?

models.title: Property reductions: make one acceptance event change the whole language
models.html:
The mental model: a behavioral switch

A reduction can construct a TM whose accepted language has one form if M accepts w and another form if M does not. Then a hypothetical property checker distinguishes the cases. The wrapper is fixed code; the language it ends up recognizing depends on the embedded simulation's behavior.

The target here is REGULARTMREGULAR_{TM}REGULARTM​: given a TM description, decide whether its accepted language is regular. The input is not a DFA with visibly finite-state behavior. It's an arbitrary TM, and the question is whether some DFA recognizes the same language.

Build the two cases into one machine

Given ⟨M,w⟩, construct M₂. On input x:

  1. If x is in K={0n1n:n≥0}K=\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}K={0n1n:n≥0}, accept immediately. K has a terminating membership test, even though it is not regular.
  2. Otherwise simulate M on w, accepting x if that simulation accepts.

If M rejects w, M₂ may reject on that second branch; if M loops, M₂ loops there. Either way, those x's are not accepted.

Identify the two languages exactly

If M accepts w, every x in K is accepted by step 1 and every x outside K is eventually accepted by step 2. Thus L(M2)=Σ∗L(M_2)=\Sigma^*L(M2​)=Σ∗, which is regular.

If M does not accept w, only step 1 contributes accepted strings. Thus L(M2)=KL(M_2)=KL(M2​)=K, which is nonregular by the pumping proof.

A REGULAR_TM decider would therefore answer yes exactly when M accepts w. That would decide A_TM, contradiction. This time the answer is not flipped. Decide the direction from the case analysis, not from a memorized rule that “reductions negate the answer.”

Why the nonregular base language is doing real work

K supplies a known no-instance of the target property, while Σ* supplies a known yes-instance. The simulation switches between them. If both cases produced regular languages, the target checker could not reveal the source answer. If the wrapper accepted extra strings in the no-case, you would need to re-prove the resulting language nonregular; hand-waving about “mostly K” is not enough.

Also distinguish “nonregular” from “undecidable.” K is nonregular but decidable. That is why step 1 can be an ordinary finite algorithm. The target property of arbitrary TM languages is the undecidable task.

Equivalence gives another route

EQTMEQ_{TM}EQTM​ asks whether two TMs accept the same language. Compare an arbitrary M against a fixed machine that rejects every input. Their languages are equal exactly when L(M) is empty. So an equivalence decider would give an emptiness decider, which the previous deck ruled out.

Again, the reduction handles accepted languages, not identical running times or identical step-by-step behavior. Two machines can recognize the same language while one rejects a nonmember and the other loops on it.

Keep: construct a clear property switch; prove exactly what language appears in both cases; then read off the contradiction.

One connected check: Why is it valid for the wrapper to decide membership in a nonregular language K, and why would that not be valid if K had no decider?

models.title: Computation histories: a finished run can be checked locally
models.html:
Replace “run the machine” with “inspect a claimed run”

A computation history is a finite sequence of configurations C₁,C₂,…,Cₘ. It claims that C₁ is the starting snapshot, each next snapshot follows legally from the previous one, and Cₘ is an accepting or rejecting halt. It's a transcript of the computation, with tape and head information included.

Checking such a supplied transcript is different from waiting for a machine to produce one. A looping computation has arbitrarily long finite prefixes, but no completed accepting or rejecting history. A finite checker can reject an invalid claimed history without resolving whether some other, longer accepting one exists.

Three checks make the claim precise

First verify that C₁ is the actual start configuration for the specified input. Then check every adjacent pair: did exactly the allowed write, head movement, and state change occur, with other cells unchanged? Finally check the required terminal condition, such as an accepting halt state in Cₘ.

A string with the right first and last states can still contain a fake middle step. Conversely, a sequence of locally legal steps beginning from the wrong input proves nothing about the intended instance. All three clauses matter.

This is another proof pattern: a long global claim can have a finite certificate with many small consistency checks. Later, NP uses polynomially bounded certificates; here the history can be arbitrarily long.

Bounded tape makes the configuration space finite

A linear bounded automaton, LBA, is a TM whose available tape is bounded by the input length under the course model. It may revisit and rewrite those cells, but it cannot keep expanding its workspace beyond the allotted region.

For n available cells, q control states, and g tape symbols, there are at most q n gnq\,n\,g^nqngn configurations: q state choices, n head positions, and g choices independently for each cell. The exact boundary convention can change a constant factor; finiteness is the key. Fix the input before counting—n is not one constant for all possible inputs.

Why membership becomes decidable

For a deterministic LBA, if the same complete configuration repeats before halting, future behavior repeats too, so it will loop. Simulate until accept, reject, or a repeated configuration. Finite configuration space guarantees one of these outcomes.

For a nondeterministic LBA, searching one path is insufficient. Explore the finite directed graph of configurations and ask whether an accepting configuration is reachable. Keep a visited set to avoid revisiting loops forever. This is the DFA reachability idea applied to a much larger finite graph.

The limit of this result

We have a bound for one fixed input length. It does not automatically settle whether an LBA accepts some input of any length. That problem ranges over unbounded n, so no single finite configuration graph covers all candidates. The next deck uses computation histories to show why this distinction matters.

Keep: a finite claimed run can be verified; bounded space gives finitely many configurations per input; membership and emptiness quantify over different things.

models.title: Histories in reductions: finite checks can encode an unbounded existence question
models.html:
The apparent paradox

LBA membership is decidable: for one supplied input, search a finite configuration graph. Yet LBA emptiness is undecidable: there is no general algorithm deciding whether it accepts any input. The difference is the quantifier. “Check this candidate” does not give a finite stopping rule for “no candidate of any length works.”

Given ⟨M,w⟩, construct an LBA B whose input is a claimed accepting computation history of M on w. B checks its formatting, correct start, legal adjacent steps, and accepting final configuration. It uses the candidate's own length as bounded workspace. It does not simulate M forever hoping that a history eventually appears.

Analyze the two cases

If M accepts w, its finite accepting run can be written as a history. That string passes B's checks, so L(B) is nonempty.

If M does not accept w, no valid accepting history exists. Every candidate fails at least one check, so L(B) is empty.

A decider for LBA emptiness would distinguish these cases and decide A_TM, contradiction. Each individual history check terminates, yet the existence question over histories of unbounded length remains undecidable. No contradiction at all once the two questions are separated.

Why reversed configurations show up in the CFG argument

For the CFG universality problem ALLCFGALL_{CFG}ALLCFG​, the construction uses a PDA for bad histories. A bad history has some defect: malformed syntax, wrong start, wrong finish, or an illegal adjacent step. Nondeterminism can guess a defect to check. Acceptance means at least one real defect is found.

To compare neighboring configurations using a stack, encode alternating configurations in reverse order. Pushing one configuration and reading the reversed next one brings corresponding positions together under last-in-first-out access. Without that reversal, the stack would present the first configuration backward while the next arrived forward, and the local comparison would not line up.

The PDA needs to verify a local illegal transition, including unchanged regions and the small region affected by the head. This is a construction argument; the phrase “just check the pair” stands for specific stack work, not an unlimited random-access comparison.

Why “bad histories” produces universality

If M never accepts w, every string is either malformed or fails to describe a valid accepting history. The bad-history language is then all strings over the encoding alphabet, Σ*.

If M accepts w, at least one valid accepting history exists. That string has no defect, so it is excluded. The bad-history language is not universal.

Convert the PDA to a CFG. A hypothetical CFG-universality decider would reveal whether M accepts w by checking whether the resulting grammar generates all strings. The construction must include malformed strings among the bad ones; otherwise the no-acceptance case might still omit them and fail to be Σ*.

How the earlier topics cooperate

The proof uses configurations from TM theory, stack reversal from PDA design, PDA→CFG equivalence, and the two-case structure of reductions. This is why disconnected formula memorization collapses here: the pieces have jobs in one larger argument.

Keep: a finite checker can verify candidates while existence over unbounded candidates remains hard. Bad-certificate recognition turns a missing valid history into universality.

One connected check: Why must the bad-history PDA accept malformed encodings as well as well-formed histories with an illegal step?

models.title: Big O: a budget on growth, after fixed details stop dominating
models.html:
The question changes from “can it finish?” to “how much work?”

A decider halts on every input, but its running time may grow wildly with input length. Complexity studies that growth. Let n be the length of the encoded input, and T(n) the worst number of steps among inputs of that length. We want useful comparisons without listing every constant setup cost.

f(n)=O(g(n))f(n)=O(g(n))f(n)=O(g(n)) says that beyond some threshold n₀, f stays below a constant multiple c of g. Formally, there exist c>0 and n₀ such that f(n)≤c g(n)f(n)\le c\,g(n)f(n)≤cg(n) for every n≥n₀, for the nonnegative functions under discussion.

The constants must be fixed across all sufficiently large n. You don't get to choose a new c for each n; that would make the claim almost meaningless.

Work a bound from the definition

Take f(n)=6n³+5. For n≥2, 5≤n³, so 6n3+5≤7n36n^3+5\le7n^36n3+5≤7n3. Choose c=7 and n₀=2. That proves f=O(n³). The lower-order extra 5 is absorbed into a fixed multiplier once n is large enough.

Why isn't f=O(n²)? If 6n3+5≤cn26n^3+5\le cn^26n3+5≤cn2 eventually held, dividing by n² would give 6n+5/n2≤c6n+5/n^2\le c6n+5/n2≤c. But 6n exceeds any fixed c when n is large enough. No fixed constant can contain that growth.

O(n³) is an upper bound, not necessarily a tight one. The same f is also O(n⁴). A statement can be correct and still less informative. Do not read the equals sign in f=O(g) as ordinary equality of two numerical functions; it is conventional membership-in-a-growth-class notation.

How bounds combine

For sequential phases, add costs. If one is at most c₁g(n) after n₁ and another at most c₂g(n) after n₂, their sum is at most (c₁+c₂)g(n) after max(n₁,n₂). The maximum threshold ensures both bounds are valid at once.

For a nested loop, count how often the inner work runs and its cost each time. n passes each taking O(n) steps give O(n²). But check whether the pass length shrinks; mindlessly multiplying every visible loop by n can miss a stronger bound.

Input representation is part of the problem

An integer N written in binary takes about log₂N bits; unary 0ᴺ takes N symbols. An algorithm using N iterations is linear in unary length but exponential in the binary length. Saying “linear in the number” without specifying encoding can hide the entire difficulty.

Also distinguish 2O(n)2^{O(n)}2O(n) from O(2n)O(2^n)O(2n). The former allows an unspecified constant multiplier in the exponent, such as 2^{3n}; the latter permits only a fixed multiplier outside 2ⁿ. Those are not interchangeable.

Keep: Big O is a quantified eventual upper bound on growth. Name the input-size measure and machine model before counting steps.

One connected check: In the proof that 6n³+5 is O(n³), what jobs do c=7 and n₀=2 each perform?

models.title: Little o and algorithm cost: distinguish smaller growth from the same scale
models.html:
“At most a constant multiple” versus “eventually a tiny fraction”

Big O allows comparable growth: 6n³ is O(n³). Little o is stronger. f(n)=o(g(n))f(n)=o(g(n))f(n)=o(g(n)) means that for every positive constant c, f(n)≤c g(n) eventually. The threshold may depend on c. When the ratio is defined appropriately, this is equivalent to f(n)/g(n)→0.

For √n versus n, the ratio is 1/√n, which tends to zero. Thus √n=o(n). For 6n³ versus n³, the ratio is always 6, so it is not little o. It cannot eventually fit below 0.01 times n³. The difference is the order of the quantifiers: some fixed multiplier versus every arbitrarily small multiplier.

Return to a familiar language and count actual work

To decide {0k1k:k≥0}\{0^k1^k:k\ge0\}{0k1k:k≥0} on a single tape, first check block order. A straightforward machine crosses off one zero and one one per round, repeatedly traveling across a region of length O(n). There are O(n) rounds, so the time is O(n²).

The reason isn't just “two loops.” It is the combination of how many obligations are discharged per round and how far the head travels to discharge them. Tape movement is part of the cost.

Why repeated halving can improve the bound

Instead of matching one pair at a time, compare the parity of the two remaining counts, then retain roughly half of each for another round. Equal counts have equal low-order binary bits; after removing that bit by halving, their quotients must still match. If parities differ in some round, reject. Boundary cases with no surviving symbols must be handled explicitly.

The number of rounds is O(log n), since each successful round roughly halves the live populations. But the old crossed-out cells still occupy physical tape positions. A pass may still travel across O(n) cells even when few live symbols remain. Therefore the time is O(n log n), not automatically O(n) from imagining the tape physically shrinks.

That distinction—logical population versus physical span—is exactly the kind of detail that separates a plausible story from a correct time analysis.

Multiple tapes can change the movement cost

With a second tape, copy the first block and compare it against the second in coordinated scans. Each relevant symbol needs only a constant amount of local work, so a linear-time method is possible on that model. This does not contradict the one-tape analysis: the storage layout and allowed head movements changed.

The language is the same, the yes/no condition is the same, and computability power is the same. The number of physical steps can differ. Complexity claims must name the model under which they are measured.

How to structure a time proof

Identify the input length n. Divide the algorithm into phases. For each phase, bound the number of repetitions and the cost per repetition, including resets and scans over marked cells. Sum the bounds, then simplify using Big O. If claiming little o, show the ratio or quantify over every positive multiplier; an ordinary upper bound is insufficient.

Keep: little o means vanishing relative growth. For algorithms, count physical work, not just useful-looking edits.

One connected check: Why can halving the number of live symbols leave the cost of one tape sweep proportional to the original input length?

models.title: Simulation cost: equal computability can come with a quadratic bill
models.html:
Revisit the one-tape encoding with a stopwatch

We already know one tape can represent k tapes using separated blocks and marked head positions. Now ask how much time that simulation takes. Suppose the multitape machine runs in t(n) steps on inputs of length n, with t(n)≥n and fixed k.

In t steps, each head can visit only O(t) cells, and the original input occupies at most t cells under the assumption. With a fixed number of tapes, the entire encoded configuration therefore has length O(t). This is a bound on how far the simulator may need to scan.

One simulated step is not one real step

The simulator must sweep to find the marked symbols, remember their tuple, apply the joint transition, move markers, and sometimes insert a blank cell by shifting later data. Each such phase costs O(t) on a representation of length O(t). A fixed number of phases still costs O(t).

There are at most t simulated steps. Multiply: O(t)×t=O(t2)O(t)\times t=O(t^2)O(t)×t=O(t2). Initialization is absorbed under t≥n. The constants may depend on the fixed simulated machine and number of tapes, not on the input length.

If the simulation at step i has only O(n+i) stored cells, a more detailed sum is ∑i=1tO(n+i)\sum_{i=1}^{t}O(n+i)∑i=1t​O(n+i), which is O(nt+t²), hence O(t²) when t≥n. The rough bound and the sum describe the same source of cost.

What the theorem actually promises

Every such multitape computation has a one-tape simulation with at most quadratic overhead under this construction. It does not say every one-tape algorithm for the same language must be quadratically slower. A different direct algorithm might do better. An upper-bound construction isn't a lower-bound impossibility proof.

For example, simulating a linear-time multitape method gives an O(n²) one-tape method. That demonstrates existence of a quadratic method; it does not establish that O(n²) is optimal.

Why polynomial time survives

If t(n)=nᵈ for a fixed constant d, squaring produces n^{2d}, still a polynomial. This is one reason polynomial time is a robust category across these standard deterministic tape models. A constant number of extra tapes may alter the exponent or practical speed without turning a polynomial computation into an exponential one under this simulation.

By contrast, nondeterministic simulation will involve a tree of alternative configurations, not merely one encoded configuration. The next deck counts how many branches must be explored. Different source of overhead, different bound.

Keep: representation length bounds scan cost; scan cost times simulated steps gives total cost. Equal language power doesn't mean equal speed, and an upper bound doesn't prove optimality.

One connected check: Which two separate facts contribute the two factors of t in the O(t²) simulation bound?

Name what “time” measures before counting

For a nondeterministic decider, time t(n) is the maximum number of steps along any branch on inputs of length n. It measures the longest branch, not the total number of nodes across the computation tree. Every branch must halt within that bound.

If each step has at most b choices, with b a constant determined by the machine, there can be roughly b^d paths of length d. A depth-t tree can therefore contain exponentially many candidates even though each individual branch is short.

See the difference on a small tree

With two choices per step and depth three, there can be eight length-three choice sequences: 111,112,121,122,211,212,221,222. Each branch takes three steps. A deterministic simulator that explores all choices may need to inspect all eight branches before concluding that none accepts.

Growing depth from three to thirty doesn't merely multiply the candidate count by ten. It can multiply it from 2³ to 2³⁰. That's the source of the exponential cost; no individual transition became expensive.

Derive the simulation bound

Enumerate candidate choice sequences up to length t, replay each for at most O(t) steps on a multitape simulator, and check whether any accepts. The number of candidates is bounded by a constant-base exponential in t. Multiplying by a polynomial factor such as t still gives 2O(t)2^{O(t)}2O(t).

If b=1 there is no branching and the search is much cheaper, but the exponential expression remains a valid general upper bound. Converting the resulting deterministic multitape simulation to one tape squares its running time. Squaring 2ct2^{ct}2ct gives 22ct2^{2ct}22ct, still 2O(t)2^{O(t)}2O(t). The constant in the exponent changes; the broad form does not.

What this says about power and efficiency

Nondeterministic and deterministic TMs decide the same languages because the finite tree can be searched. But the straightforward deterministic simulation may be exponentially slower than the longest nondeterministic branch. Whether every polynomial-time nondeterministic decision problem has some polynomial-time deterministic method is the P versus NP question—not settled by this expensive simulation.

An exponential simulation proves an upper bound that is sufficient for decidability. It does not prove that an exponential slowdown is unavoidable. Again: “our method costs this much” and “every possible method must cost this much” are different claims.

Connect this to a guessed solution

A nondeterministic branch can guess a short candidate and verify it. The branch length includes both guessing and checking. A deterministic exhaustive search may try every candidate. Later, the certificate definition of NP packages exactly this distinction: a supplied candidate can be easy to check even when finding one efficiently is not known.

Keep: nondeterministic time measures branch depth; deterministic search may pay for the whole tree. Do not silently substitute one quantity for the other.

One connected check: Why does a polynomial bound on each branch fail, by itself, to give a polynomial bound on the number of branches?

models.title: P: algorithms whose work is polynomial in the encoded input length
models.html:
The definition is a growth guarantee, not a compliment

P is the class of languages decided by deterministic TMs in polynomial time: for some fixed exponent k, running time is O(nᵏ), where n is input length. The machine must halt on every input and answer correctly. “Polynomial” does not mean instantly practical; n¹⁰⁰ is polynomial and can be absurdly large.

The value of the class is robustness: standard deterministic model changes have polynomial overhead, and useful efficient algorithms often fall inside it. It gives a precise mathematical boundary to investigate, not a guarantee about your laptop's response time.

PATH: search the graph without enumerating all paths

Given a directed graph G and vertices s,t, ask whether a path from s to t exists. Mark s. Repeatedly inspect outgoing edges from marked vertices and mark their destinations. Stop when t is marked or no new vertex can be marked.

On a graph s→u→t with an extra cycle u→s, marking still progresses safely: revisiting s doesn't create an endless search. A vertex needs to be newly marked only once. At most the number of vertices can be added, and each pass inspects finitely many encoded edges, giving a polynomial bound.

Correctness comes from two directions: each marked vertex has a path from s; every reachable vertex is eventually marked by following a path's edges. Termination comes from finitely many new marks. Enumerating every possible path would waste work on repetitions and cycles.

Euclid: use a preserved relation and a decreasing quantity

To compute gcd(a,b), repeatedly replace (a,b) by (b, a mod b) until b=0. The greatest common divisor stays the same because a divisor divides both a and b exactly when it divides both b and the remainder a−qb.

For 18 and 24: (18,24)→(24,18)→(18,6)→(6,0), so the gcd is 6. The remainder is smaller than the divisor, ensuring progress. More sharply, the relevant magnitude shrinks by at least a factor of two within a bounded number of iterations, giving logarithmically many rounds in the numerical magnitude.

The numbers are binary encoded. Their bit length is logarithmic in their value, so a rigorous polynomial-time claim also counts the bit cost of division/remainder operations. Treating arbitrary-size arithmetic as one free step would hide work.

A familiar language class returns

The deck states that every context-free language is in P. Earlier, CNF gave a finite exhaustive membership algorithm via 2n−1 derivation steps. That particular enumeration can be exponential; it established decidability, not the stronger polynomial result. Polynomial parsing uses shared subproblems instead of separately trying every tree.

This distinction is useful everywhere: a language may admit a slow algorithm and also a fast one. Complexity classes assert the existence of a suitably bounded algorithm, not that every algorithm for the problem is efficient.

Keep: find a reusable summary—reachable vertices, a gcd invariant, shared parsing subproblems—and prove both correctness and a bound in encoded input length.

One connected check: Why does “at most N iterations” fail to establish polynomial time when the integer N is supplied in binary?

models.title: NP: a yes-answer has a short certificate that can be checked quickly
models.html:
Start with checking, not with a mysterious acronym

Suppose someone hands you a proposed Hamiltonian path in a graph: an ordered list of vertices. You can check that it starts and ends where required, visits every vertex exactly once, and uses an actual graph edge between each adjacent pair. The list may have been hard to find, but checking a supplied list is a concrete finite job.

A certificate is that extra proposed evidence. A verifier is a deterministic algorithm that checks the original input together with the certificate. NP consists of decision languages where yes-instances have certificates of polynomially bounded length that can be verified in polynomial time.

For no-instances, every permitted certificate must fail. A verifier that accepts some bogus witness would certify the wrong language.

Think “show me the route and I'll check it.” The certificate supplies the route; the verifier checks the graph's actual edges and the once-per-vertex requirement. It doesn't trust the person who supplied it. A pretty-looking list gets no free pass. This is the concrete meaning of verification before the acronym starts sounding like wizard shit.

Work the HAMPATH certificate

For a graph with vertices {s,a,b,t}, a candidate [s,b,a,t] claims a path using all four exactly once. Check its endpoints, count and uniqueness of vertices, and edges s→b, b→a, a→t. If any edge is missing, reject this certificate. That does not by itself prove the graph has no Hamiltonian path; another ordering may work.

The certificate length grows with the graph encoding size. Trying all vertex orderings may take huge time, but the verifier processes one supplied ordering. Keep the quantifiers straight: some certificate for a yes-instance; no certificate for a no-instance.

NP does not mean “non-polynomial”

The name refers to nondeterministic polynomial time, which the next deck connects to certificates. Problems already in P are also in NP: a verifier can simply run the polynomial decider and ignore the certificate. Therefore membership in NP does not establish hardness or rule out an efficient deterministic algorithm.

The deck uses compositeness as a verification example. A nontrivial factor certifies that an integer is composite: check the factor bounds and divisibility. But compositeness is also in P, because primality has an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena paper establishes that prime/composite decision result. Finding a full factorization is a different task; don't slide from one claim to the other.

What about certifying a no-answer?

A Hamiltonian path is a compact witness that a path exists. The absence of one particular candidate is not a witness that no candidate exists. The complement class coNP concerns languages whose no-answers, viewed as yes-answers to the complement, have polynomial certificates.

It is not established that NP and coNP differ. So say “we have this yes-certificate” rather than “there can never be a short no-certificate.” A lack of a known method is not an impossibility theorem.

Connect to earlier proof practice

An ambiguity witness gave one string and two derivations. A computation history gave a finite run. A counterexample refuted a universal claim. These are all evidence objects, but NP adds quantitative requirements: certificate length and verification time must be polynomial in the original input length.

Keep: NP is about polynomially checkable yes-evidence. It includes easy problems and does not itself mean NP-complete.

One connected check: Why does rejecting [s,b,a,t] fail to decide that a graph has no Hamiltonian path?

models.title: Verifiers and guessing machines: two descriptions of the same resource
models.html:
Turn a certificate verifier into a nondeterministic machine

If a language has polynomially bounded certificates and a polynomial-time verifier, an NTM can guess a certificate of the allowed length, then run the verifier. A yes-instance has at least one successful guessed certificate, so at least one branch accepts. A no-instance has none, so every branch rejects.

The guess must be bounded. “Guess any finite string” with no length limit could produce arbitrarily long or nonterminating branches, destroying the polynomial-time guarantee. Guessing itself consumes time; it isn't free magic.

Reverse the construction

If an NTM decides a language in polynomial time, an accepting branch has polynomially many steps. Record its transition choices as a certificate. A deterministic verifier follows those choices, checks that each is legal, and confirms an accepting halt within the bound.

Because the fixed machine has only finitely many choices per step, each choice needs only a constant number of bits. A polynomial number of choices gives a polynomial-size certificate. The verifier doesn't search all branches; the certificate identifies one candidate branch to check.

That proves the equivalence: polynomial nondeterministic time and polynomially verifiable certificates describe the same class NP.

SUBSET-SUM: make the witness concrete

The deck uses numbers such as {4,11,16,21,27} and a target. For target 25, selecting 4 and 21 works. A certificate can be a bit vector 10010, with one bit per listed entry: 1 means select that occurrence, 0 means skip it. Add the selected numbers and compare with the target.

The input is a list of entries; repeated equal values, if present, are distinct positions. You may use each occurrence at most once in ordinary SUBSET-SUM. A certificate that reuses one index repeatedly would be solving a different problem. Check certificate length, valid entries, and the sum.

Binary arithmetic takes time proportional to bit lengths, but summing at most the listed number of integers of bounded input size remains polynomial. Exhaustively trying every subset has 2ᵐ candidates for m entries. A fast verification procedure does not by itself provide a fast search over all candidates.

Where P versus NP actually stands

P asks for a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm. NP asks for polynomially checkable yes-certificates, equivalently polynomial-time nondeterministic decision. P⊆NP. Whether P=NP remains unresolved; the Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved (checked November 1, 2026).

NP-complete means a problem is in NP and every NP problem can be transformed into it by a polynomial-time reduction. It is a special kind of completeness, not a synonym for NP. If one NP-complete problem had a polynomial-time algorithm, all NP problems would. No known polynomial algorithm is not the same as a proof that none exists.

The course's final connection

We began by asking what a machine must remember. We moved to what it can compute at all, then what it can compute within a time budget. The same habits keep paying off: specify the object, preserve its meaning through a construction, prove both directions, and account for termination or cost separately.

Keep: bounded guesses are certificates; checking one branch differs from searching the whole tree; the major separation questions remain open.

One connected check: In the verifier-to-NTM construction, why are both the certificate-length bound and the verifier-time bound necessary?

modelOverview:
Start with the one job underneath the entire course

Alright. Before another Greek letter lands on your screen, fix the job in your head: someone gives us a finite input, and we want to determine whether it follows a rule.

Take 0011. A rule might say: “zeros first, then exactly the same number of ones.” This input passes. 001 fails because one zero has no matching one. 0101 fails the order requirement even though the counts match. The rule has two conditions. Forget either and you solve a different problem.

A string is one input sequence. An alphabet is the set of symbols allowed in it. A language is the set of all strings satisfying the rule. The language is the target; a machine is our proposed checker. A machine can be designed incorrectly. Calling a circle “accept” doesn't make its decisions match the target by magic.

The course keeps changing one resource: what can the checker remember?

Imagine reading 000… and then receiving the first 1. The earlier zeros are behind you. To decide whether enough ones follow, something must preserve the number of unmatched zeros. That's the actual problem. The circles and arrows are our way of specifying the solution—or proving a proposed kind of solution cannot exist.

Model What survives from earlier input? What that buys us
DFA One of finitely many state labels A finite summary: odd/even, the last symbol, remainder modulo 3
NFA Several possible finite-state runs Convenient guesses; a DFA can track the set of possibilities
PDA A finite state and an arbitrarily growing stack Store one marker per unmatched obligation; discharge the newest one first
Turing machine A finite state, a writable tape, and a movable head Write down information, revisit it, change it and compare separated pieces

A stack is a pile whose top is the only accessible end. A tape is a row of cells you can revisit by moving a head. Those access rules matter as much as the amount of storage. “More memory” is too vague; ask what can be written, inspected, and retrieved next?

For 0011, a PDA pushes two markers while reading the zeros, then pops one per 1. State labels enforce “no zeros after ones.” The stack handles the count; the state handles the phase. That's how the parts cooperate.

Grammars approach the same target from the other direction

A checker receives a finished string. A grammar starts with an unfinished job and constructs a string using replacement rules.

Consider S → 0S1 | ε. S is the unfinished job. → means “may be replaced by.” The vertical bar separates choices. ε means produce no symbols.

S
0S1       add one zero before the unfinished job and one one after it
00S11     repeat that same wrapping move
0011      replace the remaining S by ε

Every wrapping adds a matched pair, and every zero is placed before the unfinished middle while every one is placed after it. The rule builds equality and order into the structure. The PDA's stored markers are another way to manage those unfinished obligations. Grammar ↔ PDA conversions make that connection exact.

CNF then changes the grammar's internal building blocks while preserving its finished strings. It is like reorganizing a recipe into smaller instructions: the meal must remain the same. We will explain exactly what corresponds, so the analogy doesn't have to carry the proof.

A proof is the explanation that survives every input

Watching 0011 work tells us about 0011. To justify the whole PDA, we need a statement that remains true throughout every run: during the matching phase, the stack has one marker for each earlier zero not yet matched by a one. That statement connects the changing machine to the fixed language rule.

To use it, check three things: it starts true; each allowed move preserves it; the final acceptance condition means the rule is satisfied. We also show every valid string has a successful run. This is the bridge from “I can follow the diagram” to “I can prove the diagram works.”

The pumping lemma goes the other way: finite memory forces some long runs to repeat a state, creating a reusable loop. If reusing that loop necessarily breaks the target language, no DFA could have been its correct checker. The loop is forced by the resource limit; the contradiction is between the checker's behavior and the target rule.

Where the later chapters go

Once a tape gives us a general model of an algorithm, we ask a bigger question: does any algorithm solve this problem and always finish? Decidability studies that. Reductions show that a solver for one problem would give a solver for another. Complexity then asks how the number of steps grows with input length. “A solution exists,” “it eventually finishes,” and “it finishes quickly” are three different claims.

Use the deck guides in course order or jump to the concept blocking you. Each names the question, builds the mechanism, runs a concrete example, unpacks the notation, and explains the connection forward. The later-chapter guides are available because this is a guide to every published deck; their presence does not make them confirmed Midterm 2 scope.

For your current CNF question, start with CNF 1: preserve the finished strings while changing the recipe. Work from the meaning of a variable that can finish empty. The deletion rules will then have a reason behind them.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤5-state PDA for 0ᵐ1ᵐ⁺ⁿ0ⁿ, m,n≥1; satisfy normalization conditions already.
items.guide: Separate the first matched 0/1 block from the later matched 1/0 block. The middle phase can pop old zero markers then push markers for trailing zeros. Show the three preconditions.

items.prompt: Convert that PDA to CFG wrapped rules; give push/pop tables.
items.guide: Pair each push with every pop of the same stack symbol; include the bottom-marker pair. Only the wrapped family is requested.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤2-state PDA for 0ᵐ1ⁿ, m≥n≥0, with Γ={0}; give diagram and formal definition.
items.guide: Push on zeros; switch on the first one and pop on ones. Both ordinary phases accept because leftover zeros and ε are allowed.

items.prompt: Prove no one-state PDA with Γ={0} recognizes that language.
items.guide: Use acceptance of ε and 01, then replay an accepting 01 run to force acceptance of 0101. Explain why stack operations remain legal.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤3-state DPDA, including reject state; give δ.
items.guide: Remove choices, retain both accepting phases, reject zeros after ones, and check all four-way table conditions.

items.prompt: Simulate the supplied PDA on 000111 using a tree.
items.guide: Keep branches for the competing 1 transitions with different stack effects. A single path is explicitly insufficient.

items.prompt: Find a counterexample to that PDA for 0ᵐ1ⁿ, m≤n, and draw its tree.
items.guide: Check zero-only inputs and too few ones; acceptance in an ordinary state need not empty the stack. The paper supplies 0 and 001 as examples.

items.prompt: Repair the PDA using ≤4 states and one accept state; trace the counterexample.
items.guide: Use a bottom-marker check before final acceptance; preserve ε and strings containing only ones.

items.prompt: Convert S→A|0A, A→SAS|ε to CNF, showing all four stages.
items.guide: Track both nullable S occurrences and the induced A→S unit rule. The full worked lesson follows this question.

items.prompt: Design a ≤9-state outside-in TM for w#wᴿ with restricted Γ; trace 01#10 and 010#0 fully.
items.guide: Remember the erased left bit in the state; find and erase the matching rightmost bit. Check # and exhaustion on both sides; count both halting states.

items.prompt: Use the prescribed inside-out TM strategy with ≤8 states and special initial-symbol marks; trace both strings.
items.guide: Use the left boundary marks to know when matching is complete; verify extra separators and the string #. Follow the specified strategy.

items.prompt: Give a ≤4-state two-tape TM for the same reversal language and trace both strings.
items.guide: Copy the left side to tape 2, then compare the right side while scanning that copy backwards. Show both head positions at each joint step.

items.prompt: Adapt the square-length pumping proof using i=3 and the lecture witness.
items.guide: With |y|=k, bound the new length p²+2k strictly between p² and (p+1)².

items.prompt: Can the same witness use i=0 if square lengths exclude n=0?
items.guide: Treat p≥2 by adjacent-square bounds; treat p=1 separately, where ε is now outside the language.

items.prompt: Give the full truth table for ¬(A∧B∧C) and (A∧B)⇒¬C.
items.guide: Write eight rows. Both formulas are false only when A,B,C are all true.

items.prompt: Decide regularity for nonempty binary strings with average bit value ≤0.9; explicitly give s and i.
items.guide: Use a boundary ratio such as 1⁹ᵖ0ᵖ, then add only ones. Cover all legal loop lengths, including |y|=p.

items.prompt: Decide regularity of 0ʰ1ᵏ with h>5k and positive h,k.
items.guide: Choose s=0⁵ᵖ⁺¹1ᵖ and delete a nonempty zero-only loop. The strict inequality then fails.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤2-state PDA for binary strings whose number of ones is divisible by six; formal definition required.
items.guide: Store nonzero remainders in the stack alphabet and use the accepting control state for remainder zero. Zero symbols leave the remainder unchanged.

items.prompt: Give a CFG for the same language with ≤5 rules and ≤3 variables.
items.guide: Generate groups of six ones with arbitrary zero blocks in every gap; include the all-zero/empty case. Count alternatives as specified.

items.prompt: Convert S→CS|ε, C→SCS|CS|1 to CNF with stages.
items.guide: S is nullable. Both occurrences in SCS matter; remove C→C and induced units. The second worked task covers this grammar.

items.prompt: Identify the language of the supplied PDA and explain it.
items.guide: The marker stack matches halves by length; a forced 1 must appear in the second half. Distinguish this from matching the halves symbol by symbol.

items.prompt: Normalize the PDA without changing Σ or Γ; construct all CFG rule families.
items.guide: Replace the no-stack-change edge by a matched push/pop through an intermediate state. Include wrapped, concatenation, and empty rules; do not add a forbidden stack symbol.

items.prompt: Convert hamburger grammar H→bCb, C→mC|CbC|ε into a PDA by the prescribed procedure.
items.guide: Push production right sides in reverse order, include terminal-matching loops and the bottom-marker finish.

items.prompt: Convert that grammar to CNF with the prescribed stages.
items.guide: C is nullable in several positions; CbC creates Cb, bC and b. Isolate b,m in longer right sides and binarize.

items.prompt: Determine ambiguity of bmbmb in that grammar.
items.guide: Give two complete leftmost derivations, differing in whether the outer C first uses mC or CbC.

items.prompt: Prove 0.5n≤m≤1.5n iff n choices from {1,2,3} can sum to 2m.
items.guide: One direction is a bound on the sum. The other needs an explicit choice of counts of 1s/2s or 2s/3s, including n=0.

items.prompt: Complete the specified ≤7-state PDA with Γ={0,$} using that idea.
items.guide: Push two markers per zero; nondeterministically pop one to three per one; accept exactly when the bottom marker is reached.

items.prompt: Draw full simulation trees for 001 and 011.
items.guide: The first rejects, the second accepts. Include all nondeterministic pop choices, not merely the successful path.

items.prompt: Read the language of the supplied two-state PDA.
items.guide: Recognize that accepting final states permit unused stack markers: m≥n, not m=n.

items.prompt: Normalize it using ≤6 states and a stack alphabet of at most three symbols.
items.guide: Use a separate drain path rather than adding free pops to active computation states; then repair any no-op stack move.

items.prompt: Give wrapped CFG rules and push/pop tables for the normalized machine.
items.guide: Account for original matching pops, drain pops, bottom-marker pops, and any dummy-symbol pair.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤4-state PDA for strings containing 01101, using Σ=Γ={0,1}.
items.guide: Use state plus stack-top combinations to encode progress along the fixed pattern, then consume any suffix in an accepting phase.

items.prompt: Define an equivalent NFA for a PDA with a uniform bound m on stack cells.
items.guide: States are (control state, stack string of length ≤m). Start with empty stack; accepting pairs have accepting control states. Define both pop and no-pop transition cases.

items.prompt: Give a ≤7-state two-tape TM computing x⊗y from x#y while restoring tape 1; follow alphabet restrictions.
items.guide: Remember the current bit of x on tape 2 while scanning y, emit the product block, then restore that bit in its marked tape-1 position.

items.prompt: Simulate on 01#10 with joint tape configurations.
items.guide: The output is 0010 and tape 1 must end unchanged. Only movement-only sequences may be compressed as the question permits.

items.prompt: Identify the languages of B,D,X in the supplied grammar.
items.guide: B yields b*, D yields c*, and X yields aⁱbⁱ for i≥1. Explain bases and recursive contributions.

items.prompt: Use those results to identify the languages of Y and S in detail.
items.guide: Y equates a/c counts with at least one pair; S unions that branch with the a/b-equality branch and free trailing cs.

items.prompt: Determine ambiguity of a²b²c².
items.guide: Use two leftmost derivations through the XD and Y start branches.

items.prompt: Convert the grammar to CNF in the specified nullable/unit order.
items.guide: D and B can disappear; add the induced alternatives before removing units. Retain all conditions while introducing helpers.

items.prompt: Convert the simplified S→Y, Y→aBc|aYc, B→bB|ε grammar into a PDA.
items.guide: Use stack substitutions in reverse order and matching loops for a,b,c. The hint expects nine nodes.

items.prompt: Complete the fixed PDA for positive block lengths a,b,c forming an arithmetic progression.
items.guide: Use a+c=2b. Two pops per 1 cancel initial markers; after the bottom is reached, two pushes per remaining 1 prepare the final block. Handle odd/even leftover phases.

items.prompt: Draw simulation trees for 012 and 00112.
items.guide: 012 accepts; 00112 fails the count relation. Preserve mandatory positive blocks and all transition branches.

items.prompt: Identify the language of the supplied PDA.
items.guide: One 1 accounts for up to two zeros; include odd zero counts and zero zeros. The language is 0ᵐ1ⁿ with n≥m/2 and nonnegative counts.

items.prompt: Repair a no-op stack transition without changing states or alphabets.
items.guide: Replace the final-state loop with a push followed by an already available matching pop, preserving input consumption.

items.prompt: Give all wrapped rules with matching-symbol pairing tables.
items.guide: Cross every push with every matching pop, including less obvious paths through reused states.

items.prompt: Explain why the original PDA is not deterministic.
items.guide: Exhibit an actual four-way conflict between a zero push and an ε bottom-marker pop.

items.prompt: Modify the original into a DPDA without changing Q,Σ,Γ; complete δ and F.
items.guide: Remove the conflict while separately preserving ε and all-one inputs. Complete missing combinations with qᵣ as required.

items.prompt: Design the prescribed ≤6-state TM matching adult/child boarding and exit events.
items.guide: Mark the first cell F, remember event type in state, find a later matching exit, mark it ×, and return. Respect prefix feasibility and empty input.

items.prompt: Trace the TM on A+A+A−A− to halting.
items.guide: Show each state, tape edit, and head position through the final accept transition.

items.prompt: Give leftmost derivations of jjb and bbbb in the supplied grammar.
items.guide: Always expand the leftmost variable; ε vanishes from the resulting string.

items.prompt: Decide whether j is ambiguous in that grammar.
items.guide: A nullable B may disappear directly or split into two nullable Bs, giving distinct leftmost derivations.

items.prompt: Convert to CNF with the exact requested ε and unit removal order.
items.guide: Track B,J,S nullability and preserve S₀→ε. Show the intermediate grammars, not just the final normal form.

items.prompt: Complete the provided CFG-to-PDA draft without adding states.
items.guide: Match each long production to its reverse-push chain, sharing only compatible remaining pushes.

items.prompt: Fill the PDA δ table from the supplied diagram for 0ᵐ1ⁿ0ⁿ.
items.guide: Each nonempty output is a set of (state,push) pairs. Read the input and pop fields separately.

items.prompt: Fill the modified DPDA table including reject completion.
items.guide: Use single pairs instead of singleton sets. Check the four potentially applicable entries for each actual input/top combination.

items.prompt: Draw the full simulation tree on 01112.
items.guide: Track both the state and ordered stack through the phase boundaries and ε pop moves.

items.prompt: Explain the language of the supplied seven-state PDA.
items.guide: The first component matches m zeros with m ones, m>0; the second matches 2n additional ones with n twos, n≥0.

items.prompt: Identify failed normalization conditions; repair using the same Q,Σ,Γ and resimulate.
items.guide: The no-stack-change edge is the issue. A permitted push followed by a matching pop can preserve the phase change without extra states.

items.prompt: Convert the normalized PDA to wrapped CFG rules with pairing tables.
items.guide: Group by Δ₁,Δ₂,$ and enumerate the Cartesian product of pushes and pops for each symbol.

items.prompt: Complete the ≤9-state binary-to-quaternary TM for even-length x# by the given five-step algorithm.
items.guide: Process each two-bit pair as 2xᵢ+xᵢ₊₁, erase its source cells and append one base-four digit. The example bit string 11011000 represents decimal 216; the paper’s 213 label is inconsistent.

items.prompt: Fully simulate on 11#.
items.guide: It should finish with two blanks, #, and output digit 3. Show all return scans and the halting transition.

items.prompt: Give leftmost derivations of ghgghg and gg in the supplied grammar.
items.guide: Track the leftmost remaining variable and nullable G,H carefully. A derivation is an ordered sequence, not a list of rules used.

items.prompt: Determine ambiguity of ghg with reasons.
items.guide: Compare the gG and HhGg start branches and produce two complete leftmost derivations.

items.prompt: Perform only the first three CNF stages, following the specified removal order.
items.guide: Do exactly the requested stages; the problem explicitly omits binarization and terminal replacement. Repeated H occurrences create multiple nullable alternatives.

items.prompt: Convert the CFG to the fixed PDA draft, sharing states as needed.
items.guide: Reverse-push chains with identical suffix work can merge. Check that sharing does not create an unintended production.

items.prompt: Draw the full simulation tree for 1010 in the supplied PDA.
items.guide: Preserve guesses at the inner-block boundary; the accepted branch ends with empty working stack and complete input.

items.prompt: Identify the PDA language using reverse and bit-flip notation.
items.guide: The inner and outer stacks match reversed, flipped symbols. The outer pushed block ends in 1; the inner pushed block starts and ends in 0. Watch the overbars in the PDF: text extraction drops them.

items.prompt: Give wrapped CFG rules and tables for all five stack symbols.
items.guide: There are nine push/pop pairings: one for Δ₁, two for Δ₂, four for Δ₃, one for Δ₄ and one for $.

items.prompt: Build a ≤6-state PDA validating the specified $$$ comment syntax.
items.guide: Track opening/closing delimiter counts and require the newline immediately after closing. Distinguish ordinary text from comment content and respect Γ.

items.prompt: Show an accepting path for a$$$b$$$△.
items.guide: This subpart requests a path, not a full tree. Include stack updates for all six dollar symbols and the required newline.

items.prompt: Design the ≤11-state masking TM following the supplied procedure and input promise.
items.guide: Keep the current a/b in control states, find its mask bit, append only on 1, and return through the two separators.

items.prompt: Fully simulate on ab#01# through halting.
items.guide: The output is b after the second #; both input and mask positions are erased. The worked simulator uses the official diagram’s transitions.

method:
Reading an explanation and producing a proof from a blank page are different skills. This workbook trains both. The target is strong performance on unfamiliar exam questions, including exact procedures and complete justification.

Start with a model you can run in your head

For a new deck, first identify the question it solves and the objects involved. Then follow one complete example with the changing information visible. Connect each symbol to that example, explain why each step preserves the intended meaning, and reconnect the result to the next concept. The 49 deck guides and complete mental-model edition follow this structure. The worked lessons now begin with the relevant model too.

A mental model earns its keep when it lets you predict a new case and explain a changed condition. “A stack is a to-do list” is only the entry point: you must also know top-first order, what each transition changes, and what counts as completion. Analogies are explicitly mapped to the mathematics and stopped where they stop helping.

This sequence applies the worked-example, explicit-teaching, concrete-to-abstract and proof-explanation guidance cited below. It is not a newly validated universal method. The conversational language is a learner preference; the learning claims come from actual attempts and later recall, not the number of slang words or pages read.

The daily loop

  1. Retrieve before rereading. Start with one previously studied task. Write what you remember on paper. Then check it.
  2. Learn one complete example. Read the problem, its purpose, each transition or proof step, and why that step is justified. Follow the linked slide pages when the original diagram matters.
  3. Close it and produce. Solve a related task without copying the example. If you need help, use the hint; record the attempt as assisted.
  4. Repair the first broken link. Was it notation, the mechanism, the procedure, choosing a method, or proving the claim? Relearn that link, then attempt a different example.
  5. Return after a delay. Aim for the next day, roughly three days later, then a week later. These are adjustable defaults, not a scientifically optimal schedule. Mix related topics after you can attempt their basic procedures.

The daily page suggests one lesson and shows locally due practice. It doesn't turn a click or a streak into a claim of mastery. Your attempt history distinguishes needs work, assisted, independent once, and later recall. These are self-reports; this static site does not grade mathematical proofs.

Why this design

Worked examples and explicit modelling reduce the amount a novice must invent at once. Guidance should then fade into independent work rather than remain a permanent stream of answers. The AERO guides and the worked-example meta-analysis support that sequence, with important differences across learners and tasks. AERO explicit teaching, AERO scaffolding, Barbieri et al., 2023.

Retrieval practice and spacing generally improve later access to knowledge. Trying to reconstruct a proof or diagram can reveal gaps that rereading hides. Transfer to changed problems needs deliberate practice too; recalling a familiar sentence is not enough. Agarwal et al., 2021, Carpenter et al., 2022, Latimier et al., 2021.

The latest review checked here, published October 29, 2026, finds classroom benefits of retrieval, spacing and interleaving, with variation across contexts and limited evidence for some moderators. Those are population-level findings, not a promise about one exam or an optimal schedule for one student. Ruitenburg et al., 2026.

For proofs, ask what licenses a crucial step and how it connects to the claim. Research on self-explanation training supports proof comprehension; it does not establish that reading explained proofs automatically produces independent proof-writing skill. This is why the workbook has both a complete proof and a fresh task. Hodds, Alcock & Inglis, 2014.

Feedback should identify the error, the violated condition, and the next correction. “Wrong” and “great job” alone give little direction. Wisniewski et al., 2020. Explanations are useful when they connect reasons; demanding an explanation of every tiny step can add load. Rittle-Johnson, 2024. Concrete examples and formal statements should be explicitly connected. IES practice guide.

AI can help during practice while leaving independent performance weaker if it supplies answers too freely. One high-school mathematics field experiment found this risk and evidence that tutoring safeguards mitigated it. That result motivates hidden solutions and independent retests here; it does not diagnose any particular student's result. Bastani et al., 2025.

What demanding theory courses actually recommend

Stanford CS103 separates creative problem-solving from formal proof writing, explicitly teaches assumptions and conclusions, and checks variable scope and justified claims. Its exam review advises working on weak material and writing an answer before consulting solutions. We adopt those observable course practices. They are teaching guidance, not evidence that every high-scoring student follows one secret routine. Guide to proofs, Proofwriting checklist, Exam review, pages 3–6.

There is no established single “best” method for every learner and every task, and university prestige is not causal evidence. The strongest practical combination here is accurate modelling, meaningful independent attempts, specific feedback, delayed retrieval, and varied exam tasks. We adjust it from demonstrated work rather than claiming it already works for you.

A practical study block

Use about 45–60 minutes as a starting structure: 5–10 minutes recalling an earlier task, 15–20 minutes following one worked example, 15–20 minutes attempting and checking a fresh problem, and a few minutes recording the next repair. These times are planning choices. If a concept breaks, spend the block repairing it; reading more pages doesn't compensate for a missing dependency.

For daily reading on a phone, study the explanation and trace a small example. For exam practice, use paper and close the lesson. During a mixed mock, set the timer, keep solutions shut, and review only after the block. Use the attempt record to note solution exposure. A problem whose answer you remember is useful recall practice, but is not a fresh independent test.

What a 90+ target requires

Aim to complete representative unseen or meaningfully changed questions under the actual exam constraints, with correct constructions, complete proofs, and enough time to check the requested format. Review with the supplied rubric and official solutions, and ask for a mathematical review of your own written work when available. An answer that “looks familiar” is not evidence of that level. No reading-completion percentage or practice score guarantees 90+.

Before an exam: confirm current scope and logistics; account for every requested subpart; respect state and alphabet limits; test ε and shortest legal inputs; check all nondeterministic branches when a tree is required; finish TM simulations; name the contradiction or prove both directions as appropriate.
mock:
This is a 100-point practice set written for this workbook, based on recurring task types. It is not an official exam or a prediction. Some methods deliberately resemble the lessons; use a historical paper you have not studied for an additional independent check. Set your own time limit; Midterm 2's exact duration is still unverified.

Write your answers on paper with the solutions closed. If you open a hint or worked answer, label that portion assisted. Score against the detailed obligations, not whether your answer looks similar. The suggested rubric is for diagnosis and is not the instructor's grading policy.

Problem 1 · Grammar and normal form · 25 points

Let Σ={a,b}, V={S,A,B}, and

S → AB | A
A → aA | a
B → bB | ε

(a) Give a leftmost derivation of aab. (4)

(b) Prove this grammar is ambiguous using aa. Give two leftmost derivations. (6)

(c) Convert to CNF. Show a new start, ε elimination, unit elimination, and final helper rules. (15)

Review Problem 1 after your attempt

(a) S⇒AB⇒aAB⇒aaB⇒aabB⇒aab. (b) S⇒A⇒aA⇒aa, and S⇒AB⇒aAB⇒aaB⇒aa. The start choices differ and both derivations are leftmost.

(c) Add S₀→S. Only B is nullable. Removing B→ε adds S→A (already present) and B→b; the grammar now has S→AB|A, A→aA|a, B→bB|b. Eliminate units S→A and S₀→S: S₀→AB|aA|a; S→AB|aA|a; A→aA|a; B→bB|b. Introduce U→a and W→b: S₀→AB|UA|a; S→AB|UA|a; A→UA|a; B→WB|b; U→a; W→b. No start ε rule is permitted: the original language contains at least one a.

Rubric: 4 for a valid leftmost derivation; 6 for two distinct leftmost derivations of the same string and the conclusion. CNF: new start 2, correct nullable alternatives and ε removal 4, unit elimination 4, legal final shapes 3, all stages shown 2. A language-changing omission needs correction even if a few strings still derive.

Problem 2 · Build and justify a PDA · 25 points

Construct a PDA for L={0m1n2n∣m≥0,n≥1}L=\{0^m1^n2^n\mid m\geq0,n\geq1\}L={0m1n2n∣m≥0,n≥1} with at most five states and Γ={X,$}. Give its states, start, accepting set, transitions, and a proof of both directions. Trace 01122 through acceptance, and explain why 002 is rejected.

Review Problem 2 after your attempt

Use Q={s,p,r,t,f}, start s, F={f}, Σ={0,1,2}. Moves: s —ε,ε→$→ p; p —0,ε→ε→ p; p —1,ε→X→ r; r —1,ε→X→ r; r —2,X→ε→ t; t —2,X→ε→ t; t —ε,$→ε→ f. All unspecified δ entries are ∅; each listed PDA output is a singleton pair set.

Every accepting run consumes only zeros in p, at least one 1 to reach r, and at least one 2 to reach t. X markers count unmatched ones; reaching f requires all removed. Thus every accepted string has the required form and counts. Conversely, every such string can take m zero loops, n pushes, n pops, and the bottom-marker finish.

Trace: (s,01122,ε)→(p,01122,$)→(p,1122,$)→(r,122,X$)→(r,22,XX$)→(t,2,X$)→(t,ε,$)→(f,ε,ε). For 002, after the zeros the machine remains in p with next symbol 2, for which there is no move. It rejects.

Rubric: correct construction under constraints 10; formal components and transition types 4; soundness and completeness 6; full accepting trace 3; rejection explanation 2. Recheck ε and inputs with no ones: n≥1 is essential.

Problem 3 · PDA-to-CFG conversion · 20 points

A normalized PDA has states {s,p,r,f}, start s, sole accept f, and transitions:

s — ε,ε→$ → p
p — a,ε→X → p
p — b,X→ε → r
r — b,X→ε → r
r — ε,$→ε → f

(a) State why the normalization conditions hold. (4)

(b) Define the variables and start variable, give every wrapped rule with a pairing table, and specify the other two rule families. (12)

(c) Derive aabb from the start variable. (4)

Review Problem 3 after your attempt

(a) f is the only accepting state, and its only entrance pops $ after all X markers. Every transition pushes or pops exactly one symbol. (b) Variables Aᵢⱼ for i,j∈{s,p,r,f}; start Aₛf. Pair $ push s→p with pop r→f to get Aₛf→Aₚr. Pair X push p→p on a with pop p→r on b to get Aₚr→aAₚpb; pair it with pop r→r on b to get Aₚr→aAₚrb. Other families: Aᵢⱼ→AᵢₖAₖⱼ for all i,j,k and Aᵢᵢ→ε for all i. (c) Aₛf⇒Aₚr⇒aAₚrb⇒aaAₚpbb⇒aabb.

Rubric: normalization 4; variables/start 3, three correct pairings 6, two remaining families 3; valid derivation 4. A wrong inner index changes the meaning even if the surrounding terminals look right.

Problem 4 · Turing-machine construction · 20 points

Input is promised to be w# followed by blanks, where w is a nonempty binary string. Compute the bitwise complement of w in place, leave # unchanged, and halt immediately to the right of #. Use only L/R moves and at most two working states, plus accept and reject. Give a complete transition table over Γ={0,1,#,⊔}, trace 01#, and justify halting. Explain what changes if the input promise is removed and ε must be rejected.

Review Problem 4 after your attempt

Under the promise, one working state q suffices: on 0 write 1,R,q; on 1 write 0,R,q; on # write #,R,accept; on blank write blank,R,reject. Trace: q01#⊔⇒1q1#⊔⇒10q#⊔⇒10#q_accept⊔. After k scanned bits, exactly the first k bits are complemented and the remainder unchanged. Each move goes right, so the finite input reaches # and halts.

Without the promise, specify the desired valid format first. If it must be nonempty binary w followed by exactly one # and then blank, use a separate initial state requiring 0 or 1, and a state after # to check blank. A straightforward strict validator uses three working states: initial, scan, and check-after-separator. This is a construction, not a minimality claim; do not assume the original two-state constraint is automatically retained. The question asks what changes, not to force an unjustified minimal state count.

Rubric: table with correct writes/head movement 8; entire trace 4; invariant and halting 5; promise/validation distinction 3. The trace alone does not establish correctness for all promised inputs.

Problem 5 · Pumping with a changed boundary · 10 points

Prove L={0m1n∣m>2n, n≥1}L=\{0^m1^n\mid m>2n,\ n\geq1\}L={0m1n∣m>2n, n≥1} is not regular. Explicitly give the witness string and pumping repetition, and cover every legal split.

Review Problem 5 after your attempt

Suppose L is regular with pumping length p≥1. Choose s=0²ᵖ⁺¹1ᵖ∈L, of length 3p+1≥p. For every split s=xyz with |xy|≤p and |y|>0, y=0ᵏ for some 1≤k≤p. Choose i=0. Then xy⁰z=0²ᵖ⁺¹⁻ᵏ1ᵖ has at most 2p zeros and p ones, violating m>2n. This contradicts pumping, so L is nonregular.

Rubric: assumption/arbitrary p 1; valid long witness 2; all-splits argument 3; specific pumping count and failed condition 3; contradiction/conclusion 1. An argument choosing a single convenient split is incomplete, even if its arithmetic is right.

After the mock

Keep the first attempt. Write corrections separately. Record which portions used hints or solutions. Pick one changed problem for each substantive error and retry it later without the answer visible. Use the official papers' requirements for final calibration; this rubric does not override the course's warning that incomplete proofs generally receive no partial credit.
